PRD.when: When the owner asks how to beat one rival's product, a rival is taking sales, or the store is about to launch against an established competitor or change its price, offer or page. Not for weekly price tracking or a map of rivals' ads.
PRD.tune: prices are compared at the door, with delivery fees, duties and taxes; review themes are counted and quoted rather than summarised; every way to beat the rival is priced against the store's own gross profit; and delivery, payment and other-language reviews are read as their own signals.
PRD.title: Competitor product teardown
PRD.outcome: a one-page teardown of one rival product (price paid at the door, offer, promise, proof, counted review praise and complaints, weak spots) and a ranked plan of 3 to 5 ways the store can beat it, each checked against the store's gross profit and the law on comparisons.

PRD.when: When the owner wants a winning product to sell: a new store choosing a first product, an existing store wanting fresh candidates, or before a supplier sourcing trip.
PRD.tune: free first-party sources replace paid spy tools; every trend needs a second dated source; the margin screen compares delivered gross profit with the cost to win a buyer instead of a flat markup; and platform gaps by country and refused pay-on-delivery orders change which picks survive.
PRD.title: Find trending products
PRD.outcome: a ranked shortlist of 5 to 10 rising products, each with its trend evidence, rival count, estimated landed cost, gross profit per order and a pass or fail on whether that profit can pay for a buyer, ready to hand to a demand test.

PRD.when: When the owner asks "is this niche worth it?" or "is this market too crowded?", is choosing between two or three niches for a new store, or wants to enter a new category or country. Not for finding product ideas: this judges one niche.
PRD.tune: every figure is labelled measured, estimated or proxy so a hint never passes as a fact; the verdict turns on cost to win a buyer against delivered gross profit, not on size alone; crowded niches are split into owned and same-looking; and marketplace-led countries are sized across marketplaces such as Amazon or Mercado Libre, not just Google.
PRD.title: Niche size and competition check
PRD.outcome: a two-page niche report: a demand range with its working, a map of who owns the niche and how tightly, the likely cost to win a buyer against the gross profit the store would earn, and a verdict (enter, enter with a named angle, or avoid) with the one angle that could work.

PRD.when: When the owner asks what to sell next, one hero product carries the store, repeat orders are flat, or buyers keep asking for something the store does not sell. Also before a supplier visit. Not for testing demand for a product already picked.
PRD.tune: candidates come from counted buyer requests and second-order data, not trend lists; repeat is read only on cohorts old enough to show it; gross profit per order holds a veto; and the brief ends in a demand test, so no stock is bought on a guess.
PRD.title: Plan the next product
PRD.outcome: a scored list of 5 to 10 candidate products drawn from the store's own buyers and data, one pick and a runner-up, and a one-page launch brief for the pick that a supplier, a designer and the ad team can all work from.

PRD.when: When rivals keep running sales or undercutting the store, Google Shopping or marketplace sales dip for no clear reason, or before setting sale prices. Gives a weekly watch with a react rule per product. Not for setting the store's own base prices.
PRD.tune: every product gets a price floor from gross profit before any rival is tracked; flags are sorted into short sales and real resets so the store stops chasing temporary cuts; pulling ad spend and answering with value come before cutting price; and each market's "was" price and all-in price rules sit in the same sheet.
PRD.title: Track competitor prices and offers
PRD.outcome: a weekly price and offer sheet for 5 to 20 key products against 3 to 5 named rivals, with change flags, a price floor per product, and one written decision per flagged line (hold, answer with value, pull spend, or match within the floor), ready to review in 15 minutes.

PRD.when: When the owner asks "will this sell before I order stock?": a supplier quote with a minimum order is on the table, or a new product or big reorder is planned, and nobody knows if buyers will pay. Tests with a pre-order, waitlist or small ad.
PRD.tune: the go and no-go lines are set from the store's own gross profit per order before any spend; only money taken can trigger a stock order; the US dry-test rule and prepaid-only pre-orders (no pay on delivery) are built into the setup; and warm list buyers are kept apart from cold ad buyers so the result is not flattered.
PRD.title: Validate demand before buying stock
PRD.outcome: one test plan (test type, page, ads or messages, spend cap, dates) with go and no-go lines fixed in advance, and after the test a one-page decision sheet that says order, change and retest, or drop, with the numbers behind it.

PRD.when: When you have a category in mind but no product, and want one run from buyer complaints to a scored pick.
PRD.tune: Feed it reviews from Amazon and from three to five rival Shopify stores, plus a real landed cost from a supplier quote so the last step can score margin. Do not jump straight to the score: the gap step should change one thing buyers notice, not three. Read PRD-0001, PRD-0002 and PRD-0006 before you start.

PRD.when: When you want to open a store or add a line and have a market in mind but no product yet.
PRD.tune: Favour problems people pay to fix again and again, and drop any that only support a cheap one-off item. Check who already advertises to each problem in the Meta Ad Library for your selling country before you shortlist. Read PRD-0012 and PRD-0013 first so the top five lean toward repeat buys and parcel-friendly goods.

PRD.when: When you want proof of unmet demand in a category before you design or source anything.
PRD.tune: Paste one- to three-star reviews from Amazon and the top Shopify rivals, sorted by star, and keep the review lines next to each pain. A badly rated subcategory with weak search volume is a trap, so confirm search demand before you call it a gap. Check PRD-0002 so the fix is one clear change, and AVT-0009 for buyers who already spent money on failed fixes.

PRD.when: When your category looks the same everywhere and you need the one difference that would make buyers switch.
PRD.tune: Give it prices, pack shots, claims and review counts for three to five leaders, plus any shift in taste you see among your buyers. Pick one change only, since a new format, price and claim at once confuses shoppers. Read PRD-0001 and PRD-0002 first, then BRD-0011 to turn the gap into a position.

PRD.when: When you want products other stores already sell with ads and you have no paid spy tool.
PRD.tune: Use the free Meta Ad Library set to your selling country, and log how long each ad has run and how many stores run it. A viral video with no ads behind it is not proof, and one-hit products fade fast, so read PRD-0003 before you order stock. Pass the shortlist to the saturation and scoring checks next.

PRD.when: When you have one to three product ideas and want a go or no-go before you spend on stock or ads.
PRD.tune: Feed it the landed cost from a real supplier quote, the price rivals charge, parcel size and weight, and whether buyers reorder. A product that can only sell cheap rarely funds paid ads, so check PRD-0006 first and PRD-0013 for repeat and gifting demand. Use your real shipping rates for each market you sell in, not the supplier's estimate.

PRD.when: When a product looks promising and you need to know how many stores already run ads for it.
PRD.tune: Run it in the Meta Ad Library for each country you plan to sell in and date the result, since counts change week to week. It misses Amazon and TikTok Shop sellers, so check those by hand. A crowded field can still be won with a better offer, so read PRD-0002 and OFF-0035 before you drop the idea.

PRD.when: When a product or category is trending and you need to know if it is a fad before you buy stock.
PRD.tune: Give it five years of Google Trends data, not one, plus the selling season in your country. If your store already rides one hot product, use the range question to plan what comes next. Read PRD-0003 on how hero products decay and PRD-0001 on picking big, known categories.

PRD.when: When you found a rival store selling your product and want to know if the market is big enough to chase.
PRD.tune: Use visit estimates from a traffic tool and the rival's real price and bundle mix from their store, then read the result as a range, not one number. A store with heavy paid traffic can show big sales and little profit. Check PRD-0017 on how channels split and PRD-0006 before you size your own plan.

PRD.when: When you already sell and must choose your next product with more ideas than cash.
PRD.tune: Feed it your Shopify order export, repeat rate by product and ad results for any test of the new item. A launch that sells to your own email list but not to cold traffic has not proven it can win new customers, so read PRD-0012 first. PRD-0011 warns against splitting cash before the hero product is fully backed.

PRD.when: When your range has grown and shoppers or ads no longer say clearly what you sell.
PRD.tune: List every SKU with sales, margin and the job it does for the buyer, using your Shopify product sales report. Do not add a SKU only because a rival has one. Read PRD-0011 on backing one hero and PRD-0007 on line extensions before you approve a launch.

PRD.when: When you want to sell a new kind of product under your current store name.
PRD.tune: Give it what your brand means today, in buyers' words from reviews, and the new product. Do not stretch the name just to save on ads, because the new line can blur what the core product stands for. Read PRD-0008 and PRD-0007 first, and BRD-0012 if a new name is needed.

PRD.when: When you want a steady monthly routine for finding and screening your next product, not a one-off hunch.
PRD.tune: Each month give it saved Ad Library captures, marketplace best-seller ranks and your cost notes, since it cannot browse. Keep a watch list so a product that has filled up with rivals is dropped before you order. Read PRD-0003 and PRD-0012 so its picks favour products that win new buyers and last.

PRD.when: When you want to test real demand with a pre-order or waitlist page before you place a factory order.
PRD.tune: Set the pass mark in paid pre-orders or deposits, not email sign-ups, and send a small Meta test to a Shopify pre-order page. State the ship date and refund terms plainly, since late pre-orders hurt trust and can breach payment provider rules. Check PRD-0006 so the test price matches the price you plan to sell at.

PRD.when: When you are turning an everyday annoyance into a product on a small budget and want to think it through.
PRD.tune: Bring the problem, who else has it and your cash limit, and ask where to pay experts and where to do it yourself. Her record is about one hero product and getting it seen, so pair it with PRD-0011 and PRD-0003 on hero focus and decay.

PRD.when: When an owner asks whether the category is growing or shrinking, before putting more cash into stock or ads in it, or when choosing what to add next to a working range.
PRD.tune: the store's own monthly sales sit beside the market so a store problem is not called a market problem; Google Trends is read as share of searches against a steady reference term over five years and twelve months by country and state; no call is made unless two kinds of dated source agree; add-on products are ranked only after a margin check, with stock and ad timing worked back from the season.
PRD.title: Category demand direction check
PRD.outcome: a one-page grow, hold or avoid call with dated evidence and what would change it, a seasonality map for each market the store sells in, and a ranked list of 5 to 10 adjacent or add-on products with direction and a rough margin check.

PRD.when: When a quarter ends, before a buying round, or when the catalogue has grown and nobody knows which products earn their place.
PRD.tune: contribution is counted after returns and ad cost on in-stock days, every kill is checked for the buyers it would strand and planned in waves, and every kill carries a ledger of the stock, cash and purchase orders behind it.
PRD.title: Range review: kill, keep, fix or grow
PRD.outcome: One sheet with a row per SKU (sales, contribution margin after returns, trend, class, lifecycle, returns and reviews), a kill, keep, fix or grow call with the reason and first step, and the stock and cash left behind each kill call.

PRD.when: When a product comes in sizes or colours and you need to decide what to make and how much of each.
PRD.tune: every tolerance is tested against the grade step so sizes never overlap, size shares come from in-stock days with stockouts and exchanges put back, and every minimum order gap gets a priced fix instead of quiet over-buying.
PRD.title: Size grading and variant plan
PRD.outcome: A grading table with tolerances per size, the colours and sizes to make, the quantity split from your sales data or size returns, and a check against each variant's MOQ.

AVT.when: When the brand sounds like every rival and the owner wants a clear "what we stand against" line the store can prove. Use before a repositioning or a new round of ads. Not for the full positioning and message pillars.
AVT.tune: the opponent comes from counted complaints across reviews and forums, not a workshop; a candidate is dropped unless the store holds operational proof it does otherwise; the test budget and keep-or-cut rule come from the product's gross profit per purchase and store-side orders; and the adopted...
AVT.title: Brand opponent statement
AVT.outcome: a one-line 'we oppose X because Y' statement (or three candidates to test), backed by a habits table and counted customer quotes, with candidate cards and a test plan for the owner to approve.

AVT.when: When the owner asks why people really buy, ads talk to nobody in particular, or the customer picture has never been checked, before new ads, pages or flows. Builds buyer types from surveys, reviews and interviews. Not for running the interviews themselves.
AVT.tune: every buyer type stands on counted survey, interview and review codes; the five slots are tagged on live ads and checked against store-side cost per purchase versus break-even, not opinion; false winners are caught by the click gap; and gaps are ranked by buyer share times gross profit per purchase.
AVT.title: Buyer decision map
AVT.outcome: buyer type briefs built from surveys, reviews and interviews, a codes table, a tag table of current ads, a gap table ranked by money, and a survey and interview kit, ready to guide new ads and pages.

AVT.when: When the owner wants to talk to real customers, or the team argues about why people buy and nobody has asked them. Use before new ads, a page rewrite or a new product, or when sales stall. Gives the invite, script and summary sheets.
AVT.tune: the sample deliberately includes refunders, refused deliveries and near-buyers; the script follows the purchase from first thought to first use instead of asking opinions; consent, WhatsApp template and language rules for each market are built in; and every finding is a counted reason with exact phrases that...
AVT.title: Customer interviews
AVT.outcome: a recruiting message (email and WhatsApp versions), a 30-minute interview script, a one-page summary template for each call, and a cross-interview sheet that turns 12 to 20 calls into counted buying reasons with exact buyer phrases, ready for ads, pages and product decisions.

AVT.when: When the owner wants ideas from what people say online: comments, DMs, Reddit, forums, creators' comment sections and marketplace reviews. Run monthly before product, ad or content planning, or when posts feel out of touch. Not for mining the store's own reviews for ad angles.
AVT.tune: listening is aimed at buyer pain, not brand mentions; no idea passes without two independent sources; every quote is kept exact, linked and stripped of personal data; and product ideas carry a rough gross profit case instead of a vibe.
AVT.title: Social listening for product and ad ideas
AVT.outcome: a monthly memo with five product ideas and five ad or content ideas, each backed by quotes from at least two sources, plus the idea log sheet with every quote's link, date and code, ready for the product and creative teams.

AVT.when: When your ads or product page sound generic and you cannot say who the buyer is in one breath.
AVT.tune: Search Reddit and niche forums in the buyer's own problem words, plus your reviews and rivals', and paste exact quotes rather than summaries. Keep to the 60-minute box so research does not stall the launch. Read AVT-0006, AVT-0007 and AVT-0011 first.

AVT.when: When you want to know what rival products leave out and which promises buyers no longer believe.
AVT.tune: Paste Amazon and rival-store reviews split by star, and pull out the one- and five-star reviews that mention money spent on other fixes. With fewer than about 100 reviews, treat each point as a lead, not a pattern. Read AVT-0009, AVT-0008 and AVT-0010 first.

AVT.when: When you have reviews and survey answers but do not know which kinds of buyer they come from.
AVT.tune: Feed it your review app export, post-purchase survey answers and rival reviews, and count self-describing phrases such as "as a nurse". A group that shows up once is not a segment. Read AVT-0016 and AVT-0013 first.

AVT.when: When you sell a product many stores sell and bigger rivals own the obvious buyer.
AVT.tune: Give it rival ads from the Meta Ad Library and long Amazon reviews with photos or video, then size each new group with a Reddit search. If your product is the same as the leader's, a new buyer group is the cheaper win than a new mechanism. Read AVT-0014, AVT-0012 and AVT-0013 first.

AVT.when: When your avatar is a list of ages and incomes and your ads still miss.
AVT.tune: Feed it buyer stories, support tickets from your helpdesk and survey answers, so each card ties a job and a trigger to a real quote. Watch for odd uses of your product, which can be separate jobs and even new SKUs. Read AVT-0003 and AVT-0005 first.

AVT.when: When your reviews are short and you want to call five to eight recent buyers to learn why they bought.
AVT.tune: Paste the Shopify orders for each buyer you will call, with first product, discount code and days to reorder, so each call starts from facts. Ask about the timeline from first thought to purchase, never which features to add. Read AVT-0003, then AVT-0017 and AVT-0024 for how many calls are enough.

AVT.when: When you have a customer list and want to hear from buyers and non-buyers before you pick angles, offers or the next product.
AVT.tune: Pull buyers and non-buying subscribers from Klaviyo and promise no sales pitch in the invite. Use a reward everyone gets plus a prize draw, and check the rules on prize draws in each market you sell in, such as the US or UK. Read AVT-0018, AVT-0025 and AVT-0021 first.

AVT.when: When you get orders but cannot say why people bought or what nearly stopped them.
AVT.tune: Run the survey on the Shopify thank-you page and as a Klaviyo email, and ask what they tried before your product. When you read results, weight the most loyal and the least happy buyers over the middle. Read AVT-0021 and AVT-0019 first.

AVT.when: When your product quiz has about 100 answers and you have not read them as a whole.
AVT.tune: Export quiz answers from your quiz app or Klaviyo profile fields about every 100 submissions. The share of people naming failed past fixes shows how aware they are, so read that before picking a hook. Read AVT-0023, AVT-0022 and AVT-0020 first.

AVT.when: When ads show strong returns but repeat orders and profit stay weak, and you want to know who your best buyers really are.
AVT.tune: Feed it the Shopify customer and order export with discount codes, first product and UTM source. Sale-only buyers often never come back, so do not let them shape your avatar. Read AVT-0021 and OFF-0008 first.

AVT.when: When you are about to test a new buyer group and want the ad, page and photos to speak to the same person.
AVT.tune: Paste the buyer sketch with its quotes, the ad, and the product page text and images. Adding the group's name to the hook alone fails, so every part must match. Read AVT-0015 and AVT-0012 first.

AVT.when: When a poll or survey says people love an idea and you are about to launch, rename or reprice because of it.
AVT.tune: Paste the questions, answers and sample size, then compare them with what buyers actually did in Shopify. Stated love rarely matches orders, so turn the answer into a pre-order or click test before you act. Read AVT-0019 first.

AVT.when: When you have notes from buyer interviews and no clear pattern for why people switched to you.
AVT.tune: Use notes from calls with recent buyers, not reviews, and mark what pushed them off the old fix and what nearly held them back. These forces become ad and page angles, so keep the exact quotes. Read AVT-0003 and AVT-0009 first.

AVT.when: When new reviews arrive every month and you want your buyer file kept current without reading each one.
AVT.tune: Give it each month's review export from your store, Amazon and your review app, along with your org context. When low reviews rise, it should split product faults from wrong-fit buyers, since they need different fixes. Read AVT-0016 and AVT-0008 first.

AVT.when: When you want to think through the real job a buyer hires your product to do.
AVT.tune: Bring buyer stories and the odd ways people use your product, and ask about situations and struggles rather than age and income. Pair it with AVT-0003 for the interview method and AVT-0005 for jobs that can become new SKUs.

OFF.when: When the owner says order value is stuck, asks where to set free shipping, or wants bundles or buy-more-save-more deals; also when a sale is planned or the free-shipping line was set from the average order. Not for picking a single free gift.
OFF.tune: every offer is judged on gross profit per session, not order value; the threshold comes from the peaks of the store's own order distribution; bundle discounts are funded from the real cost of the nth unit; and each discount carries its own break-even line before anyone switches it on.
OFF.title: Offer, bundle and free-shipping threshold design
OFF.outcome: a recommended free-shipping threshold, bundle tiers, gift, upsells and discount rules modelled on gross profit per session, with an order value chart, offer and upsell tables, a set-up list and an offer model sheet.

OFF.when: When shops or companies that showed interest stop replying, or the owner asks what to send wholesale or gifting leads after a pitch, sample or quote, and nobody knows who was last contacted. Not for finding new shops and writing the first pitch.
OFF.tune: sequences are split by stage so a sampled or quoted lead never gets a cold-lead message; every touch must add a named new asset; the money gate means follow-ups never need a discount; and the sequence keeps going after the first order, timed to the stockist's sell-through so reorders arrive...
OFF.title: B2B sales follow-up sequence
OFF.outcome: five written sequences (no reply, interested, sampled, quoted, first order placed) for retail and corporate leads, each with 3 to 5 touches, send days, channel, the one new thing each adds and the one ask, plus stop and re-try rules and a tracker, as drafts the client approves before any send.

OFF.when: When the owner asks what price to charge shops or distributors, needs a wholesale price list and trade terms, or is about to pitch first stockists or a distributor. Not for quoting or invoicing one bulk order.
OFF.tune: wholesale prices are worked back from the store's own retail price with VAT or sales tax handled the way each market shows prices; every SKU is checked against what it earns online after ad cost; credit terms are capped by the supplier's float; and the pricing policy protects the retail price without crossing resale price law.
OFF.title: Wholesale price list and terms
OFF.outcome: a wholesale price sheet for every SKU the store will sell to trade, with a pass or fail margin check per line, and a one-page terms sheet ready to attach to pitches and quotes, both approved by the client before anyone sees them.

OFF.when: When the owner wants bulk gift orders from companies for Diwali, Christmas, year-end or client and employee gifts, usually 6 to 10 weeks before the season, and needs priced gift boxes and a pitch to company buyers.
OFF.tune: the first leads come from company buyers already in the store's orders; every box is priced with per-address shipping and kitting labour shown; order-by dates work back from a delivery the store can meet with a season cap; and the starter box is shaped around the US gift limit without giving tax...
OFF.title: Corporate gifting sales
OFF.outcome: a one-page gifting offer with three priced boxes and order deadlines, a 40-company target sheet with the buyer role and reason for each, a pitch email and a LinkedIn note, and a quote template, all drafted for the client to approve before anything is sent.

OFF.when: When the owner asks what offer to run for a new product, range or store going live in the next 2 to 8 weeks, to win first buyers without teaching them to wait for discounts.
OFF.tune: the price is tested against what a store with no reviews can defend before any perk is chosen; the perk is picked by the barrier stopping the first buyer and by what it teaches buyers, not by habit; one perk only, with a written full-price-day switch; and every cap and end date must be provable...
OFF.title: Launch offer design
OFF.outcome: a one-page launch offer sheet: the launch price, one launch perk with its exact terms, start and end date, who qualifies, the unit cap, the cost and contribution per order, the break-even ROAS, the full-price-day plan, and three offer lines for ads, page and email, all checked against margin and stock.

OFF.when: When the owner wants buyers on subscriptions or auto-reorder for products people use up (coffee, supplements, skincare, pet food, cleaning refills), or asks what subscribe-and-save discount to give. Not for reorder reminder emails without a subscription.
OFF.tune: frequencies come from units per pack and daily use, not round numbers; the margin model runs 12 months by cohort with churn and failed payments; cancel stays as easy as sign-up under US, UK and EU rules; and buyers who mostly pay on delivery get prepaid packs instead of subscriptions that cannot be charged.
OFF.title: Subscribe and save program
OFF.outcome: a one-page subscription offer (eligible products, discount, frequencies, gift, skip and cancel rules), a cancel-flow table with a save action per reason, a margin model sheet by month, the product page placement, and a launch checklist, ready for the client to approve and set up.

OFF.when: When a distributor, reseller or sales agent wants to carry the brand in a region, channel or country, and the owner asks what terms to agree or has a draft contract to check. Not for the wholesale price list.
OFF.tune: every term has a walk-away, not just a wish; exclusivity is always tied to minimums that switch it off; the margin stack is checked down to the shelf price; trademark and marketplace accounts stay with the store; and late-payment rules and tax invoicing sit inside the payment terms.
OFF.title: Distributor agreement checklist
OFF.outcome: a term sheet of about 30 terms, each with the store's position, walk-away point and risk rating, a red-flag review of any draft received, the margin stack to the shelf, and a short list of questions for the store's lawyer. It is a negotiating tool, not legal advice; a lawyer reviews before anything is signed.

OFF.when: When the owner wants the products in shops and boutiques: first stockists, more shops in a city, or a list of retailers never properly contacted. Not for chasing leads already pitched who went quiet.
OFF.tune: the list starts from the store's own buyer clusters and the stockists of neighbour brands, not a generic directory; every shop is scored on payment risk as well as fit; the pitch leads with what the shop earns per unit; and nobody is pitched until the store can refill a reorder.
OFF.title: Find and pitch retail stockists
OFF.outcome: a stockist target sheet of 30 to 60 shops scored A, B or C, one pitch email and two follow-ups personalised for the 10 to 15 A-tier shops, and a ready "what we send" pack (line sheet layout, terms summary, sample rule), all as drafts for the client to approve and send.

OFF.when: When the owner wants to 'add a free gift' and needs to know which gift and at what spend, order value has stalled, or a sale needs something cheaper than a discount. Not for setting free shipping or bundle tiers.
OFF.tune: the gift is chosen from a scored shortlist that includes parcel weight and whether it helps the buyer use the product; the money model charges the gift to every order above the line, not just the new ones; uptake is shown at three levels and only launched if the middle case pays; and pay-on-delivery orders carry the gift's loss on refused parcels.
OFF.title: Gift with purchase offer
OFF.outcome: a one-page gift offer: the chosen gift and runner-up from a scored shortlist, the unlock rule (spend line, product or quantity), cost per order, change in gross profit per order and per month, stock check, the exact terms, placement on product page and cart, and the date the offer ends.

OFF.when: When buyers hesitate on a new or pricey product, the owner asks about a money-back guarantee or free exchange, the returns promise is vague, or a bolder guarantee feels too risky.
OFF.tune: the guarantee is picked from the buyer's counted fear and the product type, not from a famous brand; the cost model turns the promise into the conversion lift it must buy and the cash it ties up; the system's return rules are set to match the words; and support gets a claim rule so a bold promise...
OFF.title: Guarantee and risk reversal
OFF.outcome: a guarantee pack: the chosen guarantee and runner-up, the full terms text for the policy page, a cost model (claim rate, cost per claim, cost per order, conversion lift needed, cash held), the short guarantee line and badge text, where each goes, and the claim-handling rules for support.

OFF.when: When a sale (Black Friday, Diwali, a festival offer or a sitewide code) is planned and nobody has priced how much discount each product can take without losing money.
OFF.tune: each product gets its own ceiling from delivered cost including failed deliveries, not one sitewide guess; the sheet shows the extra units a discount must buy before anyone approves it; slow stock gets a separate cash floor so clearance logic never leaks onto full-price products; and thin products are routed...
OFF.title: How deep can we discount?
OFF.outcome: a discount ceiling sheet with one row per product (or per variant group): delivered cost, contribution per unit at full price, the deepest safe discount, the units lift needed to break even at five discount depths, and the break-even ROAS at each depth, plus a one-screen summary naming which products can carry a sale and which cannot.

OFF.when: When the owner asks which products to show first on the homepage or top of collections: grids follow default sort, top slots show sold-out best sellers, or a season or sale changes what should lead. Not for the menu or which collections exist.
OFF.tune: slots go to the products that earn the most profit per view, read on in-stock days; stock cover, size runs and returns can knock a winner out of the first screen; new products get a fair two-week trial; and the plan comes with weekly move rules so the top rows stay right as stock changes.
OFF.title: Merchandise the homepage and collections
OFF.outcome: a slot plan sheet: every homepage slot and the first 8 to 12 positions of each key collection, with the product, its merch score, stock cover and the reason; the weekly move-up and move-down rules; and a numbered set-up list for Shopify, ready for approval.

OFF.when: When the owner asks which sales to run this year and when, or is planning the next year or two quarters of festivals, promotions and full-price weeks. Not for how deep one product can be discounted.
OFF.tune: the year gets a discount budget measured in gross profit with a running total, not a list of holidays; every event is checked against each product's own ceiling; stock is worked back to a PO date and a capacity check; and full-price moments are planned between sales so the regular price stays...
OFF.title: Yearly sale calendar
OFF.outcome: a twelve-month calendar sheet with one row per promotion or full-price moment (dates, mechanic, depth, products in and out, stock needed and PO date, expected contribution, owner, approval date), a yearly discount budget with a running total against its cap, and a one-screen summary of the year.

OFF.when: When the owner thinks a price is too low or too high and wants proof before changing it, or asks 'can I raise prices without losing sales?'. Not for setting prices from costs and rivals.
OFF.tune: it never splits one product's price across visitors, and instead offers four designs that keep one price per product at a time; the profit line is written before launch so the result is judged on profit, not conversion; timed tests use comparison products to remove the background trend; and failed deliveries and repeat effects are checked after the test ends.
OFF.title: Run a price test
OFF.outcome: a one-page price test plan: the question, the design chosen and why, the variants with exact prices and terms, the profit line to beat, main metric and guardrails, run time and order count needed, the stop rule, set-up steps for approval, and a filled reading template that turns the result into contribution per visitor and per month.

OFF.when: When the owner asks what price to sell a product at: pricing a new product, repricing after cost or ad-cost changes, thin margins across the range, or before a launch or marketplace listing.
OFF.tune: the floor includes the ad cost to win a buyer, not just product cost; rivals are compared per unit with shipping; the position in the band is set by proof the buyer can check; and a floor above the market triggers a reshape, cost or drop decision instead of a price nobody will pay.
OFF.title: Set product prices
OFF.outcome: a price sheet with one row per product: delivered cost, price floor, rival price band per unit, proof level, recommended price, contribution per order and as a percentage, break-even ROAS, price per unit or per use, the shelf price each market expects (pre-tax in the US, VAT-inclusive in the UK and EU), and change from today, plus a one-screen summary of the moves.

OFF.when: When you want a better offer and do not know whether to change price, add a bundle, a gift or a subscription.
OFF.tune: Feed it gross margin per SKU, the spread of order values and repeat rate from your Shopify export. Try the free wins such as order bumps and gifts before levers that cost margin. Read OFF-0035, OFF-0014 and OFF-0015 first.

OFF.when: When you plan a sitewide sale, a code or free shipping and want to know the ad return it needs before it goes live.
OFF.tune: Use real cost of goods, shipping, payment and app fees per order, not list margin. The return you need climbs fast as a discount eats margin, so run every discount depth you are weighing. Read OFF-0005, OFF-0065, OFF-0069 and OFF-0033 first.

OFF.when: When you sell one hero product at one price and want a bigger first order.
OFF.tune: Give it unit cost, shipping cost per pack size and your current order mix from Shopify. Tie each tier to a real use, make the middle pack the default and space the savings evenly between tiers. Read OFF-0027, OFF-0049, OFF-0018 and OFF-0030 first.

OFF.when: When you want to set or fix a free-shipping or gift threshold without guessing from average order value.
OFF.tune: Export a year of order values from Shopify and set thresholds from the peaks, not the mean. Free shipping on a single cheap item can lose money, so test a multipack line instead. Read OFF-0013, OFF-0079, OFF-0076 and OFF-0033 first.

OFF.when: When you want cart and checkout add-ons that raise profit, not only order value.
OFF.tune: Give it products bought together and margin per SKU from Shopify, plus take rates from your upsell app if you have them. Rank each slot by take rate times added value times margin, and keep discounts out of checkout. Read OFF-0011, OFF-0009, OFF-0050 and OFF-0010 first.

OFF.when: When you are adding an after-payment offer and want to set what buyers see first and what follows a no.
OFF.tune: Use your post-purchase app results and margin per offer, and judge each slot by profit added per order, not take rate. The best offers are more of the same at a multi-unit price, or a product that fixes the next problem. Read OFF-0051, OFF-0052 and OFF-0074 first.

OFF.when: When you want a bigger order or a cheaper first sale without cutting your price.
OFF.tune: List low-cost items buyers want, with their landed cost and spare stock. A gift pays only when it lowers the cost to win a buyer by more than the gift costs, so recheck break-even with the gift included. Read OFF-0007, OFF-0073 and OFF-0078 first.

OFF.when: When you sell something people use up and want a subscription offer that wins first-order subscribers.
OFF.tune: Feed it margin, how long one unit lasts, repeat data by cohort and cash on hand. Front-load the first-order discount, give one-time buyers none, and match the delivery cadence to real use to cut cancels. Read OFF-0029, OFF-0040, OFF-0041 and OFF-0075 first.

OFF.when: When shoppers hesitate at checkout and you want to know if a stronger guarantee would pay.
OFF.tune: Give it monthly sales, refund rate by product and return shipping cost from Shopify. Work out net sales after the extra refunds before you lengthen the window, and offer lifetime cover only on goods that truly last. Read OFF-0001, OFF-0060, OFF-0064 and OFF-0056 first.

OFF.when: When your pop-up has offered the same small discount for months and few sign-ups turn into orders.
OFF.tune: Give it Klaviyo sign-up and placed-order rates, average order value and any live site offers. A one-time discount in the pop-up can undercut your subscription offer, and money-off framing often beats percent off on bigger orders. Read OFF-0026, OFF-0028, OFF-0036 and OFF-0037 first.

OFF.when: When you are planning Black Friday or a big seasonal sale and want backup offers ready before it starts.
OFF.tune: Feed it stock by SKU, margin and active subscriber count. Build the ladder of gift, bundle and deeper discount ahead of time, and give subscribers a better members-only deal so the sale does not trigger cancels. Read OFF-0068, OFF-0066, OFF-0043 and OFF-0008 first.

OFF.when: When you want a limited drop or a sale deadline that makes people act without fake timers.
OFF.tune: Use real stock counts and a real end date, and give your email list early access. Fake or always-on scarcity breaks trust and can break consumer rules in the US, UK and EU. Read OFF-0003 and OFF-0080 first.

OFF.when: When you tested two or more offers and need to know which one earns more per visitor.
OFF.tune: Paste sessions, orders, revenue and unit costs per variant from your test tool and Shopify. A higher order value can hide lower profit, so pick by profit per session and recheck break-even for each offer. Read OFF-0015 and OFF-0016 first.

OFF.when: When you set prices by feel and want one safe price test with a floor you will not cross.
OFF.tune: Give it unit costs, recent sales at each price and rival prices, and change the live price in Shopify yourself. Do not cut price on reflex when a rival does, but do test a lower price when a launch stalls, as OFF-0070 shows. Read OFF-0070 and FIN-0012 first.

OFF.when: When your offer feels plain and you want to work out what would make it hard to refuse.
OFF.tune: Bring the core product, buyer doubts from reviews and your margin, and push for bonuses and a guarantee rather than a lower price. Check any guarantee against your refund maths before you publish it. Read OFF-0002 and OFF-0001 first.

BRD.when: When a new store comes on board, store facts are out of date, or jobs keep using different prices, margins or customer facts. Builds the one checked set of files every later job reads first. Not for one product's claims and proof.
BRD.tune: the folder will not rank products until gross profit per purchase is computed to the door (with failed deliveries counted where buyers pay on delivery); every customer profile carries a count, share and date range instead of a persona sketch; every fact and rival row expires on a set date; and the ads record judges past ads against...
BRD.title: Store knowledge folder
BRD.outcome: a dated knowledge folder with a one-screen README and facts, product money, voice, customer, proof, competitor and ads files, each with a recheck date, ready for every later job to read first.

BRD.when: When the owner asks "what can we say about this product?", copy makes claims nobody can back up, or a product is about to get new ads, pages or emails. Sorts every claim by its proof. Not for checking a finished ad against ad rules.
BRD.tune: it sorts every claim into five evidence tiers and refuses to let an ingredient study become a product promise; it applies each market's category rules claim by claim with an allowed rewrite; it pairs each counted objection with a real answering review; and it ranks themes by quote counts and claim...
BRD.title: Product claims and proof profile
BRD.outcome: one product's selling profile: a claims table sorted by proof tier with allowed wording, customer quotes, objections, proof and visuals blocks, three themes, and a JSON file other skills can read.

BRD.when: When a designer, freelancer or AI image tool needs the brand's exact colours, fonts and button styles, or the site looks patched together. Reads them from the live Shopify theme. Not for a photo moodboard for shoots.
BRD.tune: it reads tokens from the published theme's own settings file instead of guessing from screenshots; it checks every real colour pair for contrast and gives a same-hue fix; it treats app widgets and image weight as part of the identity; and it ranks fixes by what buyers on the top-profit product...
BRD.title: Visual identity sheet from the live theme
BRD.outcome: a printable visual identity guide of 6 to 10 pages, a tokens.json file with a CSS variables block, and a fix table for contrast and other problems, ready for designers and image tools.

BRD.when: When copy sounds like AI wrote it, reads generic or like every other store, and is about to go live on a product page, ad, email or caption. Rewrites it in the brand's voice without changing facts or prices. Not for writing new copy from scratch.
BRD.tune: it rewrites toward the brand's measured voice and customers' own words rather than a generic style; it proves with a diff that no fact, price or claim changed; it sets the reading grade by format and buyer instead of one number; and it checks any offer line against the product's margin before the...
BRD.title: Machine-sounding copy scrubber
BRD.outcome: clean, ready-to-paste store copy rewritten in the brand's voice, with before and after reading numbers, a flag table of every changed line, a facts kept table and a voice check.

BRD.when: When a photographer, creator, agency or AI image tool is about to make photos for the store, or ads and photos look like they come from different brands. Gives a moodboard, do-and-don't rules and a prompt block. Not for the shot list and run of day.
BRD.tune: the board starts from the store's own best and worst ads, not a mood; it says what must stay fixed and what must vary so ads stay distinct for delivery; AI defaults and fake customers are named as don'ts; and the same rules travel in a prompt block and a creator brief, tested by a cold sorter...
BRD.title: Moodboard for shoots and ads
BRD.outcome: a one-page moodboard (12 to 20 references in five labelled groups), a do-and-don't sheet with fixed and variable rules, a 120-word prompt block for image tools, and a 150-word creator brief section, all saved as one shareable file (Google Slides, Figma, Canva or PDF).

BRD.when: When the owner says "our copy sounds different everywhere", writers or AI tools need to sound like the brand, or after new positioning. Sets the tone of voice, words to use and avoid, and examples per channel. Not for fixing one piece of AI-sounding copy.
BRD.tune: traits come from measured gaps between the owner's loved and disliked lines, each with a checkable marker; tone shifts by moment, including delays and complaints; every channel example sits inside that platform's limits and each market's SMS registration and WhatsApp template rules; and the guide must pass a blind...
BRD.title: Brand voice guide
BRD.outcome: a voice guide of about four pages: 3 to 4 traits with rules and measurable markers, a use and avoid word list, a tone-by-moment table, and before-and-after examples for six channels, plus a one-page cheat sheet a writer or AI tool can follow on the first try.

BRD.when: When the store wants one big campaign for a quarter, festival or relaunch instead of scattered posts and ads, or every channel says something different. Shows one idea in ads, email, site banner, social and WhatsApp or SMS. Not for a weekly calendar of ad tests.
BRD.tune: the idea is built from the store's own buyer words, provable facts and the habit it opposes, then has to pass a stretch test of ten executions before anyone designs; one line, one visual device and one proof are fixed and carried through ads, page, email, SMS, social and WhatsApp; channel volumes...
BRD.title: Campaign big idea across channels
BRD.outcome: one campaign idea on one page (the line, the visual device, the proof, the offer if any, and what it must never say), how each channel expresses it (ads, email, site banner, social posts, WhatsApp or SMS), and a rollout sheet with every asset by channel, date, owner and approval.

BRD.when: When the owner needs a name for a new brand, product or product line, wants to rename, or asks if a name is free to use. Checks domain, social handles, India and US trademarks and bad meanings in buyers' languages.
BRD.tune: names are generated wide from three briefs before any cut; trademark screens look for sound-alikes and same-meaning marks in every market the store sells in, plus unregistered marketplace sellers; meanings are checked in the buyers' own languages; and buyer testing hunts for problems rather than crowning...
BRD.title: Name a product or brand
BRD.outcome: a shortlist of 3 to 5 names, each with its meaning and reasoning, a check table (domain, handles, trademark search in each market, marketplace and search clashes, language meanings), one recommended name and runner-up, and a hand-off note for the trademark attorney.

BRD.when: When the store ships in a plain box, wants better packaging or an insert card, repeat orders are low, or a packaging supplier needs a brief to quote from. Plans an unboxing worth filming and its cost per order.
BRD.tune: the box is only allowed once deliveries and returns work; the budget is set from gross profit per order with retail and shipping packaging split; the insert card has a first-use job and a next-order job with tracked QR codes; and the brief ends in a 60-day test of repeat orders, not a mood.
BRD.title: Packaging and unboxing brief
BRD.outcome: a supplier-ready brief (box, layers, insert card, gift, materials, sizes and quantities), the insert card's final words with QR targets, a per-order cost sheet checked against gross profit, a filmable opening sequence for creators and customers, and a 60-day measurement plan for repeat orders and shared posts.

BRD.when: When the owner asks what makes the brand different, the store looks like every rival, ads, pages and emails say different things, or a brand is new or rebranding. Gives a positioning statement and message pillars with proof. Not for a one-line "what we stand against" statement.
BRD.tune: the statement is built from counted buyer evidence and a dated rival map, not a workshop; it must fail when a rival's name is pasted in; every pillar carries sourced proof and buyer phrases; and the promise is checked against gross profit and the claims rules in each market before any channel uses it.
BRD.title: Brand positioning and messaging
BRD.outcome: a one-page messaging house: a positioning statement, 3 to 4 message pillars each with its proof points and buyer phrases, a list of words and claims to avoid, and one line per channel showing how the main promise is said in an ad, on the product page, in email and on WhatsApp.

BRD.when: When your products look like everyone else's and you need a spot your rivals do not hold.
BRD.tune: Plot three to six real rivals using the prices, claims and looks on their stores and ads, then pick one corner. Look for an open place in the buyer's mind, not a gap in your own range. Read BRD-0011, BRD-0013 and BRD-0008 first.

BRD.when: When your home page tries to talk to everyone and you need one clear line on who the store is for.
BRD.tune: Give it your best customers' words from reviews and survey answers, plus the product. Write the not-for-you list too, since a promise that fits everyone fits no one. Read BRD-0011 and BRD-0001 first.

BRD.when: When you want to raise prices or stop leaning on sales and need a reason buyers will accept.
BRD.tune: Bring your buyer groups, review quotes and the real product reason you can charge more. A premium place has to be claimed first and backed up, and discount-heavy ads will undo it. Read BRD-0009 and BRD-0013 first.

BRD.when: When an AI is about to write or design anything for a store that already has a website.
BRD.tune: Point it at your live Shopify store so prices, offers, look and voice each carry a source, and rerun it after any price or offer change. Never let it adopt a rival's look as your own. Read BRD-0005 and BRD-0015 first.

BRD.when: When a store is about to make its first Facebook and Instagram (Meta) ads, has a new hero product or offer, or its ads read as generic. Ranks products worth advertising by profit and banks proof and customer words. Not for the full store knowledge folder.
BRD.tune: Run it on your store URL, then check its colours, fonts and voice against your main org context before meta-create or meta-generate use it. It reads the site as it is today, so remove stale sale banners first. Read BRD-0005 and BRD-0015 first.
BRD.title: Store profile for Meta ads: products, proof, offer and customer words
BRD.outcome: a store profile for Meta ads: products ranked by gross profit per purchase, a proof table, a customer words bank and a brand profile JSON file, ready for concepts and images.

BRD.when: When you are opening a store or a new line and need a wide pool of names that fit your market.
BRD.tune: Give it the one feeling the name must carry, your rivals' names and every market you sell in, including a sense check in every language your buyers use. Expect the best name to split the team, not please everyone. Read BRD-0002, BRD-0016, BRD-0018 and BRD-0012 first.

BRD.when: When you have two to five names and must pick one before you buy the domain or packaging.
BRD.tune: Paste the shortlist with your category and where you sell. Avoid initials-only names, score sound and spelling, and run your own trademark search in every market you sell in, since the tool cannot clear a name. Read BRD-0010, BRD-0017 and BRD-0019 first.

BRD.when: When you need one line for your header, pack and ads, or must choose between a few.
BRD.tune: Paste the tagline with your promise and key messages. An obvious line is rarely a good one, so push for one that is true but not expected. Read BRD-0021 and BRD-0011 first.

BRD.when: When you add a new range and cannot decide between a new name and your store name.
BRD.tune: List each range with its price level, buyers and sales. Put a product under the house name only when it fits the rules in PRD-0008, and run the shopping-list test in PRD-0007. Read BRD-0012 if a new name is needed.

BRD.when: When you doubt your store name, got a trademark letter, or are changing what the store stands for.
BRD.tune: Feed it branded search clicks from Search Console, direct traffic and repeat sales so the keep-or-rename score uses real numbers. Plan redirects and a clear story of why and what buyers gain. Read BRD-0020 and BRD-0010 first.

BRD.when: When your photos, pack and site look like they came from different brands and you need one look.
BRD.tune: Bring your positioning, three rival stores and images from far outside your category. Pick one colour, shape or scene you can own that works even without the logo. Read BRD-0003 and BRD-0005 first.

BRD.when: When you are redoing your box, tissue or insert and want every part to feel like one brand.
BRD.tune: Give it the product, the pack parts and the cost you can add per order. Match scent or sound to the visual mood, and get a safety check before adding scent near food, skincare or pet goods. Read BRD-0004 and BRD-0007 first.

BRD.when: When your site, emails and pack were made at different times and you suspect they no longer match.
BRD.tune: Attach screenshots of the home and product pages, a Klaviyo email, the pack and two live ads. Check that price signals back your position, above all before you move upmarket. Read BRD-0015, BRD-0009 and BRD-0005 first.

BRD.when: When several people or tools write your copy and you want each draft checked against your voice before it ships.
BRD.tune: Give it your org context and voice rules, then each ad, email or product page draft. It should fix tone and leave claims as written, and log repeat mistakes so the brief gets better. Read BRD-0021 and BRD-0011 first.

BRD.when: When you want to think through which one word your brand should own, or whether to lead a new category.
BRD.tune: Bring your category, the leader and your range, and ask whether to narrow your focus or start a new category. Pair it with BRD-0013 on being first in the mind, BRD-0008 on why better copies fail and BRD-0014 on naming an imitation openly.

SET.when: When the owner says the store feels off and wants a quick pass or fail check of Shopify settings and product pages: before launch, after a theme, app or payment change, or first in a conversion audit. Not for the go-live sign-off with test orders.
SET.tune: settings are read through a read-only app the owner controls, never a shared password or token; every fail is priced in gross profit or given a severity; each market gets its own lines for local payment methods, delivery checks and tax; checkout changes always end in test-mode orders before going live; and India's COD, UPI and GST lines go to Ishita (ishita-india-commerce).
SET.title: Store settings and product page checklist
SET.outcome: a pass or fail checklist of the Shopify store's settings and product pages, the five fixes to make first, a numbered change list for approval and a CSV to re-run after changes.

SET.when: When a new store is built and the owner asks if it is ready to go live or wants to remove the password page: a line-by-line go-live check with test orders and a sign-off. Not for checking a store that is already selling.
SET.tune: the order of blocks follows what breaks if done out of order; every pass needs proof, not a tick; the test order log covers every payment path the store offers, not just one card checkout; and launch is blocked until gross profit per order is positive.
SET.title: New Shopify store launch checklist
SET.outcome: one launch sheet of 26 numbered checks in 9 blocks, each marked pass, fail or not needed with its proof (screenshot, test order number or link), plus a test order log of at least 5 orders and a go or no-go line for the client to sign.

SET.when: When the owner wants to move from WooCommerce or another platform to Shopify without losing products, customers, orders, links or Google rankings, or is choosing the switch-over date.
SET.tune: URLs are ranked by clicks, revenue and links before mapping; the import order protects the costliest errors (subscriptions, gift cards, consent); the cut-over has a freeze window and a written roll-back rule; and the 30-day watch judges the move on gross profit per order and GA4 traffic, not...
SET.title: Move a store to Shopify
SET.outcome: a migration workbook with 5 tabs (inventory, field map, redirect map, cut-over plan, test and watch log), a dated cut-over plan with a go or roll-back rule, and a 30-day watch report template, ready for the client to approve before anything moves.

SET.when: When the owner asks which Shopify apps to install, a new store is about to add its first apps, or wants to keep app bills low from the start. Not for removing apps that already slow a live store.
SET.tune: apps are chosen job by job from the cheapest layer that works; every paid app has to beat its fee in gross profit; each one is checked for speed, crawlability, permissions and exit; and there is a written do-not-install list, including fake urgency tools.
SET.title: A lean app stack
SET.outcome: a one-page app stack for the store's stage (usually 5 to 9 apps), each line with job, choice, free alternative, monthly cost, scripts added, permissions and exit plan, plus a do-not-install list and a monthly app budget cap, ready for the client to approve.

SET.when: When the owner wants to sell in another country with local currency and prices, or foreign buyers get surprise customs bills or leave at checkout: opens one new country in Shopify Markets.
SET.tune: a country opens only if landed gross profit per order there is positive after duties, fees and returns; local prices come from that margin rather than a currency converter; duties are collected or clearly disclosed; and the market stays inactive until three test orders from that country pass.
SET.title: Selling abroad: markets and currencies
SET.outcome: a country launch sheet for one country: a go or no-go margin check, the Shopify Markets settings to enter (currency, rounding, prices, duties, shipping, domain, language, payments), a 15-line launch check with 3 test orders, and the first-month watch list.

SET.when: When a new store needs its first menu and collections (categories), or the owner asks how to group products so buyers can find them. Not for choosing which products show first in each collection.
SET.tune: the menu spine comes from counted buyer words and search terms; the tag scheme is designed before any rule so new products file themselves; every collection has an owner and a minimum size; and the structure doubles as the store's search landing pages.
SET.title: Store navigation and collections
SET.outcome: a collection map (usually 8 to 25 collections) with the exact automated rule for each, a product tagging scheme, a main menu of up to 7 items plus a mobile menu and footer, all in a sheet ready to enter in Shopify after the client's yes.

SET.when: When a new store must pick its payment gateway and methods (UPI, cards, wallets, pay later, cash on delivery), with COD limits, fees, blocked pincodes and holds on risky orders. Not for nudging COD buyers to pay online.
SET.tune: gateways are costed on the store's own payment mix, refunds and disputes, not headline rates; pay on delivery is switched on only where buyers expect it and profit after refused parcels is positive, with limits shown before checkout; and every risky order has a named reviewer and time limit.
SET.title: Payments and pay-on-delivery rules
SET.outcome: a payments sheet with the chosen gateway and runner-up costed on the store's own order mix, the list of payment methods to turn on, pay-on-delivery rules where offered (on or off, order limit, fee, blocked postcodes, confirmation step), a risky-order routine with hold and cancel rules, and a test log, ready for the client to approve.

SET.when: When a new store needs shipping zones, rates and a free-shipping line, or the owner asks what delivery time to promise buyers and where to show it. Not for choosing a courier or 3PL.
SET.tune: every zone is priced from the store's own courier invoices and packed weights; the promise is set from the 90th percentile of real deliveries, not the courier's brochure; the same words appear on all four pages; and remote-area surcharges and pay-on-delivery fees are set beside each market's delivery rules.
SET.title: Shipping rates and delivery promise
SET.outcome: a shipping set-up sheet with 3 to 6 zones, a rate for each zone and speed, one free-shipping line, a delivery promise per zone written as a date range, and the exact wording and spot for that promise on 4 pages, ready to enter in Shopify after the client's yes.

SET.when: When a new store must set up tax before real orders: India GST, HSN codes and GST invoices, or US sales tax by state. It records the accountant's answers and does not give tax rulings.
SET.tune: nothing is set on the agent's guess, because every rate traces to a named accountant answer; override collections are named by rate so mixed carts tax correctly; collection starts only after a registration or permit; a monthly watch catches threshold creep and the gap between tax collected and tax booked; and India's GST setup goes to Ishita (ishita-india-commerce).
SET.title: Taxes: sales tax and VAT setup
SET.outcome: a tax settings sheet (regions, rates, overrides, inclusive or added pricing, shipping rule) ready to enter in Shopify, a product tax map with HSN or tax codes for every product, an invoice set-up, a monthly US nexus watch, and a one-page accountant question list with the answers recorded.

SET.when: When a new store needs its shipping, returns and refund, privacy, terms and contact pages, or the current ones were copied from a template and do not match how the store really works.
SET.tune: every policy sentence traces to a signed operations fact; each promise is tested against the busiest day and the last 90 days of tickets; refund timing is stated per payment type including pay on delivery; and the lawyer gets a short, specific review list instead of a blank template.
SET.title: Store policy pages
SET.outcome: 5 ready-to-paste pages (shipping, returns and refunds, privacy, terms of service, contact), each opening with a 3 to 5 line summary box, plus the operations fact sheet they rest on, a placement list (footer, product page, cart, checkout, emails) and a short list of points for a lawyer to review.

SET.when: When you are opening a new Shopify store and want every setup step done in the right order, up to a first test order.
SET.tune: Feed it your country, your legal business name, a product list export and carrier quotes, so each step builds on real data. Do not let it skip the closing test-order step, because most launch faults only show on a phone checkout. Read SET-0003 and SET-0005 before you start.

SET.when: When you have not opened your Shopify account yet and need to choose a plan, payments and domain first.
SET.tune: Give it the country the business is registered in and the currency you plan to charge, since Shopify Payments decides whether local prices carry through checkout. Enter legal names exactly as on government ID, as a nickname can stall payout checks. Cards SET-0005 and SET-0002 first.

SET.when: When you need to choose a theme or are thinking of moving away from the one you have.
SET.tune: List must-haves from your real catalogue: number of variants, a bundle picker, a mobile gallery and filters. Judge each demo on a phone with no apps added, because every app you add later slows it. Read SPD-0001 and LPG-0034.

SET.when: When you are about to add products and need sizes, colours and packs set up so nothing breaks later.
SET.tune: Start from the supplier sheet with unit cost, packed weight and box size for each variant, since shipping and margin reports read these fields. Enter packed weight, not the bare item weight. Check SET-0007 and MEA-0023.

SET.when: When your products need collections, filters and a menu so shoppers can find things fast.
SET.tune: Give it your product export with tags and your top search terms from Shopify search or Search Console. Name collections after what people search, not internal codes, so the same pages can rank later. Read SEO-0003 and LPG-0039.

SET.when: When you are setting shipping zones and rates, or shipping seems to be losing you money.
SET.tune: Feed it label costs by zone and the spread of order values from a Shopify orders export. Save every box as a package with its empty weight, or calculated rates will undercharge on every order. Check SET-0007 and LPG-0063.

SET.when: When you are setting up tax for a new store or starting to sell in a new state or country.
SET.tune: Tell it where you have an office, staff or stock, and which markets expect prices with tax included. Run a test cart to each state you ship to and confirm the shipping line is taxed the way that state wants. Read SET-0004 and leave registration questions to an accountant.

SET.when: When you want to sell to shoppers in other countries from one Shopify store.
SET.tune: Name your payment gateway first: without Shopify Payments, local prices stop at the cart and checkout charges your base currency. Test one checkout from each market before you spend on ads there. Read SET-0002 and SET-0009.

SET.when: When you are switching on payments or think a checkout setting is costing you orders.
SET.tune: Paste your payment provider, wallet and checkout settings plus the account verification status. Turn on Shop Pay and the other wallets before any other mobile checkout change, and fix name mismatches before payouts freeze. Check SET-0008 and SET-0005.

SET.when: When your store is built and you are about to remove the password and go live.
SET.tune: Give it your settings plus the results of real test orders placed on a phone to two or three addresses. A clean desktop order proves little, since tax, shipping rate and warehouse app errors show up on mobile and on other addresses. Read SET-0003 first.

SET.when: When you have a long list of apps and want to know which to keep, swap or cut.
SET.tune: Paste your Apps list with what each one does and your PageSpeed mobile score. Look for overlap first, such as two review apps or two pop-up tools, because each one adds scripts. Read SPD-0001 and SPD-0009.

SET.when: When chargebacks are rising or you have never set rules for risky orders.
SET.tune: Give it monthly orders and chargebacks with their reasons from your payments dispute report. Below about a hundred orders a month, keep the platform defaults, because tight rules decline real buyers. Read SET-0005 for keeping the payment account healthy.

SET.when: When Shopify's built-in discounts or shipping options cannot do the rule you need.
SET.tune: Describe the rule with a worked cart, such as percentage off with a cap for large orders, or a gift at a spend level. It writes a Shopify Function, so have a developer test it on a copy before it goes live. Read SET-0001 and LPG-0072.

SET.when: When overseas orders are growing and you wonder if a local store or warehouse would pay off.
SET.tune: Give it orders, returns and shipping cost by country from a Shopify sales by country report. Compare the full cost of each order delivered, with payment fees and duties, not postage alone. Read SET-0009 and MEA-0037.

SET.when: When you are building your store on WooCommerce instead of Shopify.
SET.tune: Tell it your host, payment gateway and country, and who will handle updates and backups. Plan for speed from day one by keeping plugins off pages that have no cart. Read SPD-0014 and SET-0003.

MEA.when: When an AI agent or analyst needs safe read access to the store's ad and order data, or a data connection has broken. Not for reading or auditing the results: this only sets up the connections.
MEA.tune: access is read-only by default, with Google Ads kept read-only through the account's access level because its API has no read-only scope; secrets stay with the owner; every stored number carries its attribution setting and is re-pulled for a week; and the data is checked against the store's own...
MEA.title: Connect ad accounts and store data for AI work
MEA.outcome: read-only connections to Meta Ads, Google Ads, Shopify and GA4, with an access log, a daily results table holding a first week of data, a check table and a fix list, ready for AI audits and reports.

MEA.when: When an audit is done and the owner, a partner or an investor must decide which fixes to pay for: turns the findings into a short deck of what each problem costs. Not for the regular monthly report.
MEA.tune: every money figure built from the store's own delivered gross profit and volumes; a low, likely and high range with its method on the slide; fixes ranked by expected profit per unit of cost, with the store's own hit rates where they exist; and a payback slide that states, in words, what must...
MEA.title: From audit findings to a deck that gets fixes funded
MEA.outcome: a deck of about ten slides (Google Slides, PowerPoint or PDF) showing what each audit finding costs and what fixing it is worth, with a findings and money source sheet and a one-screen summary.

MEA.when: When the owner asks what Facebook, Instagram (Meta) and Google ads really make together, or both platforms claim the same sales: one weekly view of total ad spend against store profit. Not for checking Meta alone.
MEA.tune: gross profit after ads as the bottom line instead of blended ROAS; an over-claim ratio that shows how much the platforms double count; a channel-mix score built from four store-side checks; and a holdout sized to the store that decides cross-channel claims before money moves.
MEA.title: Blended view: what Meta and Google really return together
MEA.outcome: a weekly blended table of Meta and Google spend against store gross profit, a channel mix table with the over-claim ratio, and a holdout plan for the one channel claim worth testing.

MEA.when: When Meta Events Manager rates event match quality Poor or OK for Purchase or checkout, even though events arrive and are not doubled: fixes the customer details sent with each event. Not for missing or double-counted purchases.
MEA.tune: realistic aims per funnel event instead of one score for all; a cause for every missing key; an honest cost range in place of a made-up loss; and a same-day check in Shopify customer events and test events, then a booked 7-day re-measure.
MEA.title: Better match quality, event by event
MEA.outcome: a match quality table for every funnel event, a ranked fix list with hours and owners, and a before and after table measured on day 0 and day 7.

MEA.when: When a month ends and the owner, team, partner or lender asks how the month really went: a report that leads with profit and cash, not platform ROAS. Not for the weekly numbers sheet.
MEA.tune: contribution after ads and cash on the first screen; Shopify's definition traps corrected before any comparison; a source tag on every number with untagged numbers removed; and last month's actions graded so the report learns from itself.
MEA.title: Monthly performance report: profit and cash first
MEA.outcome: a monthly report that leads with profit and cash: a KPI snapshot, a gross-to-net bridge, a what-moved table, a channels table, graded and next actions, and a data CSV with every figure's source.

MEA.when: When sales, ROAS or cost per purchase moved sharply for a week or more across ad channels and the owner asks why.
MEA.tune: it proves the drop is real before diagnosing; it checks the store's conversion rate, stock and site in Shopify before blaming any ad account; each cause comes with the share of the drop it explains and a confidence level; and pay-on-delivery stores are judged on delivered orders.
MEA.title: Why did results change? A store-first diagnosis
MEA.outcome: a one-screen answer naming the cause of the drop, its share and money at stake, with tables proving it is real, splitting store and channel effects, and next steps with a do-not list.

MEA.when: When the owner asks whether the AI's or agency's past advice actually worked, or review dates for past ad and store recommendations have passed: grades each call against gross profit.
MEA.tune: every grade on store contribution after subtracting what would have happened anyway; a noise band that refuses to call small moves wins; hit rates read against a fair base rate; and rules the owner approves, backed by row IDs, that retire themselves when they fail.
MEA.title: Recommendation scorekeeping
MEA.outcome: a recommendation log CSV grading each past ad and store call against gross profit, an accuracy table by type, proposed rules, and a recommendation on the agent's limits.

MEA.when: When the owner asks which products really make money, or knows the store margin but not each product's profit after discounts, shipping, fees, returns and failed COD deliveries. Not for deciding which products to push or cut.
MEA.tune: failed deliveries are costed as their own loss line with units shipped but never sold; pay-on-delivery and prepaid split per top SKU where the store offers both; refunds are matured or accrued before any product is judged; and every row carries a confirmed or estimate flag, so no product is ranked on a guessed cost.
MEA.title: Profit per product sheet
MEA.outcome: one sheet (Google Sheet or `sku-profit.csv` with live formulas) with a row per product: units, net revenue, every cost line, profit per unit kept and profit share, plus a one-screen summary naming the products that lose money and the three cost lines worth fixing first.

MEA.when: When the owner wants one page of the 10 to 12 numbers to check every Monday, looks at too many numbers or the wrong ones, or a weekly review is being set up. Not for running the weekly meeting itself.
MEA.tune: every row carries its own action rule and owner, not just a target; ranges come from the store's own normal weeks; a confidence line can veto spend changes; and pay-on-delivery stores read money on delivered orders with cash still in transit held apart.
MEA.title: Weekly KPI dashboard
MEA.outcome: a one-page weekly sheet (Google Sheet or `weekly-kpis.csv` with a definitions tab) with 10 to 12 numbers, each with definition, source, owner, normal range and the action when it moves, plus a top block of three decisions for the week and a data-confidence line. Filled for the last 8 weeks so ranges are real.

MEA.when: When the owner asks how many customers come back and what a customer is worth over time (lifetime value, LTV), or needs a target cost per new customer (CAC) from real repeat numbers. Not for the monthly retention tracking sheet.
MEA.tune: undelivered, refused and refunded orders are removed before anyone becomes a "customer"; phone numbers are normalised as the identity key for guest checkouts; immature cells stay blank instead of being projected; and every lifetime value turns into an affordable CAC on gross profit with its window stated.
MEA.title: Repeat purchase and lifetime value by cohort
MEA.outcome: a cohort workbook with three tables (by first-order month, by first product, by first channel) showing customers, repeat rate and value per customer at 90, 180 and 365 days in revenue and gross profit, plus a one-screen summary with the affordable CAC per segment and one retention action.

MEA.when: When the owner asks whether a channel really brings extra sales or the store would get them anyway (incrementality), before cutting or scaling it by a lot: a holdout test by region or by weeks.
MEA.tune: the size check uses the store's own region-to-region noise before any money moves; the holdout cuts total budget by the test share so control regions are not inflated; pay-on-delivery stores read delivered orders by shipping region; and the result becomes an incrementality factor applied to platform numbers...
MEA.title: Measure channel lift with holdouts
MEA.outcome: a one-page test plan (question, regions or weeks, size check, duration, freeze list, cost cap, decision rule written before launch), the set-up list for the client to approve, and a read-out sheet that gives incremental orders, revenue, gross profit, incremental return per extra spend and an incrementality factor to apply to the platform's reported numbers.

MEA.when: When next month's budget is being set and the owner asks what a new customer really costs on Meta, Google, TikTok or creators (CAC by channel), counted from the store's own first orders.
MEA.tune: new customers are counted from the store's own first orders with failed deliveries removed; every channel gets a range from three views instead of one number; creator fees and seeded product count as acquisition cost; and verdicts use 90-day gross profit only from mature cohorts, with small upper-funnel...
MEA.title: New-customer cost by channel
MEA.outcome: a one-page table, per channel, of new customers, spend, cost per new customer as a low to high range, first-order gross profit, 90-day gross profit and a verdict, plus the blended new-customer cost for the whole store, ready to feed the monthly budget.

MEA.when: When the owner asks where buyers really heard about the store, platforms all claim the same sales, or word of mouth, influencers and AI assistants leave no click: a 'how did you hear about us' survey after purchase.
MEA.tune: pay-on-delivery buyers are reached with one approved WhatsApp or SMS question instead of a thank-you page they never see; answers are read for first-time buyers only and turned into a survey CAC set against first-order gross profit; and each channel gets a verdict that sends big budget moves to a holdout test...
MEA.title: How-did-you-hear-about-us survey
MEA.outcome: a ready survey (question, answer options in the store's channels, one follow-up, placement and display rules), the set-up list for the client to approve, and a monthly reading sheet that compares each channel's share of survey answers with its share of spend and of platform-claimed purchases, with a verdict per channel.

MEA.when: When there are too many ideas and the owner asks what to do first: ideas from audits, agents and the founder logged and ranked by profit, effort and evidence. Not for writing the 90-day plan around the chosen bets.
MEA.tune: broken things and cheap answers to big unknowns are ranked before growth ideas; every growth score starts from honest base rates and only rises with counted evidence; the person who proposes an idea never scores it; and the top five must fit real owners' hours and the cash on hand.
MEA.title: Prioritise the growth backlog
MEA.outcome: a backlog sheet with every idea logged, laned and scored, and a one-screen do-next list: the top five to start now with owner and start date, the next ten waiting, and the ideas dropped with a one-line reason.

MEA.when: When the owner asks which products to push, fix or drop, before placing the next stock order or setting next month's ad budget. Not for working out each product's profit from scratch.
