MEA.tune: every product is ranked on profit per unit of cash tied up, not revenue; demand is measured only on in-stock days; entry products that bring buyers back are protected from cuts; and every push is paced against the supplier's real lead time.
MEA.title: Products to push, fix or cut
MEA.outcome: one sheet listing every active product as push, fix or cut, with its numbers and a one-line reason, plus a one-screen summary of the 5 biggest moves and the cash they free or earn.

MEA.when: When the owner wants to track repeat customers every month and Shopify's returning customer rate moves for the wrong reasons: eight defined retention numbers with targets. Not for a one-off deep study of lifetime value.
MEA.tune: Shopify's returning customer rate is replaced with cohort numbers that only count windows that have closed; returning-customer gross profit sits beside new-customer profit so one cannot hide the other; targets come from the store's own best months, not borrowed benchmarks; and each miss points to...
MEA.title: Retention dashboard
MEA.outcome: a one-page monthly sheet of eight retention numbers, each with a written formula, the export it comes from, a target set from the store's own history, a green or red mark, and the action to take when it misses, plus a short data-confidence line.

MEA.when: When returns or failed deliveries (pay-on-delivery parcels refused and sent back, called RTO in India) feel high, profit per order looks fine but cash does not arrive, or before blocking pay on delivery, changing courier or return policy: costs the losses by product, postcode and channel.
MEA.tune: it costs a failed delivery including the ad money already spent; it reports profit per order shipped, not just per order delivered; every fix is priced against the good orders it would turn away; and postcode cells are merged to a minimum size so nobody blocks an area on noise.
MEA.title: Returns and failed-delivery cost analysis
MEA.outcome: one loss table (cost per failed delivery and per return, by product, postcode or ZIP area and channel), a ranked list of 3 to 6 fixes with money saved per month, and a one-screen summary the owner can approve.

MEA.when: When the owner asks how much to spend on ads next month: a total budget and split by channel worked back from the profit target, cash and stock. Not for moving money between Meta and Google inside a fixed budget.
MEA.tune: the budget is the lowest of three ceilings (profit, cash, stock) with the binding one named; returning profit is separated so ads are not credited with it; the ceiling stops at the marginal cost of new customers; and payout lags (including pay-on-delivery cash) and sales tax or VAT on ad spend are in the cash test.
MEA.title: Monthly ad budget from a profit target
MEA.outcome: one budget sheet for next month: the total ad ceiling, the ceiling by channel (Meta, Google, TikTok and any test), weekly pacing, and the stop line for each, with the profit, cash and stock maths that set it, ready for the owner to approve.

MEA.when: When a new store needs Google Analytics 4 (GA4) set up, or GA4 sales do not match store orders and nobody has checked it since it was installed.
MEA.tune: the check is against store orders by day with banded capture rates instead of a "tags fire" test; third-party checkouts, WhatsApp draft orders and bank or wallet payment redirects are named as separate gap causes; the post-upgrade thank-you page is treated as broken until proven; and every fix carries its...
MEA.title: GA4 setup and data check for a store
MEA.outcome: a completed setup checklist (each item set, verified or open), a 14-day reconciliation table of GA4 purchases and revenue against store orders, and a gap list where each gap has its size, cause, fix and owner, ready for the client to approve.

MEA.when: When Google Analytics puts sales in the wrong channel or Unassigned, before launching influencer or WhatsApp campaigns, or when several people build links: one UTM link-tagging rule for every channel.
MEA.tune: the medium list is mapped line by line to GA4's real channel rules, so a typo cannot hide paid spend as organic; WhatsApp, creators and QR codes get their own channels in a custom group; and a 10-minute weekly check catches drift before a month of data is lost.
MEA.title: UTM tracking for every channel
MEA.outcome: a one-page UTM rule, a value list (source, medium, campaign, content) mapped to the GA4 channel each lands in, ready templates for 10 channel types, a link builder sheet with formulas, and a weekly check sheet with pass or fail lines.

MEA.when: When a new quarter starts and the owner asks for one growth plan, not twelve: the one thing holding growth back, three bets, owners, budget and weekly checkpoints. Not for ranking every idea on the list.
MEA.tune: the constraint is found in a fixed order that checks data and unit economics before traffic; only three bets survive, each with an owner, approver and a profit range from the store's own numbers; the budget is checked week by week against a cash floor; and every bet carries its stop line before...
MEA.title: Ninety-day growth plan
MEA.outcome: a one-page plan (baseline, the constraint, three bets, owners, budget, what success looks like at day 90) plus a bets table with profit ranges, a monthly budget against the cash plan, and a 13-week checkpoint grid with the line that decides continue, change or stop for each bet.

MEA.when: When TikTok ads are about to start, or TikTok shows more or fewer purchases than the store's orders: a pass or fail check of the TikTok pixel and Events API. Not for building the first campaign.
MEA.tune: purchase events are reconciled against every Shopify order by day with a ten-order spot check, not just a green light in Events Manager; fixes come in a fixed priority order starting with double counts; Shopify's 2026 checkout upgrade is checked for silent tag loss; and consent is never loosened...
MEA.title: TikTok pixel and Events API check
MEA.outcome: a check sheet of 12 pass or fail tests with the evidence for each, a day-by-day table of Shopify orders against TikTok purchase events for 7 days, a ten-order spot check, and a numbered fix list in priority order, ready for the owner or developer to act on.

MEA.when: When the team meets weekly about ads, email, site and offers and the meeting runs long without decisions: a one-page pre-read, agenda and decision log. Not for building the weekly numbers sheet.
MEA.tune: the pack leads with contribution after ads and new-customer cost; known Shopify, GA4, Meta and Google traps are corrected in writing before the meeting; every change is split into sessions, conversion and order value and labelled real, noise or immature; and every decision carries a signal, a...
MEA.title: Weekly growth meeting pack
MEA.outcome: a one-page pre-read (five headline numbers, what changed and why, one main constraint, one win, one oddity, up to five owned actions) plus a decision log and a 30-minute agenda, ready to send the day before the meeting.

MEA.when: When you are about to raise ad spend and are not sure your tracking counts each sale once.
MEA.tune: Give it your GA4 setup notes, Meta Events Manager screenshots, how you tag links and 30 days of Shopify orders by day. Fix setup before you read any ROAS, because a leftover test event code or a missing event_id makes every later number wrong. Read MEA-0005, MEA-0006 and MEA-0042.

MEA.when: When you just set up GA4 or your purchases do not show up there.
MEA.tune: Describe your property settings, data retention, internal traffic filter and where the purchase event comes from. Set retention to 14 months on day one, since the change does not reach back. Filter key event rate to purchases before you read conversion by channel.

MEA.when: When Meta shows a different number of purchases than the store's orders, the pixel or Conversions API may be missing or double counting, before raising spend, or after a checkout, theme or tracking change.
MEA.tune: Feed it Events Manager screenshots: match quality, deduplication and server versus browser counts for Purchase. Check that one event_id travels on both the pixel and the server event and that no test code is left in the live tag. Read MEA-0001 before you promise a big recovery from a gateway.
MEA.title: Store orders into Meta, once and correctly: pixel and Conversions API check
MEA.outcome: a daily table of store orders against Meta Purchase events, a ten-order spot check, the main cause of any gap and the top three fixes in order.

MEA.when: When Facebook and Instagram (Meta) report far more or fewer sales than the store's orders, the owner asks how much of Meta's ROAS to believe, or before a Meta budget decision. Not for repairing the pixel or Conversions API.
MEA.tune: Give it Ads Manager exports with the attribution comparison columns next to Shopify new-customer orders for the same days. Report on 7-day click, because much of the view-through credit disappears when checked. Read MEA-0042, MEA-0025 and MEA-0007.
MEA.title: How much of Meta's credit is real: store attribution check
MEA.outcome: a week-by-week table of Meta against store orders, the size of the gap and its main cause, a chosen reporting basis, and store-truth factors per campaign for reading ROAS on a store basis.

MEA.when: When you are launching Google Ads or Google shows a different purchase count than your store.
MEA.tune: Give it your Shopify plan, the Google app status and any Tag Manager setup. Keep one primary purchase action with real order value and enhanced conversions, since GA4-imported purchases undercount as the primary. Read MEA-0016 and MEA-0017.

MEA.when: When you make choices from the Shopify dashboard and want to know which tiles you can trust.
MEA.tune: Paste the analytics tiles with their date range and a sales report by day. Use net sales plus shipping as cash collected, and read returning customer rate as a share of orders, not a repeat rate. Read MEA-0010, MEA-0013 and MEA-0021.

MEA.when: When you need your true margin per order before you set any ad target.
MEA.tune: Give it price, unit cost, freight in, packaging, pick and pack, postage, payment fees and expected return rate for each product. Margin must be the cost to the customer's door, not the product margin Shopify shows from the cost field. This is the trust gate, so read MEA-0023 and MEA-0037 before ranking any play.

MEA.when: When the owner asks what ROAS or cost per purchase they need to break even on Facebook and Instagram (Meta) ads, before any audit, budget change, scaling call or new offer. Needs only store exports.
MEA.tune: Paste an Ads Manager export plus the delivered margin from the margin check, never revenue alone. Check the cost per customer floor from cost per click and conversion rate before you plan to scale. Read MEA-0019, MEA-0047 and MEA-0026.
MEA.title: Store money lines for Meta ads
MEA.outcome: the store's money lines for Meta (gross profit per purchase, break-even and target ROAS and cost per purchase, offer break-evens and daily spend ceilings) in tables and a CSV or live sheet.

MEA.when: When total revenue looks fine but you cannot tell what new customers are costing you.
MEA.tune: Feed it a Shopify orders export with the new or returning flag, product costs and daily spend from Meta and Google. Make new-customer MER the headline, not blended MER, because repeat buyers hide rising acquisition costs. Read MEA-0039, MEA-0025 and MEA-0031.

MEA.when: When you only find out at month end whether a day or a week made money.
MEA.tune: Give it daily net sales, variable costs, ad spend and your 90-day return rate. Accrue returns each day at the expected rate, because Shopify books them on the refund date, and keep fixed costs out of the daily view. Read MEA-0030, MEA-0028 and MEA-0011.

MEA.when: When you want to know if you can safely raise ad spend based on what customers are worth over time.
MEA.tune: Give it Shopify revenue by first-order month, gross margin, new customers and spend. Use 30-day or 90-day gross profit per customer, not lifetime revenue, and only judge cohorts old enough to fill that window. Read MEA-0020, MEA-0054 and MEA-0048.

MEA.when: When platform ROAS looks great but the bank balance does not agree.
MEA.tune: Put Meta and Google exports for the same dates next to Shopify net sales and new-customer revenue. Be wary of small channels and retargeting that look strong because they catch warm visitors. Read MEA-0053, MEA-0040 and, if you also sell on Amazon, MEA-0029.

MEA.when: When your ad reports and your customers' own answers about how they found you disagree.
MEA.tune: Give it the how-did-you-hear answers from your post-purchase survey app and spend by channel for the same weeks. Compare each channel's share of answers with its share of spend, and make sure AI assistants are one of the answer options. Read MEA-0045 and AEO-0025.

MEA.when: When a channel's reported sales and your store's sales do not match and you need to know what the ads really add.
MEA.tune: Give it spend, new-customer revenue and new orders by region for several months. Match test regions on all three histories and keep the test well clear of Black Friday. Read MEA-0050, MEA-0033 and MEA-0034, and MEA-0041 if the store is small.

MEA.when: When sales dropped and you want to know which lever moved before you change anything.
MEA.tune: Feed it Shopify sessions, orders and AOV for both periods, plus the ad change history and returns. Split the drop into sessions, conversion rate and order value, and remember that Google's last few days always look weak. Read MEA-0009, MEA-0018 and MEA-0051.

MEA.when: When prices change after a new quote, a cost-down or a supplier switch, and the profit sheet needs the new COGS.
MEA.tune: every price carries a date, source and basis, scrap is grossed up level by level, tooling spreads drop off when paid, and the roll-up is checked against the last invoice before Shopify's cost per item is updated.
MEA.title: Living BOM with a COGS roll-up per SKU
MEA.outcome: A versioned BOM file where every price change has a date, source and reason, plus a COGS per SKU tab (factory price, tooling spread, packaging) that radek-unit-economics and zhenyu-sourcing read from.

MEA.when: When a big catalogue needs sorting by how much margin each product brings and how steady its demand is.
MEA.tune: classes are built on contribution margin and on demand cleaned for stock-outs and promotions, new and ending SKUs are kept out, the bands bend to the store's own data, and every box shows stock value next to margin.
MEA.title: ABC and XYZ classes for your products
MEA.outcome: Every SKU classed A, B or C by share of margin and X, Y or Z by demand steadiness, shown as a nine-box grid with the rule behind each class and what each box means for range, stock and promotion.

MEA.when: When planning bundles, add-ons or a line extension, or when a new product may be taking sales from an old one.
MEA.tune: pairs are ranked by lift only above a support floor, next-order pairs go to timed emails instead of bundles, contribution not order value decides the list, bundles are checked against stock, and launches are judged on net demand.
MEA.title: Basket and attach rate analysis
MEA.outcome: A table of product pairs bought together with attach rates and order sequence, margin per basket, cannibalisation checks for recent launches, and a ranked list of bundles and add-ons worth testing.

LPG.when: When Facebook and Instagram ads get clicks at a normal cost but few sales, or before a sale, launch or spend rise: checks the pages the ads land on, on a phone. Not for an audit of the whole store.
LPG.tune: Give it the live ad, the landing link, a phone screenshot and the Events Manager view for that page. Confirm the pixel records a page view after the cookie banner, then check message match and trust in the first screen. Read LPG-0064, LPG-0038 and MEA-0007.
LPG.title: Meta ad landing page check for an online store
LPG.outcome: a phone-first check of every page the Meta ads land on, with a page table, pass or fail checks, a ranked fix list with gross profit at stake, and screenshots.

LPG.when: When cold buyers from ads need a story and explanation before they will buy: a long, story-led advertorial page in the store's brand. Not for a short numbered list of reasons to buy.
LPG.tune: only true, consented stories, with no composites; a plain advertising label and a typical-results rule built in as gates; card conflicts on the opening settled in favour of curiosity over shared pain; and the page is judged against the product page on gross profit per session.
LPG.title: Story-led advertorial page
LPG.outcome: a fast, story-led advertorial HTML page in the store's brand, with images, optional Shopify template files, a claims check file and a beliefs table, ready for review and a test against the product page.

LPG.when: When cold ad traffic clicks but does not buy, or ads, pages and emails talk past what shoppers already know: matches each one to the buyer's stage, from unaware of the problem to ready to buy.
LPG.tune: stage comes from audience, query and visitor data instead of a guess; every mismatch is ranked by store-side cost per purchase; the ad, page and email are fixed together as one path; and the stage mix starts from the store's own sales and margin, not a fixed split.
LPG.title: Awareness stage message match
LPG.outcome: a stage map for each traffic source, a diagnosis of which ads, pages and emails speak to the wrong stage, new drafts written for each stage, and a pairing table that joins ad, page and email.

LPG.when: When the owner shares a page they like (screenshot or link) and wants that layout in their own brand, or an old page needs rebuilding as clean HTML.
LPG.tune: other brands' pages are used for structure only, enforced by a written rights check on copy, images, fonts, icons and overall look; the structure is improved against proven levers instead of copied blindly; and the page must pass Core Web Vitals good levels before handover.
LPG.title: Page layout rebuild in the store's brand
LPG.outcome: a structure version and a branded version of a reference page as clean HTML in the store's brand, with images, an optional Shopify section, a section inventory, a brand map and a rights check file.

LPG.when: When a product page has many views but a low add-to-cart rate, or buyers keep raising the same doubts the photos could answer. Not for page copy or an A/B test plan: this rebuilds the product photos.
LPG.tune: every slot answers a counted doubt from the store's own reviews, tickets and survey; the feed image is protected from text; images are weight-checked for speed; and the test plan is gated by the product's real monthly orders, with a before-and-after path for small stores.
LPG.title: Product page gallery audit and rebuild
LPG.outcome: a doubts table from reviews, tickets and returns, a gallery plan that answers each doubt in order, finished images in 4:5 and 1:1 folders, an alt text file and a review deck.

LPG.when: When ads land on a product page that converts poorly, or a product has more strong reasons to buy than its page shows: a short numbered 'reasons to buy' page for ad traffic. Not for a long story page.
LPG.tune: every reason answers a counted buyer doubt with traceable proof; the page ships with a speed and mobile pass at Core Web Vitals good levels; it is judged against the product page on profit per session with a sized test; and buyers see delivery time and payment options right where they decide.
LPG.title: Reasons-to-buy listicle page
LPG.outcome: a fast, mobile-first reasons-to-buy HTML page with five to seven proven reasons, images, an optional Shopify section set, a reasons table, a speed check and a comparison plan.

LPG.when: When the owner wants the store audited for conversion: visitors come but do not buy, conversion rate has fallen for weeks, or mobile converts far below desktop. Finds where buyers leave across every page and sizes each leak. Not for one ad's landing page.
LPG.tune: every fix is sized in gross profit per month with a realistic lift and a chance of working; the ship, test or research call comes from the store's own order volume; paid traffic is checked against gross profit per visitor, not a generic revenue floor; and the visuals are made with free tools from...
LPG.title: Storefront conversion audit
LPG.outcome: a funnel table by device, a ranked findings table with monthly gross profit per fix, a test plan, before and after images, a deck and a findings CSV.

LPG.when: When the store is booking a photographer or studio day and wants a shot list and brief so every hour gives usable photos. Not for a cheap phone or home shoot.
LPG.tune: frames are spent by gross profit rank, not evenly; every shot is tied to a named channel slot and the buyer doubt it answers; vertical frames are composed for Meta's current safe bands on the day; and casting comes from the store's own buyers, with the usage licence a hard stop.
LPG.title: Product photoshoot shot list and art direction
LPG.outcome: a shoot pack for one day: a numbered shot list of 30 to 50 frames mapped to their channel and slot, a props and set list, a lighting plan, a model and casting brief, a timed run-of-day, file delivery specs, and model and usage release checklists, ready to send to a photographer.

LPG.when: When paid or search traffic lands on a collection grid and few people click a product, when a collection grows past one screen of products, or when a new collection is launched. Not for ranking on Google: this turns visitors into clicks and sales.
LPG.tune: filters are ranked by counted buyer mentions and data fill rate; the first row is gated on variant stock and gross profit; every badge and pin follows a written, dated rule; and the grid is planned for a two-column phone screen first.
LPG.title: Collection page that converts
LPG.outcome: a plan for one collection page: intro copy (top and bottom), a ranked filter list with values, a default sort rule with the first six products pinned, product card rules and a card copy line for each product in the first two rows, ready for the client to approve and the theme or merchandising app to apply.

LPG.when: When buyers ask how the product differs from a rival or a cheaper option, people search 'X vs Y' or 'alternatives to X', or before running comparison ads: a fair comparison page with dated facts.
LPG.tune: alternatives and rows come from counted buyer mentions, not from what flatters the store; every cell carries a source and a date; the page admits where rivals win, which comparison rules in the US, UK and EU reward; and the same claims file feeds the store's comparison ads.
LPG.title: Comparison page against alternatives
LPG.outcome: one comparison page written in full (headline, short verdict, fact table, who-should-pick-which, why this one, FAQ, button) plus a claims file with the source and check date for every row, ready for a claims review and the client's approval.

LPG.when: When a gifting season such as Diwali, Christmas or Mother's Day is 4 to 8 weeks away and the store needs a gift guide page by recipient and budget, with delivery cutoff dates.
LPG.tune: delivery cutoffs come from the store's own 90th percentile dispatch and transit data with a buffer, not courier promises; every pick is gated on season stock and profit after wrap; recipients come from real gift orders; and each market's holiday and festival calendar, zones and pay-on-delivery cutoffs are built in.
LPG.title: Gift guide page
LPG.outcome: one gift guide page written in full (intro, recipient sections, budget bands, 20 to 40 product picks with giver-focused copy, gift options, a delivery cutoff table by region and shipping method), plus a pick sheet with stock and profit for each item, ready for the client's approval and the theme or page builder.

LPG.when: When shoppers ask which product is right for them, the store has several similar products and buyers cannot choose, or the owner wants a quiz that also collects emails or WhatsApp numbers.
LPG.tune: questions come from the facts that cause wrong purchases and returns; every result path is gated on profit, stock and honest matching; capture never blocks the answer; and quiz answers flow into email properties and avatar research instead of sitting unused.
LPG.title: Product finder quiz
LPG.outcome: a quiz spec ready to build in a quiz app or theme section: 4 to 8 questions with answer options, a scoring table that maps every answer path to one product or bundle, one results page per outcome (headline, why this fits, proof, offer, button), the capture step with consent text, the tags for email flows, and the targets to judge it by.

LPG.when: When the store needs real lifestyle photos for ads, social and product pages but has no budget for a photographer: a phone or home shoot plan. Not for a booked studio day.
LPG.tune: scenes come from where buyers say they use the product, not from mood; every frame is shot both ways so it works at 9:16 without a crop disaster; consent and home privacy are gates, not afterthoughts; and the plan keeps lifestyle images out of the one slot (the Shopping main image) where they get...
LPG.title: Lifestyle photos on a small budget
LPG.outcome: a one-day home shoot plan (scenes, a numbered 25-to-30 frame shot list, light and phone settings, props from home, timed schedule, consent forms) and a pick sheet that turns the day into 20 usable, named lifestyle images at 4:5, 1:1 and 9:16.

LPG.when: When product photos look mismatched (backgrounds, sizes or colours jump between images), collection grids look messy, files are heavy, or a new editor joins: one retouch and export standard.
LPG.tune: one fill percentage and one base line make every collection row line up; edits are split into allowed and banned so no editor "improves" the product; fixes are ordered by gross profit and channel risk; and image replacements carry new URLs so Meta and Google actually pick them up.
LPG.title: Consistent product photo set
LPG.outcome: a one-page retouch and export standard (background, light, crop, colour, allowed edits, export table), an audit sheet scoring every current product image against it, and a ranked fix list, ready for an editor or freelancer to apply in batches.

LPG.when: When the owner wants an About us page, buyers ask who is behind the brand, the current page is a mission statement nobody reads, or before founder ads and press outreach.
LPG.tune: the story is built from a recorded interview and a confirmed fact sheet, never invented; every value becomes a practice with proof; origin claims use exact wording; and a plain-text fact box makes the page the source answer engines repeat, closing on the products buyers should try first.
LPG.title: About us and brand story page
LPG.outcome: one about page written in full (headline, opening story, the difference, how it is made, the people, proof, a brand fact box, and a shop-first close), plus an interview log and fact sheet that back every line, ready for the founder's read-through and the client's approval.

LPG.when: When the same questions keep reaching support or WhatsApp, buyers leave product pages to ask something, or the FAQ was written from guesses: an FAQ from real questions, placed where they come up. Not for ready replies for support agents.
LPG.tune: every question is counted from the store's own tickets, chats and reviews; each answer is placed where the doubt arises rather than on one page; policy conflicts are surfaced instead of guessed; and answers are written to be both read by buyers and quoted by answer engines, now that FAQ snippets...
LPG.title: FAQ built from real questions
LPG.outcome: a counted question list, 15 to 40 written answers, and a placement map that puts each answer on the page or message where the question comes up (product, collection, cart, help centre, order emails), with the source and owner of every answer, ready for the client to approve and load.

LPG.when: When the owner wants the home page words rewritten: visitors land but few click into products, after a rebrand, or before sending influencer or brand traffic to the home page.
LPG.tune: every section has a named visitor, a job and a metric; the homepage is scored on view-product rate from the store's own analytics; returning buyers get their own fast path; and hero picks are gated on profit and stock before any words are written.
LPG.title: Homepage copy
LPG.outcome: a homepage written in full, section by section (usually 7 to 10 sections), each with its copy, its job, which visitor it serves, the number that proves it works, and a returning-buyer variant where it differs, ready to load into the theme editor after the client approves it.

LPG.when: When many products have supplier, copied or empty descriptions, after a rebrand, or when lots of products were added at once: descriptions for the whole catalogue from one template per type. Not for one key product page in full.
LPG.tune: each description is filled only from a fact sheet row, so missing facts become a flag list instead of invented copy; templates are set per product type with word budgets; a 10-product pilot locks the voice before the batch; and duplicate, machine-tell and fact checks run before anything is imported.
LPG.title: Product descriptions for the whole catalogue
LPG.outcome: one description template per product type, a voice sample bank, and descriptions for every product in a Shopify import CSV (Handle and Body (HTML)), with a flag sheet listing each product held back for missing facts, ready for spot checks and the client's approval before import.

LPG.when: When one product page gets traffic but sells poorly, ads send people to a page that does not match them, or a new product needs its first page: full copy for that page. Not for descriptions across the whole catalogue.
LPG.tune: the promise is picked by counted review mentions, not taste; every proof slot is tied to a named objection and a real reviewer; claims are narrowed to the evidence before writing starts; and the page is gated on positive gross profit per order and the listing rules of each market it sells in.
LPG.title: Product page copy that sells
LPG.outcome: one product page written in full (headline, subhead, proof line, 3 to 5 benefit blocks, 3 to 5 chosen reviews, details table, 5 to 8 FAQs, guarantee and buy-box lines), in page order, with a source for every claim, ready to paste into the Shopify product template after the client approves it.

LPG.when: When listing on Amazon, Flipkart, Myntra, Nykaa or Meesho, titles were copied from the supplier, or titles get rejected or cut off: one title per channel from the same facts. Not for rewriting Google Shopping feed titles from search data.
LPG.tune: every channel's title is built from one checked attribute sheet, so the product is described the same true way everywhere; each title carries a character count and a rule check against rules dated this month; marketplace titles are written only for products that make money after fees; and changes...
LPG.title: Product titles for store and marketplaces
LPG.outcome: a title sheet with, for every product, a store title, an SEO title, a Google Shopping title, an Amazon title and a title for each other marketplace it sells on (such as Walmart, Etsy or eBay), each with its character count and a pass or fail check against that channel's rules, ready for the client to approve and upload by feed, flat file or seller panel.

LPG.when: When wrong sizes or wrong use drive returns, exchanges or tickets ('does it fit?', 'how do I use it?'): size and fit guides or how-to-use guides built from return reasons, tickets and reviews.
LPG.tune: fit notes come from the direction buyers actually exchange each product, not a generic chart; every size number is measured; how-to guides are written from misuse returns and placed both on the page and in the delivery messages; and returns, exchanges and tickets per 100 orders are baselined so...
LPG.title: Size, fit and how-to-use guides
LPG.outcome: for each product type in scope, either a size and fit guide (size table in two units, how to measure, per-product fit notes, model size worn, between-sizes rule) or a how-to-use guide (steps, first-use expectations, mistakes to avoid, when to contact support), with the placement for each block and a before-and-after measure of returns and tickets, ready for the client's approval.

LPG.when: When you are about to send paid traffic to a page and want to check it keeps the ad's promise.
LPG.tune: Attach the exact ad copy and first frame from any channel, with the page it links to. Each persona or angle ad should land on a page that leads with that one benefit. Read LPG-0064, LPG-0067 and LPG-0068.

LPG.when: When you run ads to several buyer groups and need to decide which page each one should land on.
LPG.tune: Give it your live ads tagged by buyer group, awareness stage and traffic source. Social traffic needs the pain and education block early, while search traffic wants product and price first. Read LPG-0070, LPG-0050 and LPG-0004.

LPG.when: When people land on your page but leave before scrolling, and you suspect the first screen.
LPG.tune: Give it your offer, review count and rating, guarantee terms and your best ad headlines. Test the headline first and the hero image second, and put returns or guarantee lines right under the button. Read LPG-0016, LPG-0067 and LPG-0038.

LPG.when: When you are building or fixing a product page that must answer the doubts that stop buyers.
LPG.tune: Feed it answers to 'what almost stopped you buying', support tickets and low-star reviews. Plan for phones first: thumbnails, rating above the title, and price, add to cart and risk reducers in the first screen. Read LPG-0034, LPG-0048 and LPG-0042.

LPG.when: When your page has reviews but visitors still leave before buying.
LPG.tune: Give it a review export with names and photos from your reviews app, plus your top buying objections. Choose each testimonial to answer one objection and show who wrote it, since bare logos and anonymous quotes now read as fake. Read LPG-0053, LPG-0037 and LPG-0062.

LPG.when: When your product page offers many pack sizes and most buyers still pick the smallest.
LPG.tune: Give it unit cost, shipping cost per pack and current pack choices from Shopify orders. Cut to three tiers, put the money saved in each option's title and check margin per tier before you test. Read LPG-0006, LPG-0008 and LPG-0035.

LPG.when: When your product photos are mostly pack shots and shoppers keep asking about size, use or fit.
LPG.tune: Give it the current gallery, the top questions from email and chat, and review quotes. More shoppers swipe the whole gallery than scroll the whole page, so let the images carry answers and proof. Read LPG-0060 and LPG-0034.

LPG.when: When you have an ad that works and want to know if a long article-style page is worth building.
LPG.tune: Give it results from the ad running to a plain product page: spend, cost per purchase against break-even and the angle used. Build an advertorial only once the plain page roughly breaks even, and match page length to how hard the ad already sells. Read LPG-0030, LPG-0029 and LPG-0004.

LPG.when: When the readiness check says go and you need a full advertorial written and checked for cold traffic.
LPG.tune: Ground it in customer research, a buyer sheet, an offer brief, a short belief list and real reviews. Keep one editorial voice from start to end and close with a soft check-availability step. Read LPG-0057, LPG-0044 and LPG-0025.

LPG.when: When your product needs matching to the buyer and ad traffic does not convert on a plain product page.
LPG.tune: Give it survey answers, review themes and which product suits which buyer. Treat the first three questions as the hook and test them first, and aim for about 30% of starters to reach the results page. Read LPG-0032, LPG-0019 and CRO-0004.

LPG.when: When your store has grown cluttered and shoppers reach product pages but few add to cart.
LPG.tune: Attach phone screenshots of home, collection, product and cart pages, plus click map data if you have it. Remove parts that get under about 1% of clicks, and hide the discount code box when no promotion is running. Read LPG-0043, LPG-0007 and LPG-0058.

LPG.when: When collection pages get visits but few clicks into products, often because popular sizes are sold out.
LPG.tune: Give it the product order of your top collection and stock by size from Shopify inventory. Paid visitors judge a collection by its top six products, so move broken-size items down every day. Read LPG-0069, LPG-0059 and LPG-0041.

LPG.when: When your menu is messy and your best products take too many taps to reach.
LPG.tune: Give it collections ranked by sales and menu clicks from your analytics. Put a bestsellers row at the top of the phone menu, use image categories and keep links that lead away from a product off product pages. Read LPG-0039, LPG-0061 and LPG-0071.

LPG.when: When your page copy is final and you need it turned into a Shopify page you can edit yourself.
LPG.tune: Paste the approved copy and name your theme so the sections read price from the product and never go stale. Install on a duplicate theme and check on a phone before publishing. Read LPG-0013 before adding a sticky buy button to a long page.

LPG.when: When one product carries the business and cold buyers need more than a short product page to believe it.
LPG.tune: It reads the market's sophistication from rival pages and writes one stage above it, digs the mechanism out of how the product is made, answers the six objections in the order buyers raise them, and ties every line to a file in a claims log.
LPG.title: Long-form sales page for a hero product
LPG.outcome: A full sales page draft (headline options, lead, story, mechanism, proof, offer, guarantee, FAQ, close) written to the buyer's awareness stage and the market's sophistication, with a claims log tying every line to a file, ready for annabel-landing-pages to build.

SPD.when: When a fix or landing page needs a Shopify section the theme lacks, or an app's widget could be built into the theme instead: editable sections built and tested on an unpublished copy of the theme.
SPD.tune: every section is built on an unpublished duplicate and must pass Theme Check, a full editor test and a three-run mobile speed comparison against the live theme before handover; it starts from a fix that has a gross profit figure; and the owner, not the agent, publishes.
SPD.title: Shopify theme section builder
SPD.outcome: new Shopify theme section files (Liquid, settings schema, locale entries, CSS and JavaScript) on an unpublished theme, with a settings table, test results, a preview link and a one-page owner guide.

SPD.when: When big images or hero videos slow the site, images make up most of the page weight, or before a photo or catalogue refresh. Not for a full speed check of a slow site.
SPD.tune: upload rules and served-size targets are kept apart, because Shopify already resizes and serves modern formats; the first image on each template is set to load early while the rest wait; every re-export starts from masters; and no file ships until it passes a side-by-side check on a real phone,...
SPD.title: Image and video speed pass
SPD.outcome: a one-page media rules sheet (upload size, file weight targets, formats, video rules) the team and photographers follow from now on, an offender list of the heaviest images and videos on the 5 key templates with the fix for each, the theme changes for an unpublished copy, a re-export plan for existing files, and before and after page weight with a quality check on a phone.

SPD.when: When the store has too many apps, app bills keep growing, speed tests blame third-party code, or uninstalled apps left code behind: keep, replace or remove for each app. Not for picking apps for a new store.
SPD.tune: each app's speed cost is measured by blocking its domains and re-running the lab test, not guessed from its reputation; app revenue claims are checked with a holdout or off week; data exports, a theme copy, a full flow test and a 14-day rollback come before any uninstall; and leftover code from...
SPD.title: Remove app bloat
SPD.outcome: an app and code inventory (every app and leftover snippet that touches the storefront, with its measured weight and speed cost, monthly bill and what it earns), a keep, replace or remove decision for each with the reason, a step-by-step cleanup plan with data exports and rollback, and before and after speed numbers.

SPD.when: When the owner says the store or site is slow, Core Web Vitals fail, after a theme or app change, or before a big traffic push.
SPD.tune: five templates chosen by real sessions, judged on field Core Web Vitals (with INP, not the retired FID) rather than a lab score; every fix measured on an unpublished theme copy with median-of-3 lab numbers before anyone publishes; fixes scored by metric crossed x reach / hours; tracking checked...
SPD.title: Shopify speed audit and fix list for a slow store
SPD.outcome: a speed scorecard for 5 key templates (field LCP, INP and CLS on mobile and desktop, plus median lab numbers), the cause behind each failing metric, and a fix list of 8 to 15 items ranked by impact and effort, each with before and after lab numbers from an unpublished theme copy, the owner, and the date to re-read field data.

SPD.when: When your Shopify store is slow and you want fixes made in the order that wins back the most orders.
SPD.tune: Give it PageSpeed reports for the home page, top collection and top product page, your app list and theme files. Fix images first, then outside scripts, then hosting. Read SPD-0002, SPD-0001 and SPD-0004.

SPD.when: When your mobile speed score is low or Search Console warns about Core Web Vitals.
SPD.tune: Run PageSpeed Insights on a home, collection and product page and paste all three with the field data. Field data is a rolling 28-day sample of real visits, so judge a fix on lab data now and field data a month later. Read SPD-0005 and SPD-0006.

SPD.when: When a speed audit lists many problems and you need to know which ones are worth the time.
SPD.tune: Give it the problem list plus monthly sessions, conversion rate and order value from Shopify. Size each payoff from your own field data and published cases, never from a promised lift. Read SPD-0004 and SPD-0002.

SPD.when: When you have many apps and a slow mobile score and want to know which apps cost the most speed.
SPD.tune: Paste your Apps list and the third-party code section of the PageSpeed report. Stores with few outside services score far better on mobile, so cut duplicate apps before you tune the rest. Read SPD-0001 and SPD-0011.

SPD.when: When you removed an app but its script still shows up in PageSpeed.
SPD.tune: Give it the files from a duplicate theme and the name of every app you have removed. Search the theme for each app's name and delete lines on the copy first. Read SPD-0009.

SPD.when: When the first big image on your page appears late and LCP is above 2.5 seconds.
SPD.tune: Give it the hero or slider section code and the LCP element named in PageSpeed. Load the first hero image right away with high priority and never fade it in. Read SPD-0006 and SPD-0008.

SPD.when: When a bar, badge or image pushes the page down as it loads.
SPD.tune: Give it the layout shift report and the page, and name any app that adds a bar or badge. App-added free-shipping bars are a common cause, so use a theme block or reserve the space. Read SPD-0007.

SPD.when: When scripts, styles or fonts block your first screen from showing on phones.
SPD.tune: Give it theme.liquid, the apps you are keeping and your font setup. Most app code enters through the theme head, so delay only scripts you can find and leave checkout and tracking code alone. Read SPD-0011 and SPD-0009.

SPD.when: When you are about to upload product or banner images, or your image files are over 1 MB.
SPD.tune: List file names, sizes and pixel widths from Shopify Files. Shopify only lightly compresses uploads, so size images to about twice their shown width and compress before you upload. Read SPD-0008 and SPD-0013.

SPD.when: When your homepage has sliders, autoplay video or quick view, and pages feel slow.
SPD.tune: Give it home and collection page screenshots plus the theme settings for sliders, video and quick view. Swap video embeds for a light thumbnail and remove quick view that loads every product's data. Read SPD-0010 and SPD-0012.

SPD.when: When a big sale or ad push is coming and you want speed checked and protected beforehand.
SPD.tune: Give it the sale date, current scores and any apps or banners planned for the sale. Set a limit per page and test again after each new app or banner. Read SPD-0005, and SPD-0003 for cart and checkout caching rules.

SPD.when: When your store runs on WooCommerce or another self-hosted system and pages are slow.
SPD.tune: Give it your host, caching plugin, plugin list and server response time. Never cache cart, checkout or account pages, and stop WooCommerce files loading on pages with no cart. Read SPD-0014 and SPD-0003.

SPD.when: When you add apps often and want speed checked the same way every month.
SPD.tune: Give it each month's PageSpeed reports and app list so it can compare with the month before. Under about 1,000 sessions a month, run the single report reader instead. Read SPD-0005 and SPD-0001.

SPD.when: When you want to think through what a shopper is waiting for on a slow page before anyone changes code.
SPD.tune: Describe the slow moment in plain words, such as the main product image showing late on a phone, and bring any trace you have. Ask for one small change that can be undone, with a stop rule, not a promised score. Read SPD-0006 and SPD-0004.

CRO.when: When a store sells through WhatsApp, Instagram DMs or site chat and the owner asks whether chat sales are working day to day: one page of chats, reply times, orders and profit from chat.
CRO.tune: it counts only chat orders that can be proven, reports chats lost to a closed WhatsApp window, shows contribution after messaging and staff cost instead of revenue, splits any change into chats, conversion and order value before naming a fix, and refuses to act on lost reasons from fewer than 20...
CRO.title: Chat sales daily report
CRO.outcome: a daily chat sales report (one screen: 10 numbers, 3 fixes for tomorrow) and the sheet behind it with a data tab, a lost-reasons tab and a 7-day trend, filled in about 15 minutes from the inbox labels and Shopify orders.

CRO.when: When too many orders are cash on delivery (COD) or come back unpaid (RTO), or before adding a COD fee or prepaid discount: COD rules and nudges that move buyers to pay online. Not for calling or messaging buyers to confirm COD orders.
CRO.tune: COD is valued per order placed after RTO and remittance costs, by cart value band; the prepaid incentive is priced against every prepaid order, not just converts; fees and conditions must show before the payment step to avoid drip pricing; and the policy is proven with switchback weeks read on...
CRO.title: Cash on delivery and prepaid checkout for India
CRO.outcome: a COD and prepaid policy sheet (COD limits, fee or no fee, prepaid incentive and its cap, advance rule if any), the exact nudge lines and where each appears, a settings list for Shopify or the store's checkout, and a 4 to 6 week switchback test plan with a keep or drop rule based on delivered gross profit per session.

CRO.when: When the owner wants to A/B test or split test one change on a product page, collection page, home page, cart or landing page, and needs the plan before it goes live. Not for reading a test that has finished.
CRO.tune: the go or no-go on testing is computed from the page's own weekly traffic before anyone builds a variant; the ship decision is gross profit per visitor with pay-on-delivery share and failed deliveries as guardrails; repairs are separated from tests; and a test that cannot finish in 6 weeks is turned into a bolder change...
CRO.title: Store A/B test design
CRO.outcome: one test plan sheet (one screen) for one store change, with the hypothesis, primary metric, guardrails, sample size per variant, run time in weeks from the store's real traffic, the stop rule and the ship rule, ready for the client to approve before anything goes live.

CRO.when: When product pages get views but few add to cart, before paying for more traffic to a product, or to know which pages to rework first: names the likely reason per product. Not for drop-off after add to cart.
CRO.tune: products are compared with their own product type median and a view floor, not one store average; traffic, device and stock causes are ruled out before anyone touches the page; each product gets one evidenced reason and one first fix, sized in gross profit a month; and products not worth the work...
CRO.title: Products with low add-to-cart rates
CRO.outcome: a ranked sheet of the products with enough views but a low view-to-cart rate (usually 5 to 15 products), each with its rate against the store median, the likely reason backed by evidence, the first fix to try, and the gross profit a month at stake, plus a short list of products to leave alone and why.

CRO.when: When people add to cart but leave at checkout, cart or checkout abandonment looks high, or after a checkout or app change: finds where and why buyers leave and ranks the fixes. Not for messages that win back abandoned carts.
CRO.tune: the leak is sized in orders and gross profit per month by device before any fix is named; the agent does three real phone checkouts and reads the payment gateway's own success rate, so failed wallet, bank or card payments are caught as repairs; and postcode, pay-on-delivery and one-time-code walls are checked alongside tax and wallet issues in every market.
CRO.title: Fix checkout drop-off
CRO.outcome: a leak map of the cart and checkout steps with orders lost at each, the cause behind each leak with its evidence, and a fix list of 5 to 12 items ranked by gross profit recovered per month, each marked repair (ship now) or test, with who makes it and the setting or copy to change.

CRO.when: When shoppers cannot find products: searchers convert poorly, the zero-result list is long, the menu has grown messy, or new categories were added.
CRO.tune: the store's own search terms are classed into eight query types and run on a phone before anything changes; most fixes are data fixes (synonyms, tags, metafields, redirects) rather than a new search tool; menu gaps are found from search demand; and words from the languages your buyers use, written in English letters...
CRO.title: Fix site search and navigation
CRO.outcome: a search term sheet (top terms classed by type and marked works, weak or fails), a ranked fix list of synonyms, product data, redirects, menu and filter changes with searches affected and gross profit at stake, and a before and after target for zero-result rate and searcher conversion.

CRO.when: When buyers in chat say it is too expensive or cheaper elsewhere, chats stall on price, or agents give away discounts to close.
CRO.tune: one question splits budget, worth and comparison before any answer; a smaller option protects margin before a concession is considered; the concession ladder is public, owner-signed and costed in gross profit per order; and cheaper-elsewhere claims are checked on total cost and like-for-like,...
CRO.title: Handle price objections in chat
CRO.outcome: a price objection kit: the diagnosis question, 9 written answers (3 per objection, short and full), a value fact sheet, a cheaper-elsewhere check, an owner-approved concession ladder with the gross profit cost of each step, and a tracker of price chats, closes and margin given away.

CRO.when: When buyers of expensive items such as jewellery, furniture or mattresses ask many questions, hesitate to pay, or want to see the product first: a booked consultation or video call that closes the sale.
CRO.tune: consults are switched on only where gross profit per call beats the cost of the call; the booking button sits only above a price line; the camera lists are specific to jewellery and furniture; and the close allows a clean no with one follow-up, never a chase or fake scarcity.
CRO.title: Consultation call for high-ticket products
CRO.outcome: a consult kit ready to run: a money check, booking page copy, a pre-call form, confirmation and reminder messages, a one-page prep sheet, a full call script with show-on-camera lists, three closes, a follow-up rule, and a tracker of calls, closes and gross profit per call.

CRO.when: When the store adds or rethinks live chat on the site, chat is busy but few chats turn into orders, or the chatbot annoys buyers: where chat shows, when to invite, when a person takes over. Not for writing the reply library.
CRO.tune: chat invites fire only on buying signals and never on checkout; every recommendation carries the buyer's own words and a real review; the bot is fenced to one-answer facts with hand-off triggers; and chat is judged on gross profit per session with chat on versus off, not on chat conversion.
CRO.title: Live chat pre-sale playbook
CRO.outcome: a one-page chat operating plan plus its working parts: a page-by-page trigger table, the opening lines, a 3-question discovery script, a recommendation formula with examples, a bot and hand-off rule card, a staffing grid by hour, and a 4-week test sheet that reads gross profit per session with chat on and off.

CRO.when: When mobile sales are far below desktop, after a theme change, or before sending more Instagram or TikTok traffic: a walk through the whole store on a real phone that records every blocker. Not for a data-led audit of all devices.
CRO.tune: five scripted buyer paths on a real mid-range phone over mobile data, not a resized desktop window; every issue weighted by how many mobile sessions see it and capped by the store's measured mobile gap in gross profit; and local checks (low-end Android, delivery checker, local payment methods, WhatsApp buttons) sit beside Safari and wallet checks.
CRO.title: Mobile conversion audit
CRO.outcome: a phone journey log with screenshots of 5 buyer paths, a blocker list (every issue rated blocker, major or minor) and a fix list of 10 to 20 items in order of gross profit at stake, each with the page, the fix, the owner and whether it is a repair or a test.

CRO.when: When a test has reached its planned end date and the owner asks whether it won, when someone claims a big win, or before rolling a variant out to all traffic.
CRO.tune: the verdict has four outcomes, including "invalid", with the split check done by hand from the export; the money is gross profit per visitor planned on the low end of the range; refunds returns and failed deliveries are counted by order cohort, after the return window; and the winner is rebuilt in the theme and...
CRO.title: Store A/B test readout
CRO.outcome: a one-page verdict (win, lose, unclear or invalid) on one finished store test, with the validity checks, lift and 95% range, gross profit impact per month, guardrail table, the ship decision and a 4-week watch plan, plus one row for the store's test log.

CRO.when: When carts are abandoned and the store has WhatsApp or SMS consent but no chat follow-up, or chat leads go quiet after getting a link: who to message, when, and how to answer replies. Not for writing message templates alone.
CRO.tune: quiet chat leads are recovered free inside the open window instead of with paid templates; each group is judged on extra gross profit from a holdout, not attributed revenue; message 1 helps rather than discounts; and Instagram is kept to replies because the platform does not allow cold DMs.
CRO.title: Recover carts by chat
CRO.outcome: a cart recovery plan for chat channels: an audience table, a timing card with at most two messages per cart, the written messages (opted-in WhatsApp, SMS, and quiet chat leads), a reply guide, a suppression list, a cost check and a holdout test sheet.

CRO.when: When the owner wants to see what visitors actually do on a page (session recordings, heatmaps, Hotjar or Clarity), traffic is too low to split test, or a page underperforms and nobody knows why.
CRO.tune: sessions are picked by segment with buyers as a comparison group, so behaviours buyers share are not mistaken for problems; every observation is coded on one tag sheet and a pattern needs at least 3 of 20 sessions plus a second kind of evidence; privacy masking and consent (EU, UK, US states and other markets) are checked before any session is watched.
CRO.title: Session recording and heatmap review
CRO.outcome: an observation log of 60 to 120 coded sessions, a pattern table (each behaviour with how often it appears, on which page and device), heatmap readings for the key pages, and a ranked fix list of 5 to 12 items, each with its evidence from two sources, gross profit at stake and whether it is a repair or a test idea.

CRO.when: When the owner wants bigger orders from cart and post-purchase offers: order value has stalled, an upsell app shows offers nobody takes, or a new slot such as post-purchase is added.
CRO.tune: pairings come from the store's own baskets (attach rate and lift) and second orders, not an app's generic suggestions; each slot gets one offer ranked by added gross profit after discount and shipping; mechanics that dark-pattern rules in the US, UK and EU treat as deceptive are banned up front.
CRO.title: Cart upsells and cross-sells
CRO.outcome: a pairing table (for each top product: the offer in each slot, its price, the rule behind it and the added gross profit per exposed order), a rules sheet the upsell app or theme can follow, a setup sheet ready for approval, and a holdout plan that shows after 4 weeks whether the offers really add profit.

CRO.when: When a store opens WhatsApp for sales, moves off the founder's personal phone to a business setup, or adds click-to-WhatsApp ads: profile, catalog, quick replies and labels. Not for broadcasts and marketing messages.
CRO.tune: the catalog is chosen by chat demand and gross profit, not uploaded whole; labels are a sales pipeline the daily report can count; every entry point carries its own source; and the account choice is costed against WhatsApp's 2026 pricing rather than picked by habit.
CRO.title: WhatsApp sales chat setup
CRO.outcome: a set-up WhatsApp sales channel ready for its first chats: account type chosen with the reason, profile filled, a catalog of 10 to 30 products, greeting and away messages, 15 to 25 quick replies loaded, 11 pipeline labels, hours and a reply target, tracked entry links for each source, and a signed-off 10-chat test sheet.

CRO.when: When new visitors do not trust the store: they convert poorly, ask 'is this legit?', or cold traffic is about to be sent.
CRO.tune: doubts are counted from the store's own surveys, tickets and reviews and sorted into eight buyer questions; every reassurance line must point to a dated fact the store can keep; fake counters, resetting timers and quote-less press logos go on a remove list; and each market's online seller disclosure rules are checked.
CRO.title: Trust and reassurance audit
CRO.outcome: a doubt map covering 8 buyer doubts across every page type, each with what the store shows now, the evidence buyers feel that doubt, and the exact reassurance line or element to add, where it goes and the fact or proof that makes it true; plus a top-10 action list in order of sales at stake and a short list of trust elements to remove because they are false or unprovable.

CRO.when: When chat orders are mostly single items, or agents push add-ons buyers resent: when and how to suggest one bundle, upgrade or add-on in a sales chat.
CRO.tune: each chat offer is ranked by added gross profit per offer made; the agent card says when not to suggest as clearly as when to; nothing is added without a yes and a read-back; and risky pay-on-delivery baskets stay small instead of being grown.
CRO.title: Upsell and cross-sell in chat
CRO.outcome: a chat offer sheet for the store's top products (one upgrade, one add-on and one bundle each, ranked by added gross profit), a when-and-when-not card, 3 wording patterns with filled examples, and a weekly tracker of offers, take rate, added gross profit and refunds.

CRO.when: When buyers seem unsure at cart or checkout, after shipping or returns changes, or tickets show doubt: writes the small words (delivery dates, COD notes, returns lines, error messages). Not for finding where buyers leave checkout.
CRO.tune: each line answers a counted doubt at the exact step it happens; delivery wording comes from the store's own 90th percentile transit data; every fee shows before the last step, in line with drip pricing rules in the US, UK and EU; and each line is mapped to what the store's Shopify plan can actually edit.
CRO.title: Cart, checkout and shipping microcopy
CRO.outcome: a microcopy sheet of 20 to 40 lines, each with its exact wording, its location (product page, cart drawer, cart page, checkout step, confirmation page, shipping email), the doubt it answers, its source policy or data, and how to edit it on the store's Shopify plan, ready for the client's approval and loading on a duplicate theme or in checkout settings.

CRO.when: When chat replies on WhatsApp, Instagram or site chat are slow, inconsistent or never ask for the order: 15 to 25 ready pre-sale replies. Not for price pushback or questions about existing orders.
CRO.tune: replies are ranked by the store's own chat counts, every one ends with an order step, each carries a dated fact source and a real review that answers the same doubt, and follow-ups are timed to WhatsApp's 24-hour window instead of paid templates.
CRO.title: Chat sales scripts
CRO.outcome: a reply library of 15 to 25 pre-purchase questions, ranked by how often buyers ask them, each with a short reply, a full reply, a clarifying question, a proof line, the fact source and the hand-off rule, ready to load as quick replies or saved replies.

CRO.when: When you have a test idea and need to know if your traffic and orders can prove it.
CRO.tune: Give it monthly orders, sessions and conversion rate for the page from Shopify and GA4. Under about 30 orders a month, do research instead of tests, and small stores should only test big changes. Read CRO-0011, CRO-0005 and CRO-0024.

CRO.when: When conversion is poor and you want proof of where and why before you test anything.
CRO.tune: Feed it GA4 funnel exports, Shopify sessions by device and the survey or recording tools you have. Check the purchase event first, since broken tracking sends the research the wrong way. Read CRO-0003, LPG-0040 and MEA-0002.

CRO.when: When you have heatmaps or session recordings and do not know what to look for.
CRO.tune: Export scroll maps, click maps and rage click rates from Microsoft Clarity or Hotjar for your top product and collection pages. Treat rage clicks under 1 to 2% of sessions as normal and look for sections that get many clicks but few viewers. Read CRO-0022, CRO-0023 and LPG-0051.

CRO.when: When shoppers visit your product page but few add to cart and you do not know why.
CRO.tune: Say what you sell and how many orders you get a day, then run the on-page survey on the product page with the biggest drop. Turn the top answers into test ideas, not instant fixes. Read LPG-0042 and CRO-0018.

CRO.when: When you want buyers to tell you what made them buy and what almost stopped them.
CRO.tune: Keep the thank-you page survey to two questions: what made you buy today, and what almost stopped you. Feed the near-miss answers into test ideas and page copy, and list AI assistants in the how-did-you-hear question. Read CRO-0018, LPG-0042 and AEO-0020.

CRO.when: When you have more test ideas than traffic and need to choose by evidence, not opinion.
CRO.tune: Paste each idea with the research behind it, plus traffic and gross profit per order. Rank by expected gross profit: chance of a win, likely lift, profit per order and traffic exposed, minus build cost. Read CRO-0013, CRO-0012 and CRO-0020.

CRO.when: When your store has modest traffic and small tests keep ending with no clear winner.
CRO.tune: Give it monthly sessions and orders and your top pages by revenue. Below about 300,000 sessions a month, test whole new pages, offers or product page redesigns rather than small tweaks. Read CRO-0019, CRO-0001 and CRO-0011.

CRO.when: When you want to run a test on Shopify and need to know what your plan and tools allow.
CRO.tune: Tell it your Shopify plan, theme and testing app. Stores not on Plus cannot test checkout with browser tools, flicker can inflate a variant's lift, and the same product should never be sold at two test prices. Read CRO-0016, CRO-0008 and CRO-0009.

CRO.when: When the owner wants to test whether one Meta ad, offer, page or audience beats another, or whether to trust a past test.
CRO.tune: Give it daily spend, cost per purchase and purchase volume from Ads Manager so the test is sized honestly. Use a Meta A/B test or a lift study instead of comparing two ad sets by eye. Read CRO-0005, CRO-0015 and MEA-0033.
CRO.title: Test design for a store's Meta ads
CRO.outcome: a sized Meta test plan with the question, hypothesis, budget, dates, cell setup and decision rules, or a clear answer that the store is too small to test, plus a test log row.

CRO.when: When a test has ended and you need to know if the result is real before you roll it out.
CRO.tune: Give it visitors, orders and revenue for each version by day, plus the planned sample size and dates. Check for an uneven traffic split and early stopping, and judge on revenue or profit per visitor, not conversion rate alone. Read CRO-0007, CRO-0017 and CRO-0010.

CRO.when: When you tested offers or bundles and need to know which one earns more profit per visitor.
CRO.tune: Paste sessions, orders and revenue for each offer with unit cost, shipping and the cost of any gift or discount. A bigger pack or gift can lift revenue while cutting profit, and revenue per visitor needs far more traffic to read. Read CRO-0014 and MEA-0047.

CRO.when: When you test often and want one log that ranks ideas, runs one test at a time and reads each result.
CRO.tune: Give it your store numbers each month and every test's dates and results as they end. Expect most tests to lose, since a 30 to 35% win rate is very good. Read CRO-0020, CRO-0012 and CRO-0015.

CRO.when: When you shipped several test winners and total sales did not rise to match.
CRO.tune: Name the changes or channel you doubt and give it traffic and order counts. Hold a share of visitors back from all shipped winners for a few weeks to see what they really add together. Read CRO-0012 and MEA-0033.

CRO.when: When you want a second view on a page's message or a test plan, grounded in what buyers say.
CRO.tune: Bring the page, the survey answers and the test plan, and ask it to challenge the hypothesis before anything is built. Do not use it for exact statistics; pair it with the verdict check. Read CRO-0003 and LPG-0042.

CRO.when: When a test lift looks too good to be true and you need to explain the uncertainty in plain words.
CRO.tune: Give it the result ranges, sample sizes and the claim someone wants to make from the test. Ask it to say what the numbers do not show before anyone plans around the lift. Read CRO-0012, CRO-0006 and CRO-0017.

MCR.when: When a batch of ad images is about to be made or shot and past versions came out too alike or too random, or nobody knows which look sells. Sets mood, light, angle and photo style. Not for the image prompt for one ad.
MCR.tune: styles ranked on gross profit per ad from the store's own results, with production cost and a store-side order check; a spread rule that separates big and small settings so variants count; a truth gate that keeps AI away from products judged on colour, texture or fit; a batch size capped by what...
MCR.title: Visual direction for an ad batch
MCR.outcome: a visual direction for one ad batch: a main, test and avoid photo style chosen from the store's own results, a lock or vary spec for every variant, and a contact sheet, ready for designers or image tools.

MCR.when: When an ad idea or image is ready and the owner wants ad text to test: three to five full copy versions, each answering a different buyer doubt, for Meta, Google or TikTok. Not for headlines only, or for coming up with the ad idea.
MCR.tune: each set is tied to a ranked buying objection and a dated facts row, so the test teaches which argument sells; a line-by-line compliance pass covers Meta, FTC, ASA and local ad rules before the owner sees it; and the number of sets comes from test cash and target cost per purchase, read on store orders.
MCR.title: Ad copy test sets
MCR.outcome: three to five complete ad copy sets for one concept, each answering a different buying objection, with a compliance log and a test plan for the first two sets, ready to load into Meta, Google or TikTok.

MCR.when: When the layout, look and words for one ad are approved and the image is about to be made in an AI image tool, or AI images keep drifting off brand. Writes the one ready prompt. Not for making the finished ad files.
MCR.tune: a model choice made by what the image needs, with the real product photo always as the reference; a hard rule that no review, rating, customer or price is ever generated; a version ID and reason-coded log that turns approvals into brand prompt rules; a link from each approved image to its ad ID...
MCR.title: Ad image prompt compiler
MCR.outcome: one copyable, model-ready image prompt for one ad, a separate avoid list, the reference files to attach, a recommended image tool with a fallback, and an updated prompt log, ready to generate.

MCR.when: When many new Facebook and Instagram ads launch but Meta spends on only a few, or results stall because new ads look too much like old ones. Scores how different the live ads really are. Not for the keep or cut call on each ad.
MCR.tune: diversity is weighted by spend, not counted by ads; every weakness carries spend and gross profit at risk per month from the store's own target cost per purchase; targets scale with the store's spend band instead of a fixed format count; and Meta's own flags are recorded while our clusters are...
MCR.title: Look-alike ad check for an online store
MCR.outcome: a diversity score for the live Meta ads, a cluster table of near-identical ads weighted by spend, a fingerprint sheet, a risk table and a ranked production queue of briefs for the next creative round.

MCR.when: When an ad sells once people watch but its first seconds fail to stop the scroll, and it needs new hooks to test: the opening line, on-screen text and first visual. Also for briefing creators and voice talent.
MCR.tune: openers are ranked by the store's own past results by tactic and voice, judged on store cost per purchase; every spoken line goes to a real person who can say it truthfully, with synthetic audio kept to internal previews; the batch passes a repetition check and an approved-claims check; and a...
MCR.title: Ad opener writer for an online store
MCR.outcome: a ranked table of openers (spoken line, on-screen text, first visual, voice and delivery notes) for an ad body that already sells, with recording sheets per speaker and a test plan, saved as one file.

MCR.when: When designers, creators or AI tools need real ad examples to brief from (a swipe file of good ads sorted by type), or the library needs its monthly refresh. Not for what named rivals run now, or the category's long-running ad formulas.
MCR.tune: every offer entry is priced against the store's own gross profit per purchase before anyone briefs from it; run length is read with the Ad Library's real limits (live-only outside the EU, no spend shown, retargeting look-alikes); the library keeps links and our notes, never copies; and size is...
MCR.title: Ad swipe library for an online store
MCR.outcome: a sorted swipe library sheet and folder index of ads worth learning from, a list of real gaps, and brief starters naming which entries and elements to borrow for the next three briefs.

MCR.when: When the owner wants a UGC or influencer-style video ad but has no creator, budget or time, and an AI presenter could stand in. Gives the script, hooks, presenter and clip prompts. Not for new openers on a video ad that already sells.
MCR.tune: it first asks whether real buyers or a priced creator would beat an AI presenter; the presenter is barred from first-person buyer claims and every outcome is a sourced real review shown on screen; stills are approved before any video spend; and the ad must beat the store's best current video on...
MCR.title: Creator-style video ad with an AI presenter
MCR.outcome: a production-ready creator-style video ad package: a locked script with hook variations, a presenter reference set with slot map, clip-by-clip prompt cards or a creator brief, a QC log and a test plan.

MCR.when: When a video ad that sells is losing reach or its hook rate is falling, and the owner wants about ten fresh talking-presenter hooks without a new shoot. Not for a whole new creator-style ad, or openers with no one speaking.
MCR.tune: openers are only made for a body that already hit target cost per purchase; angles come from the account's hook rate and purchases together; AI presenters may never speak as customers and carry market-by-market disclosure; and every clip passes a product-accuracy check before it reaches the owner.
MCR.title: Talking-presenter openers for a proven ad body
MCR.outcome: about ten talking-presenter openers for a proven video ad body, each with a line, cue word and prompt card or phone brief, plus a QC log and a round-by-round test plan.

MCR.when: When a launch, season or sale needs fresh lifestyle or campaign photos for one product, on brand and in every size for site, email, ads and social. Works with a real shoot, creators or AI. Not for planning a cheap phone shoot at home.
MCR.tune: the cast comes from counted customer evidence, not a mood board; products are gated on gross profit per purchase and stock for the campaign's length; shots differ by person and situation so they add real reach; and every frame passes a logged product, hands, faces and claims check before the...
MCR.title: Campaign photo set
MCR.outcome: a finished campaign photo set for one product, in folders by ratio for site, email, ads and social, with truth and casting sheets, a shot list, a check log, a review deck and a rights register.

MCR.when: When all the store's ads look the same, or it is entering a new category and wants the ad formats that keep running for others (from the Meta Ad Library and TikTok) before making ads. Not for what named rivals run right now.
MCR.tune: formulas need three ads from two advertisers and run length is always labelled a proxy; every formula is checked against the store's product, allowed claims and production capacity; formats are compared on expected gross profit per creative from the store's own margin; and the report links to...
MCR.title: Category ad formula teardown
MCR.outcome: an HTML report and ad log of the category's long-running ad formulas, a formula table with confidence and store fit, and adaptation briefs for the top three, ready for a creator or editor.

MCR.when: When the store keeps making the same kinds of ads and wants a running plan of which buyer, stage and theme combinations are still untested, updated before each batch. Not for a one-off deep dive when results stall, or for producing the batch.
MCR.tune: cells are ranked by the gross profit per purchase of the product promoted times buyer share and proof strength, not by emptiness; a cell is only "dead" after two distinct concepts fail at full spend checked against store orders; near-duplicates are collapsed so the grid shows real variety; and...
MCR.title: Creative gap grid
MCR.outcome: an updated creative grid of buyer type, awareness stage and theme showing each cell's status and results, a ranked list of open cells, and this month's production list with a naming rule.

MCR.when: When cost per purchase has risen for weeks, new ads are not fixing it, and the team feels it has tried everything. A one-off deep dive into what the ad account has and has not really tested. Not for the monthly planning grid.
MCR.tune: the tested list comes from the account and a lane counts as tested only after 3x target cost per purchase, so under-tested ideas are not written off; untested lanes are scored on buyer size, the gross profit per purchase of the product, proof held and policy risk, with proof or policy failures...
MCR.title: Creative gap map for an online store
MCR.outcome: a one-off map of what the ad account has and has not tested, lane scores, five brief cards, the top ten gaps and a revival list, saved as a dated gap map file and concept history.

MCR.when: When the store is sending product to a creator, influencer or customer and needs a natural-sounding UGC video script and brief to send, with shots, alternate hooks, usage rights and disclosure. Not for the shoot day plan: this writes the script.
MCR.tune: every claim must pass two checks, the store's approved list and what this creator has actually experienced; the creator fee is shown against gross profit per purchase as orders needed to pay it back; and the brief carries the logistics that decide whether the video can ever run as an ad: raw...
MCR.title: Creator video script for an online store
MCR.outcome: a creator video script table with exact lines, on-screen text and shots, a claims check, delivery notes, a shot list, alternate openers, and a creator brief ready to send once approved.

MCR.when: When the owner asks what rivals say and offer everywhere (Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, Google and Amazon) to find crowded and open angles before a creative batch, launch or sale. Not for Meta-only rival ad research or one rival product.
MCR.tune: it maps rivals on Shopping, Search and Amazon as well as social, with free tools; every finding carries an expiry date; open lanes must pass the store's own evidence before they become briefs; and every rival offer is priced against the store's gross profit per purchase before anyone suggests...
MCR.title: Cross-channel competitor map
MCR.outcome: a dated map of rival ads and offers across Meta, TikTok, Google and Amazon: a rival list, ad log, marketplace table, theme heat map, offer check and five to seven briefs for open lanes.

MCR.when: When a new ad needs its opening image decided, or a strong ad has a weak first frame that does not stop the scroll. Mocks up and checks frames at phone size for image or video ads. Not for the hook words or opener clips.
MCR.tune: two or three frames are mocked up and checked at real phone size for a one-second read, contrast and safe zones before one is chosen; the product is always a real photo and every number on the frame must match the live page today; and the pattern is picked from the concept's awareness stage and...
MCR.title: First frame design for an online store
MCR.outcome: a frame spec for the chosen first-frame pattern at 4:5 and 9:16, a candidate check table, mock-up files and a short phone-shoot path, ready for a designer or editor.
