MCR.when: When an ad idea is chosen and the open question is the headline: five truly different headlines with character counts for Meta, Google, Shopping and TikTok. Also for Google ad or landing page headlines. Not for full ad copy sets.
MCR.tune: the number of headlines comes from test cash and target cost per purchase, not a fixed count; every line must match a dated facts row and a real customer phrase; one character table covers Meta, Google and TikTok at once; and the winner is read on store orders, never on CTR.
MCR.title: Headline angle set for one concept
MCR.outcome: five truly different headlines for one concept with character counts for Meta, Google, Shopping and TikTok, a list of struck lines, an optional Google pack and a test plan for the first pair.

MCR.when: When the store needs a batch of polished image ads for new customers and AI tools keep misspelling or burying the text. Builds a clean base image with real type set on top. Not for a quick set of ads from one product photo.
MCR.tune: a real money forecast (test spend, daily budget, expected winners) before any image is made; a read zone that fits both the 4:5 crop and Meta's Reels caption band; a free automatic check for overlap, safe zones, size and contrast; insights admitted only with two sources.
MCR.title: Layered static production
MCR.outcome: 4 to 12 finished cold-audience statics as PNG files at 1080 x 1920 and 1080 x 1350, with HTML sources, a layout check file, a buyer profile, angle and concept tables and a test spend forecast.

MCR.when: When buyers do not get why the product works and the owner wants an animated explainer video ad that shows the problem, then the product as the fix, with the science checked first.
MCR.tune: nothing is produced until each link of the mechanism has a primary source that applies to this product's dose or design; a second check catches visuals that overclaim; the destination page is matched to the opening; and the film is judged against the store's best video on store orders.
MCR.title: Animated mechanism explainer ad
MCR.outcome: a production package for a 30 to 40 second animated explainer ad: a checked source log, an angle table, a timed script, a style card, shot cards, a freelancer brief, a QC log and a test plan.

MCR.when: When the owner asks which new ads to make next month, or the account needs its next month of ads and nobody knows how many it needs or can afford to test.
MCR.tune: batch size set by the lowest of test budget, spend-level need and team capacity instead of a fixed count; slots only for products with known gross profit and stock; a duplicate filter on concept key and big visual settings before anything is made; weekly launches with read dates and a keep or cut...
MCR.title: Monthly ad batch sprint
MCR.outcome: a sized monthly ad batch with a plan table, one brief card per ad, finished files at 1080 x 1350 and 1080 x 1920 or a prompt file, and a weekly launch schedule with read dates.

MCR.when: When the owner says "make more ads like the ones that worked": the account has clear winning ads and needs more in that style, or a new product should borrow it. Not for refreshing one tired winner.
MCR.tune: winners chosen by gross profit per ad on new customers with a Shopify check, not from memory; a style profile built by comparing winners with losers, so it holds only traits that earn; a plan sized by the test budget and split into remakes, fixes and new ideas; a stock gate on the target product.
MCR.title: New ads from the store's own winners
MCR.outcome: a winners table checked against store orders, a trait table, a saved visual style profile, a concept plan, and new statics at 1080 x 1350 and 1080 x 1920 with pre-launch verdicts.

MCR.when: When a new ad or batch is finished and the owner asks "is this ready to run?" before any money is spent. Checks the muted opening, claims, proof, call to action, landing page, policy and size. Not for the ad account setup checks at launch.
MCR.tune: hard checks that tie every claim to a dated proof row and every price to a same-day page capture; an offer check that needs the product's gross profit per purchase; a log that pairs each verdict with store-side results and changes the checks only after enough ads; a manual path and a model path...
MCR.title: Pre-launch ad check
MCR.outcome: a pass or fail verdict on six checks for every draft ad, fix notes for each failing line or frame, a prelaunch log CSV and a list of claims the owner must prove or drop.

MCR.when: When the store has one good product photo and needs a few ad images from it this week, in every size for Meta, TikTok, Pinterest and Google. Not for resizing an approved ad, or a bigger pack of images for posts.
MCR.tune: the product is always the original photo, checked side by side at magnification and by a free automated comparison; every word is checked character by character against approved copy; every platform size is its own layout; images go only to products the store profits on and can ship.
MCR.title: Ad image variations from one product photo
MCR.outcome: three to six ad image variations from one product photo, built for every placement the store runs, in one folder per placement, with an asset manifest, an edit log and copyable prompts where needed.

MCR.when: When the owner asks for new ad ideas: the queue is empty or every new idea copies the winner, and the team needs ranked directions today, each backed by proof the store holds. Not for angles mined only from reviews.
MCR.tune: ideas start from a dated inventory of the store's real proof and anything it cannot back drops out; proof strength counts double in the rank next to the gross profit per purchase of the product; stock and policy filters run before scoring; and the list ends with the proof to collect next, so the...
MCR.title: Proof-scored ad ideas for an online store
MCR.outcome: a ranked table of ad ideas the store can prove, a parked list of the next eight, a dropped list with reasons, a proof inventory and the proof to get next, saved as one dated file.

MCR.when: When the owner wants new static image ads for a product and has no designer, or the account keeps running the same two or three formats.
MCR.tune: formats chosen from a scan of the store's own ad mix rather than taste; a proof requirement per format that blocks fake reviews and unpriced offers; outside ads used for structure only; a format scorecard graded on store-side purchases and hit rate, so the next pick is better.
MCR.title: Proven static formats on the store's own product
MCR.outcome: a static ad built from one of twelve proven formats on the store's real product, with an ad spec or review deck, files at 1080 x 1350 and 1080 x 1920, and a gap table showing why that format.

MCR.when: When the product needs explaining and the owner wants a podcast-style video ad where two hosts talk through a buyer's doubt and its answer, clearly labelled as staged.
MCR.tune: the conversation must resolve a real objection from the store's own reviews; it is labelled as staged and paid on screen and never borrows a real show; a written consistency spec and a frame-pair checker hold the hosts steady across clips; and the ad is judged against the store's best video on...
MCR.title: Staged podcast-clip ad
MCR.outcome: a production package for a staged two-host podcast-clip ad: a timed script, a host reference grid and consistency spec, clip cards, an editing recipe and a test plan.

MCR.when: When an image ad's idea and words are approved and need a layout before design: where the product, headline, proof and button go in each size. Also when a finished ad keeps getting cropped or covered. Not for resizing a finished ad.
MCR.tune: zones measured in pixels inside each platform's safe area and checked to add up; a worked shared box that tells you when one master can serve feed and Reels; a free wireframe render that tests overlap and phone readability before design; an offer zone that only exists once the offer's break-even...
MCR.title: Static ad layout blueprint
MCR.outcome: three or four layout variants for a static ad with pixel-measured zones inside each placement's safe area, wireframe PNGs with HTML source, designer notes and a recommended variant.

MCR.when: When a new image ad for cold buyers is next and drafts keep coming out as a product in the middle of a nice background. Decides the idea, headline and visual twist before any prompt. Not for the layout or the image prompt.
MCR.tune: headlines built from exact customer phrases before any picture; a stop type that must filter for buyers rather than grab everyone; a history check that blocks remakes of the store's own losers and near-copies of live ads; a log that ties each idea to store-side results.
MCR.title: The visual idea behind a static ad
MCR.outcome: one concept card for a static ad that sets the buyer's problem, angle, headline, reason why and visual idea, with five test results, a history check and a log row, before any prompt is written.

MCR.when: When the account's ads all look alike and the owner wants to try a fun animated format, like clay, comic or a talking product, testing one scene before paying for the full ad.
MCR.tune: the format is a capped bet that cannot outrank the proven baseline; one scene is tested before a full film is made; the verdict is gross profit per ad after production cost, not novelty or clicks; and the real product stays exact at the reveal in every style.
MCR.title: Stylised animated ad formats, tested one scene first
MCR.outcome: a one-scene test of a clay, comic or talking-product ad format, with a scene table, style card, prompt cards, a stage 1 result against the current format, and a money table.

MCR.when: When video ads spend but do not sell, people drop off, and nobody knows if the hook or the middle is failing. Says keep, fix or cut per video and which seconds to re-edit. Not for the daily TikTok ad check.
MCR.tune: the sort uses store-side cost per purchase against the store's own target before attention, so a selling video is never re-edited; bars come from the account's own medians by placement, with one hold definition; leaks are placed in seconds from the quartile drops; and fixes are ranked by gross...
MCR.title: Video ad retention fix for an online store
MCR.outcome: a keep, fix or cut verdict for each video ad with spend, second-by-second edit sheets for the ones to fix, and an approval list, saved as a report and a verdicts CSV.

MCR.when: When the store launches new Facebook, Instagram or TikTok ads most weeks and the owner asks what to make this week, chosen on results. Plans the week's slots, briefs and replacements for tired winners. Not for a whole month's batch or a quarter's roadmap.
MCR.tune: concepts are ranked by the expected gross profit of the product they sell, not by ROAS; test slots are counted from the store's own target cost per purchase so no test is launched that cannot reach a read; a repeat checker rejects lost angles against a logged concept key; and every tired winner...
MCR.title: Weekly creative sprint for an online store
MCR.outcome: a weekly creative plan: a slot table sized to the budget, one brief card per slot, successors for tired winners, a repeat checker log, an updated angle log and a numbered approval list.

MCR.when: When a video ad that sells needs fresh hooks that work with the sound off and need no presenter: satisfying close-ups from the product's world, like pouring or folding. Not for talking-presenter openers.
MCR.tune: every moment must link to a benefit in real reviews, so attention converts; a frame-by-frame product and physics check with a free tool rejects any drift before the owner sees it; and each new opener must beat the current one on store-side cost per purchase, not hook rate.
MCR.title: Wordless openers from the product's world
MCR.outcome: about ten five-second wordless vertical openers from the product's world, with a moment table, shot cards, a frame check log and a test plan against the control opener.

MCR.when: When product photos are few, messy or mixed, products get rejected in Google Shopping or the Meta catalogue, or before listing on Amazon or another channel. Builds plain, text-free product photos that meet each channel's rules. Not for redoing a product page gallery.
MCR.tune: it decides the base set per sales channel instead of one generic shoot; it fills gaps in order of gross profit per purchase; it never lets a tool redraw the product and logs a five-point fidelity check for every file; and it leaves a named, registered library that later jobs reuse.
MCR.title: Product image library by channel
MCR.outcome: an audit of every product's base images against each channel's rules, a shot plan for the gaps, a fidelity log and an asset register CSV, so plain product photos are ready for every channel.

MCR.when: When the store has 20 or more ads with results and the owner asks what its winning ads have in common, part by part. Builds a house checklist and a remake map for one winner. Not for the verdict on one test.
MCR.tune: the checklist is learned from the store's own winners and losers on store cost per purchase, with sample minimums and an honest association-not-cause label; a part only counts if it appears clearly before most viewers leave; proof only counts if it is on the approved claims list; and the ask and...
MCR.title: Ad structure map for an online store
MCR.outcome: a part-by-part comparison of the store's winning and losing ads, a house checklist backed by evidence, ad maps of every judged ad, a remake map for one winner and a fix list for losers still spending.

MCR.when: When the owner wants a video ad made with AI over several scenes or clips, or AI clips keep changing the product, person or look between shots. Locks the look and plans each clip. Not for a creator-style talking ad.
MCR.tune: four cards are locked and pasted unchanged into every prompt; every clip starts from an approved still so spend goes only on frames the client has seen; the hero product shot is always real footage or a real photo composite; and person references need signed consent, with no AI presenter ever...
MCR.title: Shot list for an AI-made video ad
MCR.outcome: one scene-by-scene plan for an AI-made video ad: four locked cards (product, person, style, voice), a scene table with a first-frame prompt and a motion prompt per clip, continuity rules, a spend cap, and a review log, ready to generate in any image and video tool.

MCR.when: When the product makes a visible or measurable difference, when competitors run comparison ads, or after an ad was rejected for misleading or health claims. Not for everyday static ads that show no before-and-after or comparison.
MCR.tune: every number or photo on the ad is traced to an evidence file and rewritten down to what that file says; objects are preferred over bodies to show the change; charts carry their sample and source on the ad itself; and every risky layout ships with a policy-safe backup so one rejection does not...
MCR.title: Before-and-after and comparison chart ads
MCR.outcome: a claim-to-evidence sheet and 3 to 5 static ad specs (layout, every word, data labels, source line, policy notes), each with a policy-safe backup version, ready for a designer to build and for the client to approve.

MCR.when: When an ad test has finished and the owner asks "which ad won?", before moving a winner into the main campaign, or when the team argues. Calls each idea win, lose or not enough data on store profit. Not for designing the test.
MCR.tune: every verdict is on store-matched purchases and gross profit after ad cost, with a spend bar set in the store's own money; tests that changed mid-window, sale-week distortion and refused pay-on-delivery orders are handled before anyone calls a winner; and each verdict turns into three named next ads that...
MCR.title: Creative test readout
MCR.outcome: a one-page readout with every tested concept marked win, lose or not enough data on store gross profit after ad cost, the reason in one line, and the next three ads to make from each concept, plus a learning log row per concept for the tag sheet.

MCR.when: When a video ad is about to launch and nobody has watched it muted, people scroll with sound off, or text keeps getting hidden by buttons. Writes captions and on-screen text, including Hindi or Hinglish.
MCR.tune: it starts and ends with a muted test by a fresh viewer, not a style checklist; it writes a headline layer that carries the point before word-for-word captions; safe zones are checked frame by frame with each platform's own overlay rather than one remembered number; and the script for each buyer language is chosen per audience.
MCR.title: Captions and on-screen text for sound-off viewing
MCR.outcome: a caption and text sheet for one video ad: a muted-watch record, a timed headline layer, a word-accurate caption file (SRT), style rules for size, contrast and position, and a safe-zone check for each placement, ready for the editor to apply.

MCR.when: When the owner wants "us versus them" ads and the product truly beats rivals on price per use, materials, warranty or a test, without a takedown, a rejected ad or a legal letter.
MCR.tune: the comparison target is chosen per market, with the stricter rules on denigration and implied rivals (UK, EU and others) handled up front; every line carries dated evidence for both sides and a recheck date, because a rival's price change can make a live ad false; tax is stated the same way on both sides; and...
MCR.title: Us-versus-them comparison ads
MCR.outcome: three to five comparison ad concepts (hook, comparison line, visual, proof shown, must-nots, market), a claims sheet with dated evidence for both sides of every comparison, and a list of lines that need a lawyer's eye before they run. This is general practice, not legal advice.

MCR.when: When ad names are a mix of dates, initials and "final v2", and nobody can tell which angles, creators or formats win. Sets one naming rule, tags and UTMs that link ads to store orders. Not for UTM setup across all channels.
MCR.tune: the concept ID ties each ad to its brief and result; names are checked by a formula, not by memory; the ad name travels into Shopify orders through UTMs so tags can be read on store gross profit, not platform return; language and AI use are fields, which multilingual stores and disclosure rules need;...
MCR.title: Ad naming and tagging system
MCR.outcome: one naming rule (written out with examples) for campaigns, ad sets and ads; a tag sheet with a fixed code list for every field; a check formula that flags bad names; UTM settings that carry the ad name to store orders; and a results tab that sorts gross profit after ad cost by any tag.

MCR.when: When the store has happy buyers but no video reviews, or creator ads feel staged, and the owner wants real customer testimonial videos with consent. Gives the ask messages, release form, questions and edit template. Not for collecting written reviews.
MCR.tune: the thank-you is fixed before any video arrives so it can never depend on what the customer says; every testimonial is tagged to the buying objection it answers; edits cut for length but never join words; and the ask runs through consented post-delivery journeys, including WhatsApp templates in...
MCR.title: Customer testimonial videos
MCR.outcome: a working testimonial system: an ask list of customers, three ready ask messages (email, WhatsApp, box insert), a release form, a one-page recording guide, eight interview questions, an edit template that turns each video into a 20 to 40 second ad, and a rights log, ready for the client to approve and start sending.

MCR.when: When raw creator or founder footage has arrived and the owner wants several ads from it, an editor keeps returning one ad per shoot, or a test needs comparable versions. Plans five cuts that differ on purpose. Not for organic Reels and Shorts edits.
MCR.tune: the five variants are designed as three clean reads (opener, length, ending) instead of five random edits; every ending uses only the live offer and real review counts; and the read-out judges each ad on store purchases and gross profit after the shoot cost, not on click rate.
MCR.title: Five ads from one shoot
MCR.outcome: an edit plan for five video ads from one shoot: a footage log, a variant matrix (opener x length x ending), a timed cut sheet per ad, export settings and a naming row for each, ready to hand to any editor.

MCR.when: When the owner wants a carousel (swipe) ad: a product needs more than one image to explain, a single image ad is not selling, or to show a bundle, routine or range. Plans 3 to 7 cards.
MCR.tune: the carousel's job is chosen before any card is drawn; card 1 is written three ways and tested as a standalone ad while the rest stay fixed; the story lives on the image because Meta cuts card text at about 20 characters; and the winner is read on cost per purchase against the product's own...
MCR.title: Carousel ad that tells a story
MCR.outcome: a carousel spec sheet with 3 to 7 cards, each with its job, on-image words, image direction, card headline, description and link; the primary text; and a first-card test plan with two or three opening cards, ready for a designer or image tool to build at 1:1 (and 4:5 where the placement allows).

MCR.when: When the store runs or is about to launch Meta catalog ads (dynamic product ads, Advantage+ catalog) with plain product shots, or catalog ads show old sale prices. Designs frames, price and badge overlays. Not for setting up the catalog campaign.
MCR.tune: every badge is a written rule tied to a feed field, so it switches off by itself when it stops being true; the Google image stays clean while Meta gets the frame; sale prices cannot outlive the sale because dates are a gate; and loss-making products are kept out of prospecting before any design...
MCR.title: Catalog ad frames and overlays
MCR.outcome: 2 to 3 frame templates (transparent PNG layouts with zones marked), a badge and overlay rule table tied to feed fields and product sets, and a filled audit sheet listing every product in the catalog with the badges it may show, ready for the media buyer to switch on.

MCR.when: When a sale, festival offer, launch or seasonal promotion needs banners for the homepage, announcement bar, email and ads, all with the same terms and end date. Not for arranging the homepage and collections.
MCR.tune: one locked offer sheet feeds every banner and is checked against a real test checkout; the hero has a weight budget and loads first; the post-sale hero and swap-out times are made before the sale starts; and sale marks stay off the product images that feed Google and Meta.
MCR.title: Sale banners and homepage hero
MCR.outcome: a locked offer sheet plus 8 to 10 finished banner specs for one promotion (desktop hero, mobile hero, announcement bar, collection banner, email header, Meta 4:5 and 9:16 statics, and the post-sale replacement hero), with exact words, sizes, file limits and a swap-out schedule.

MCR.when: When the store has a real origin story but its ads sound like every other brand, or the founder will record once and wants many ads from it. Writes three founder video scripts with hooks.
MCR.tune: every line of the founder's story carries a proof file or gets cut before a script exists; the founder can be on camera, a voice, a pile of evidence or a labelled stand-in, so shyness never blocks the ad; one recording session is planned to yield dozens of hook and body versions and a second...
MCR.title: Founder story ads
MCR.outcome: three founder ad concepts and their timed scripts (30 to 60 seconds each, with 3 to 5 hook options per script), a story fact sheet with a proof file or a cut for every claim, and a one-page recording plan for a single session.

MCR.when: When any AI-made or AI-edited image or video is about to be used in an ad, product page, email or marketplace, and needs checking that the product looks right. Catches wrong logos, labels, colours, shapes and text. Not for making the images.
MCR.tune: video is checked by a fixed frame rule that catches mid-motion drift; generated seals, ratings and prices are treated as false claims, not design flaws; each defect has the cheapest repair route, usually putting the real product or real text back in; and drifting prompts are retired so the same...
MCR.title: Product accuracy check for AI images and video
MCR.outcome: a signed accuracy check for each generated image or clip: a product truth card, a frame sampling rule, a 12-point pass or fail sheet, a defect log with the repair route for each defect, and a sign-off line, ready to attach to the asset before it goes to launch.

MCR.when: When the owner says "use our reviews for ad ideas", ads have run out of fresh angles, or a product has its first 50 or more reviews. Ranks ten angles, each with exact buyer quotes.
MCR.tune: every count has a stated denominator and is never sold as market share; angles are ranked on gap against the store's own live ads and on gross profit per order and stock, not on mention count; review permissions and other-language quotes are handled before an angle depends on them; and each...
MCR.title: Ad angles mined from your reviews
MCR.outcome: a ranked list of ten ad angles in one table, each with 2 to 3 exact buyer quotes (review ID and date), the product it sells, the objection it answers, its evidence count and a first test headline, plus a coded quote bank file the ad team can reuse.

MCR.when: When a video ad needs music or sound, a creator's trending sound is about to run as a paid ad, or an ad got a copyright claim or was muted. Picks tracks the store is licensed to use.
MCR.tune: every track is cleared per platform and per paid use, with proof saved in a rights log; creator post sounds are checked before any paid promotion; the product's own recorded sounds come before library effects; and the free path is each platform's own library, with paid tools only when their...
MCR.title: Music and sound for ads
MCR.outcome: a sound plan per ad: the sound's job, the chosen track with licence proof, a timed sound effects list, voice and music levels, a sound-off fallback check, and a rights log row, ready for the editor and safe to run as a paid ad.

MCR.when: When shoppers add to cart and leave, cold ads get clicks but few sales, or before a price rise. Makes one ad for each top reason buyers hold back, each with the proof that answers it.
MCR.tune: objections are ranked by how close to purchase they bite, from the store's own abandoners, buyers and refused deliveries; an objection with no honest answer goes to the owner as a fix instead of becoming an ad; each ad's proof is reused on the product page, abandon email and WhatsApp; and hooks are...
MCR.title: One ad per top buying objection
MCR.outcome: five ad concepts in one table, one per top objection, each with the proof that answers it (with its file), the customer type who voices it, the hook and beats, the format, and where it runs; plus the ranked objection list with counts, and a matching review or proof for the product page and abandon messages.

MCR.when: When the store has good product photos but little video, or needs b-roll or short clips fast. Turns existing photos into 3 to 6 second motion clips, with a free no-AI path. Not for a full AI video ad.
MCR.tune: each move is graded by how likely it is to damage the product before any credit is spent; low-risk clips are made free by hand with no generator; drifted takes are repaired by putting the real product cut-out back on top; and prices, printed price labels and offers are never drawn by a model.
MCR.title: Motion clips from product photos
MCR.outcome: 6 to 10 short motion clips planned from the store's own product photos: a photo pick sheet, a move plan sorted by risk, one prompt per clip that works in any image-to-video tool (plus a free manual path), and an accuracy log, ready to use as ad b-roll, openers or product page video.

MCR.when: When a new quarter or peak season starts and ads are still planned week to week and keep running late. Lays out twelve weeks of ad ideas tied to launches, seasons, stock and budget. Not for this week's or this month's batch.
MCR.tune: concept volume is the lowest of what the test budget, winner churn and the makers can carry, not a fixed quota; every row carries the product's gross profit and stock cover, so no ad is planned for a product that loses money or runs out; sale-week readouts switch to signals that are not bent by...
MCR.title: Quarterly creative roadmap
MCR.outcome: a twelve-week roadmap sheet with every planned concept on a dated row (buyer, angle, format, product, offer, brief date, live date, test spend, readout date), a one-screen summary of the quarter's creative bets, and the three review dates where the plan gets rewritten from results.

MCR.when: When a creator, founder or staff member is about to film product videos on a phone at home, past shoots came back dark, echoey or missing shots, or one shoot must feed a month of ads. Not for writing the script.
MCR.tune: the shot count is sized from how many openers and bodies the account can actually test; proof shots must be single continuous takes so demos stay honest; the shoot fee is booked as production cost against the ads it makes; and the notes cover noise hours, takes in each buyer language and WhatsApp compression.
MCR.title: At-home UGC shoot plan
MCR.outcome: one shoot pack a creator can open on their phone and follow: a two-hour run sheet, a numbered shot list of 25 to 40 shots (openers, bodies, product proof, b-roll, second setting), a light and sound setup card, phone settings, and a file hand-in rule, ready to send with the script.

MCR.when: When the product is easiest to believe by seeing it work, long ads lose people before the proof, or a TikTok Shop listing needs a short demo video. Writes a 15-second demo script, a 6-second cut and a shot list.
MCR.tune: the demo must work three times off camera before it is filmed; every on-screen result has a proof sheet saying how and when it was shot; TikTok Shop demos are ranked on sales per thousand views; and the notes tie the demo to cutting refused pay-on-delivery parcels and returns.
MCR.title: Fifteen-second product demo ad
MCR.outcome: one fifteen-second demo script with second-by-second beats, a six-second cut, a shot list of 6 to 10 shots, and a proof sheet showing how each on-screen result was filmed, ready for a creator or staff member to shoot on a phone.

MCR.when: When a new product, flavour, colour or size launches in 4 to 6 weeks, or a past launch went live to silence. Plans teaser, reveal, proof and last-chance ads with dates. Not for a gifting season plan.
MCR.tune: the lead angle is smoke-tested before launch day instead of guessed; each stage has a switch rule in the store's own money, not a fixed day count; the proof stage fills only with real reviews and disclosed creators as they arrive; and the last-chance stage runs only on a real, kept deadline, with...
MCR.title: New product launch creative kit
MCR.outcome: a dated launch kit with four ad stages (teaser, reveal, proof, last chance), two to four concepts per stage with hooks and proof, the audience and placement for each, the rule that moves the launch to the next stage, and the asset list with due dates.

MCR.when: When a long-running winning ad is getting expensive (cost per purchase climbing) and the owner asks if it is tired, before rebuilding it. Checks fatigue first, then gives six refreshes that each change one part. Not for making many new ads in the winners' style.
MCR.tune: fatigue is only called after the auction, site, offer, tracking, season and budget are ruled out, so the store does not rebuild an ad that was never the problem; each refresh changes exactly one named part that is big enough to count as new; the original keeps selling until a refresh passes the...
MCR.title: Refresh a tired winning ad
MCR.outcome: a one-page fatigue check on one winning ad with a verdict (tired, not tired, or unclear) and the evidence, and if tired, six refresh briefs that each change one part of the ad, ranked, with a test plan that keeps the original running until a refresh proves itself.

MCR.when: When an approved ad exists in one size only and needs every size for Meta and Google (feed, Stories, Reels, display), or Stories and Reels cover its words. Rebuilds each size, not just crops. Not for new ad images from a product photo.
MCR.tune: each size is rebuilt from layers against the current 35% bottom band instead of cropped; Google gets a clean image with the words moved to its text fields; the set loads as one ad so delivery is not split; and an offer's qualifying line is never cut to make it fit.
MCR.title: Resize one ad for every placement
MCR.outcome: one folder with 6 to 7 export files of the same ad (Meta 4:5, 1:1 and 9:16; Google 1.91:1, 1:1 and 9:16, plus an optional Google logo), each checked against its safe area and a phone-size read test, and a one-page sheet that says which file goes in which placement slot.

MCR.when: When the owner wants to turn real customer reviews into image ads (review cards, screenshots, quote on product), or before reusing a review someone found online.
MCR.tune: each review is matched to a real order and logged with a dated screenshot before design starts; the edit rule is trim-only with meaning kept; standout results need the typical result beside them; and permission is asked without any reward tied to a positive review.
MCR.title: Ads made from real reviews
MCR.outcome: a review evidence log of 6 to 10 approved reviews (source, order match, permission, objection answered), plus 4 to 6 finished ad specs (review card, screenshot-style, review wall, quote-on-product) with exact words, layout and placement sizes, ready to build and run once the client approves.

MCR.when: When Diwali, Rakhi, Black Friday, Christmas, Valentine's or Mother's Day is 6 to 10 weeks away and no ads are planned. Plans ads by phase and works every deadline back from the last day to order. Not for writing the gifting ad copy.
MCR.tune: the plan is worked back from a last order date built on the store's slowest courier lane and real peak packing, not a calendar date; after-cutoff creative is made in advance so the store keeps selling things that still arrive; concepts speak to the giver; and gift orders are pushed to prepay to avoid refused parcels.
MCR.title: Gifting season creative plan
MCR.outcome: one season plan with the real order cutoff date, four phases of ad concepts (early, peak, last days, after the cutoff), an asset list by channel and size, and a deadline sheet with every brief, asset and go-live date worked back from that cutoff.

MCR.when: When TikTok ads are live and the owner wants a steady flow of new winning ads, or results hang on one or two old ads. Sizes the weekly test to the budget and calls winner, wait or cut. Not for the daily TikTok spend check.
MCR.tune: the week's slots are counted from the store's allowed cost per purchase before any video is made; one decision metric (store-confirmed purchases at allowed cost) picks winners while the rest only diagnose; agency starting lines are replaced by the store's own baseline; and next week's briefs come...
MCR.title: TikTok ads creative test plan
MCR.outcome: a weekly test sheet: the number of test slots the budget funds, the concepts and hooks going in, the campaign layout, the day 1, 3 and 7 reads, and the winner, wait or cut call for each ad, plus next week's brief list, ready for the owner to approve the spend.

MCR.when: When the product is a gift, a kit with several parts or has packaging worth showing, or buyers ask what arrives in the box. Plans an honest unboxing video ad from a real order.
MCR.tune: the ad starts from a real order through the live store, so parcel, delivery and contents on camera are true; packaging cost is put into gross profit before the ad promises it; a slow or damaged delivery stops the ad and goes to the client; and the notes protect each market's required price and pack labels and the real courier parcel.
MCR.title: Unboxing video ad
MCR.outcome: one unboxing ad plan: a 30 to 45 second script with a 15 second cut, a shot plan of 12 to 16 shots with sound notes, a packaging prep list, and an honesty sheet that lists what must be shown exactly as buyers receive it, ready to film.

MCR.when: When a video ad, explainer or product clip needs a voiceover, narration sounds read rather than spoken, or before cloning or buying an AI voice. Writes the timed script and picks the voice.
MCR.tune: the script is sized from the chosen voice's measured pace, not a template word count; the speaker's role is fixed before writing so no hired or synthetic voice poses as a customer; voice clones need written consent; and the final voice is picked by a blind listen over the real cut on a phone...
MCR.title: Voiceover script and voice choice
MCR.outcome: one timed voiceover script that fits the locked cut to the second, marked for pauses and emphasis, with a pronunciation list; a voice brief usable for a human actor or an AI voice; and a voice record (who, consent, usage, disclosure), ready to record.

MCR.when: When one ad idea is approved and a designer, editor or creator has to make it without a call, or briefs keep coming back wrong. Writes a one-page brief for that single ad. Not for briefing a whole batch.
MCR.tune: the brief starts from the test and a money line built on gross profit, not from a mood board; the offer and page are checked live and dated; every proof line points to a file a reviewer can open; and the must-nots carry the real US, UK, EU and Meta rules, so the ad is not rejected after the money is spent making it.
MCR.title: One-page creative brief for a single ad
MCR.outcome: one filled brief of about one page (under 500 words) for one ad that a designer, editor or creator can produce from without a call, plus a three-line note for the media buyer saying where the ad goes and what result decides it.

MCR.when: When the owner needs TikTok video ad scripts for one product, TikTok ads look like resized Facebook ads, or a test or monthly batch needs fresh concepts. Writes five native scripts with hooks. Not for planning the TikTok test.
MCR.tune: five scripts in five native formats instead of one script in five wordings; every spoken claim is tied to a proof line or a sourced customer quote; the contested spoken CTA is built as a cuttable test, not a rule; and each market gets openers in its buyers' own language, with pay-on-delivery and tax-inclusive price lines only where true.
MCR.title: TikTok ad scripts
MCR.outcome: a set of five scripts for one product, each 15 to 45 seconds, each with three spoken openers to test, timed beats, the exact on-screen text per beat, a caption, a call to action, a shot note and the claims it relies on, plus a one-screen summary with the order to test them. Ready to send to creators or to shoot in-house.

MCR.when: When you need next month's ad ideas to be truly different, not more versions of the one ad that already works.
MCR.tune: Feed it product reviews, post-purchase survey answers and your top ad names from a Meta export, and ask for each concept to differ in persona, angle or offer. The store trap is calling a new colour or pose a new concept; read MCR-0022 and MCR-0050 before choosing cells.

MCR.when: When you are setting next month's creative plan and need to know how many new ads to make.
MCR.tune: Give it monthly Meta spend, target cost per purchase and your hit rate from the last 60 to 90 days of ads, not a guess. Small stores often copy big-brand quotas they cannot produce, so check the spend bands in MCR-0058 and MCR-0082 first.

MCR.when: When results have gone flat across many ads and you think they might all be the same idea.
MCR.tune: Paste every live ad with its persona, angle, offer and format, plus cold frequency from the Meta export. Treat near copies as one ad, because Meta groups them; read MCR-0078 and MCR-0040 before you brief anything new.

MCR.when: When the owner asks which Facebook and Instagram ads to keep, scale, fix or cut, costs creep up and tired ads are suspected, or for a weekly or monthly ad review. Judged on store cost per purchase. Not for the daily account check or budget calls.
MCR.tune: Run it on an ad-level Meta export with spend, frequency, click rate and purchases over at least 14 days, plus the ad files. Its benchmarks are generic, so judge fatigue against your own past winners and check MCR-0036 and MCR-0060 before adding formats for their own sake.
MCR.title: Meta creative review for an online store
MCR.outcome: a scale, keep, fix or cut verdict for every live Meta ad on store cost per purchase, a concept map, a gap list, an asset check and a numbered approval list.

MCR.when: When you have a long list of video hooks and need to pick the few worth filming.
MCR.tune: Give it the hooks, the buyer each one targets and the 3-second view rate of past hooks if you have it. Score the spoken line, on-screen text and first shot separately, and drop hooks that stop the scroll but attract non-buyers (MCR-0026, MCR-0028).

MCR.when: When your founder is willing to film and you want a month or more of founder ads from one shoot.
MCR.tune: Feed it real reviews, the founder story and product proof, then let it build the hook-by-body grid before the shoot. Keep founder ads as one part of the mix, not the whole account, and start the script with a claim and its proof (MCR-0006, MCR-0008).

MCR.when: When you need a still image ad for Meta and want a proven pattern that fits cold or warm buyers.
MCR.tune: Give it the product page, review quotes and the buyer's awareness stage. Make each static either fully clear or a deliberate curiosity gap, and send curiosity statics to a page that teaches (MCR-0019, MCR-0024).

MCR.when: When you have a finished image ad and want a second opinion before you put money behind it.
MCR.tune: Attach the image and the exact product or collection page it sends people to. A clever headline with a page that does not explain it is the common store miss, so check MCR-0019 and MCR-0080 first.

MCR.when: When your best ad is losing spend or return and you want to bring it back before starting from zero.
MCR.tune: Give it the ad's weekly spend, return and frequency since launch from the Meta export, plus the script. Try new openers or a new setting with the same body before writing off the idea (MCR-0012, MCR-0047).

MCR.when: When one video ad is winning and you want versions of it for other kinds of buyers.
MCR.tune: Feed it the winning script, review quotes grouped by buyer type and the product's ingredients or features. Change only the persona and the matching proof, keep the structure, and give each version a page that matches (MCR-0073, MCR-0074).

MCR.when: When your product needs explaining and short ads are not turning into sales.
MCR.tune: Give it the mechanism, review quotes in customers' own words and every proof point you can back. Use a long video only when buyers do not understand the product yet, then test several hooks on one working body (MCR-0033, MCR-0031).

MCR.when: When you have a few ads that sell, yours or a rival's, and want to know what they share before you brief more.
MCR.tune: Paste ten or more winners with spend and how long each ran, tagged by segment, angle, hook and format. Swap one part at a time, and try your winning ideas in new formats before inventing new ideas (MCR-0051, MCR-0052).

MCR.when: When the owner wants to see what rivals run on Facebook and Instagram (the Meta Ad Library): when briefing new Meta concepts, when a rival seems to be winning the auction, or before a launch or sale.
MCR.tune: Pick rivals one or two sizes bigger than you, and study ads that have run longest rather than the newest ones. Never copy their words or images, and treat formats that every guru now teaches as past their peak (MCR-0034, MCR-0062).
MCR.title: Rival ad research for an online store
MCR.outcome: a rival roster, a competitor ad log from the Meta Ad Library, a long-runner table, an offer check against store profit, a gap table and the top test idea with its cost.

MCR.when: When most of your spend sits on two or three ads and you want to spread the risk across sources and formats.
MCR.tune: Give it your live ads with spend, source (AI, creator, in-house), format and awareness stage. Aim for many distinct formats with spend spread across them, and split effort between remaking winners, fixing near misses and new bets (MCR-0036, MCR-0042).

MCR.when: When an ad is not reaching new people, or the picture and the words seem to speak to different buyers.
MCR.tune: Attach the ad image or script with its primary text and the page it sends to. Keep one ad on one awareness stage, and make sure most of your ads speak to people who do not know you yet (MCR-0056, MCR-0057).

MCR.when: When Facebook and Instagram ad ideas are written and need images, or an AI-made ad image must be checked against the real product, logo and price before it runs. Not for a quick set from one product photo, or resizing a finished ad.
MCR.tune: Use the real product, logo and price from the store only; check product fidelity before anything is shown to the client; size 4:5 and 9:16 with safe zones.
MCR.title: Meta ad images that show the real product
MCR.outcome: Meta ad image files that show the real product, logo and price, in a folder per concept, with an asset manifest, designer briefs where needed and a short list for the owner to confirm.

MCR.when: When the store's Meta concepts need in-use or lifestyle shots it does not have, or someone wants to use AI product images. Not for turning a product photo the store already has into ads.
MCR.tune: Keep the product exact (label, colour, shape); skip AI product images where the look is what the buyer judges, and disclose where needed.
MCR.title: Product photos for Meta ads that keep the product exact
MCR.outcome: an AI safety rating per product, a shot plan, finished product photos with a manifest in folders by product and shot, and a phone shoot guide if one is needed.

ADC.when: When agents, freelancers or agencies propose ad account changes and the owner needs to approve them under firm spend limits. Not for deciding which changes to make.
ADC.tune: tiers set by gross profit at stake and how hard a change is to undo, not by who asked; one-word approvals tied to an ID that expire; spend limits that live in the platform's own settings; and an append-only log that feeds the store's scorekeeping.
ADC.title: Ad changes the owner approves, with spend limits that hold
ADC.outcome: an approval matrix with spend limits, numbered change proposals the owner can answer yes or no in chat or email, and a change audit log file, ready for agents, freelancers or agencies to work under.

ADC.when: When the owner wants alerts before ad costs spike: the store spends daily and keeps finding fatigue, cost rises or tracking problems only after revenue drops.
ADC.tune: thresholds come from each ad set's own 28-day baseline with evidence-card floors; persistence, volume and a 72-hour cooldown keep noise out; stock cover and tracking drift sit beside ad metrics; and the rules are back-tested on the store's history before any lead time is promised.
ADC.title: Early-warning watch on ad metrics
ADC.outcome: a one-screen daily digest of ad metric alerts with severity and money at stake, plus a baseline sheet, a back-test report and setup notes, ready to run each morning before trouble shows in revenue.

ADC.when: When a new batch of Facebook and Instagram (Meta) ads is ready to go live and must be built without setup mistakes: placement, naming, links and tracking. Not for judging the ad itself (hook, claims, proof).
ADC.tune: a placement rule that keeps new ads out of winning ad sets; a 13-point check that includes stock and price on the live page, not just the link; a duplicate test against Meta's own grouping; and the read rule written before launch so results cannot be bent later.
ADC.title: New ads live without setup mistakes
ADC.outcome: a launch batch table, a 13-point pre-publish check per ad with fixes, and a filled bulk import sheet with every new ad built paused, ready to load into Meta once the owner says yes.

ADC.when: When the owner wants more ad spend but cost per purchase must stay under a fixed ceiling: cost caps, bid caps and target CPA or ROAS on Meta and Google. Not for deciding whether the store is ready to spend more.
ADC.tune: a gate that asks whether a cap fits this store before building one; a cap derived from gross profit and the store-truth factor with break-even as a hard ceiling; a spend-and-cost grid instead of guesswork; and a cap log that feeds the store's own scorekeeping.
ADC.title: Capped campaigns: spend more without passing a cost ceiling
ADC.outcome: a clear call on whether to use a cost cap, a cap worked out from store gross profit, a paused campaign build table for Meta or Google, and a cap log for tuning it over time.

ADC.when: When the owner asks how to split one fixed monthly ad budget between Meta (Facebook and Instagram) and Google by profit, and which campaigns give or get money. Not for setting how big the total budget is.
ADC.tune: one store basis for Meta and Google with a factor per channel, so the platforms stop double claiming; contribution from each product group's own gross profit instead of ROAS; marginal cost of the last money as the scale test; and hard stock and cash checks before any money moves.
ADC.title: Split one ad budget between Meta and Google by profit
ADC.outcome: a proposed Meta and Google split of one fixed monthly budget, judged on store gross profit after ads, with campaign marks, a dated move plan with undo steps, and low, base and high scenarios.

ADC.when: When someone checks the Meta and Google ad accounts each working day and needs a steady 20-minute routine before touching budgets. Not for TikTok ads, which have their own daily review.
ADC.tune: break-even pulled from delivered gross profit, not product margin; breakages and stock first, with "no change" as the default call; a written rule for every cut; and a decision log with predictions so each call can be graded later.
ADC.title: Daily ad account review
ADC.outcome: a five-line daily note, a review table of every campaign, ad set and ad against break-even with a clear call and rule, and a decision log row appended each day.

ADC.when: When a month starts and the owner asks for one plan for ads and email together: a Day 1 to 30 calendar of ads, emails, SMS or WhatsApp sends and offers, with the budget split by buyer stage.
ADC.tune: the budget split is computed line by line from the store's gross profit, cash, stock, audience sizes and frequency, never a fixed percentage; flows are checked before campaigns; one offer timeline binds ads, email and site; and market notes cover pay on delivery, failed deliveries and WhatsApp.
ADC.title: 30-day plan across ads and email
ADC.outcome: a dated 30-day calendar of ads, emails and texts by shopper stage, a budget table built from gross profit, one offer timeline, and creative and email brief lists, ready for the month.

ADC.when: When the owner wants one clear score for how healthy the paid ads are across Meta, Google and TikTok, monthly or after taking over or fixing the accounts.
ADC.tune: the score is withheld until gross profit per purchase can be computed and capped when tracking fails; every point carries file, row and number from plain exports; one score spans Meta, Google and TikTok; and pay-on-delivery stores are scored on delivered orders.
ADC.title: Paid ads health score for a store
ADC.outcome: a 0 to 100 health score with a letter grade for Meta, Google and TikTok, area and check tables tied to evidence, and an action plan with owners and access levels.

ADC.when: When the owner asks whether to spend more on ads after a campaign has beaten its target for two weeks: checks profit, stock, cash and creative, then sets how fast to raise spend. Not for moving money between campaigns.
ADC.tune: warehouse, support and stock tests that profit cannot override; demand after the raise, not today's, drives the stock and capacity checks; marginal cost of the last sales as the stop rule; and a weekly cash line beside every scaling step.
ADC.title: Is the store ready to spend more, and how fast?
ADC.outcome: a readiness table testing every winning Meta and Google campaign on eight limits, a saturation watchlist, a dated scaling timeline with stop rules, and a readiness file, ready for the owner to approve the first raise.

ADC.when: When new ads are ready and the campaign they belong in is hitting its target, so they must go in without resetting learning or starving the winners.
ADC.tune: a dated snapshot that doubles as the rollback point; a placement table that sorts ad sets by status before any ad goes in; a freeze list so new ads are never judged in the same week as a budget move; and winners reused by post ID instead of being edited.
ADC.title: Add new ads to a live campaign safely
ADC.outcome: one change plan for one live campaign: a before-snapshot, a placement decision for every new ad, a list of settings frozen during the change, the edit order, and a watch sheet with the rollback rule, ready for the client to approve.

ADC.when: When a store is about to run its first Facebook and Instagram (Meta) sales campaign and every setting must be chosen before launch.
ADC.tune: every setting has a written reason and an approval box; the budget and cost goal come from delivered gross profit, not a round number; a new campaign must earn its place against consolidation; and the built draft is checked against the signed sheet before anyone switches it on.
ADC.title: Meta campaign launch sheet
ADC.outcome: one launch sheet (a table per level: campaign, ad sets, ads) with every Meta setting filled in, a reason for each non-default choice, a one-screen approval summary, and a paused draft built to match it once the client says yes.

ADC.when: When the owner wants retargeting for site visitors, cart abandoners or past buyers on Facebook and Instagram, when retargeting looks too good to be true, or when existing customers soak up prospecting money.
ADC.tune: "no separate retargeting budget" is the default and must be argued away with three conditions; existing-customer money is sized from customer count, frequency and CPM; refused deliveries are kept out of the customer list; and owned channels are checked before paying to reach past buyers.
ADC.title: Meta retargeting and exclusion audiences
ADC.outcome: an audience build list with exact definitions, a use-or-exclude matrix for every campaign, a written verdict on separate retargeting budget (yes, small, or none) with the money figure behind it, and the frequency lines to watch.

ADC.when: When new ad copy is ready to load and the owner worries it will be rejected or break the law, especially health, beauty, supplements, baby, pay later or EMI, or green claims: a line-by-line risk check. Not for appealing a rejected ad.
ADC.tune: spoken lines, captions and translations are checked like headlines; every rating names the rule and the evidence on file; each block comes with a rewrite that keeps the selling point the proof allows instead of a vague hedge; and each market's ad rules (FTC, ASA and CAP Code, EU consumer law, dark patterns, tax-inclusive prices) are checked too.
ADC.title: Ad copy policy and claims check
ADC.outcome: a line-by-line check sheet for each ad (every sentence, headline and spoken line), each marked block, fix or pass, with the claim type, the evidence held, the platform rule or law it touches, and a ready rewrite; plus a one-screen summary listing what must change before launch and what needs a lawyer or the client's proof.

ADC.when: When the Meta account has more campaigns and ad sets than its budget can feed, has grown messy, or nobody can say why each campaign exists.
ADC.tune: the number of ad sets is sized from the purchases the budget can buy; every split must name a business reason; old and new run side by side with the old winner paused last and a written rollback number; and the merge is judged on store new-customer orders.
ADC.title: Consolidate a messy Meta account
ADC.outcome: an inventory of every live campaign and ad set with a keep, merge or pause call, a target structure on one page, a dated switch order, a list of what to pause and when, and a before-and-after scorecard read on store orders.

ADC.when: When one or more ads show Rejected in Ads Manager, or the ad account, page or business is restricted or disabled.
ADC.tune: each rejection is traced to the exact line, image or page before anyone resubmits; the fix sweeps every similar live and draft ad, not just the one Meta caught; appeals are short factual templates the client approves; and restrictions are never dodged with new accounts.
ADC.title: Fix rejected ads and account restrictions
ADC.outcome: a fix sheet with one row per rejection or restriction (what, where, cause, fix or appeal, evidence), appeal texts ready to paste, a list of other live and draft ads with the same problem, and the rules added to the store's pre-launch check.

ADC.when: When the owner wants to start TikTok ads, restart a dead account, or stop boosting posts and run a proper sales campaign. Not for writing the TikTok video scripts.
ADC.tune: the budget comes from the store's own allowed cost per purchase instead of TikTok's suggestion or an agency's fixed number; launch waits for one real order to reach TikTok exactly once; stores are told plainly where TikTok ads cannot reach their buyers, such as countries where TikTok is banned; and day 14 is decided on store-side new...
ADC.title: First TikTok ads campaign
ADC.outcome: a launch pack: the account set-up checklist, a pixel pass on a real order, one drafted sales campaign (every setting listed), the ad list with names and sizes, and a 14-day check sheet with what to look at each day and the decision on day 14, ready for the owner's yes.

ADC.when: When one person holds all the keys to the business account and ad account, when taking over an account, after a hack or lockout scare, or before a peak season.
ADC.tune: the plan starts from who owns each asset, not who can log in; agencies get partner access so they can leave without taking the ad account; the backup set is ready to run with dataset and payment in place; and it draws a hard line between continuity and dodging a restriction.
ADC.title: Meta account backup and access plan
ADC.outcome: an asset ownership map, a people and roles table with the target state, a list of changes in order for the client to make or approve, a ready backup set (ad account, Page, shared dataset, payment), and a one-page recovery runbook for the five common failures.

ADC.when: When most orders are cash on delivery (COD), many parcels come back unpaid (RTO) or it varies by ad, or Meta's results look far better than cash collected: Facebook and Instagram ad buying judged on delivered, paid orders.
ADC.tune: break-even is set on gross profit per placed COD order, not per delivered one; the confirmed-order signal is designed around Meta's 7-day event limit instead of a delivery event that arrives too late; refused buyers are kept out of seed audiences; and every campaign is read two weeks later on...
ADC.title: Meta ads for cash-on-delivery stores
ADC.outcome: an RTO table by campaign and ad, a money sheet with gross profit per placed COD order and the true break-even cost, a signal design (events, timing, values) for the developer or app, a test plan with its read date, and a weekly read sheet on delivered gross profit, all for the client's approval.

ADC.when: When Black Friday, Cyber Monday, Christmas, Diwali, a local festival or national holiday, or a brand sale is three to six weeks away and every channel needs one day-by-day plan. Not for deciding how deep each product's discount can go.
ADC.tune: build-up spend is judged on new customers rather than same-day ROAS; every day has a written scale, hold or cut guard plus a platform spending limit as the hard stop; stock and warehouse capacity sit on the same calendar line as spend; and courier cutoffs before each market's peak days, pay-on-delivery confirmation and SMS consent rules are built in.
ADC.title: Peak sale week plan across channels
ADC.outcome: one sale-week calendar from build-up to after-sale: for each day the offer, the ad budget per channel, the creative live, every email, SMS and WhatsApp send, the stock check and the cost guard, with an owner per line, ready for the owner to approve.

ADC.when: When the store has influencer or creator content and wants to run it as Facebook and Instagram ads from the creator's handle (partnership ads), or nobody knows if those ads beat brand-handle ads. Not for TikTok Spark Ads.
ADC.tune: signed usage terms come before any platform permission; creator fees are priced from their views against the store's own Meta CPM; every permission has an end date and a revoke step; and the creator handle must beat the store's handle on store orders in a matched test before more money moves.
ADC.title: Creator partnership ads on Meta
ADC.outcome: a signed-off usage terms sheet per creator, a permission sheet (creator, permission type, status, ad codes, end date), the partnership ads built paused, and a handle test plan with its read rule and dates, ready for the client's yes.

ADC.when: When the store wants an Advantage+ shopping (sales) campaign, Meta's most automated sales campaign, without letting it spend the budget on people who already bought.
ADC.tune: the existing-customer cap is sized in money from the store's own customer count, not a default percentage; it uses Meta's current two ad set method and checks the campaign still counts as Advantage+; and the first two weeks are judged on store new-customer orders, not Meta's blended return.
ADC.title: Advantage+ sales campaign setup
ADC.outcome: a fit verdict, a filled settings sheet for one Advantage+ sales campaign with two ad sets (existing customers capped, everyone else excluding them), the creative list, and a 14-day check calendar, all ready for the client's yes.

ADC.when: When starting Meta catalog (dynamic product) ads, when they show wrong prices or sold-out items, or before a sale.
ADC.tune: product sets are cut by gross profit and stock cover, not by collection; a price and stock truth test on a real sample must pass before any ad runs and repeats at every sale change; and catalog spend is capped and read on 7-day click because its reported return leans on buyers who were coming...
ADC.title: Meta catalog ads setup
ADC.outcome: a checked catalog, a product set list with the rule behind each set, a settings sheet for the catalog ads, a feed check report with every mismatch fixed or listed, and a daily and weekly feed routine.

ADC.when: When TikTok ads spend every day and someone must check them: a 15-minute daily check that corrects TikTok's sales count against store orders and makes scale, hold or cut calls. Not for testing new TikTok creative.
ADC.tune: breakages and stock are checked before any performance call; TikTok's purchases are corrected by a weekly store-truth factor from Shopify orders; raises are judged on the cost of the extra purchases, not the average; and every change carries a prediction that is graded later.
ADC.title: TikTok ads daily review and scaling
ADC.outcome: a daily review note (breakages found, store-adjusted numbers, and a scale, hold or cut call for every ad group and every ad over its test spend) plus a change list for approval and a running decision log, in 15 minutes a day.

ADC.when: When influencers or creators have posted about the product on TikTok and the store wants to put ad money behind those posts (Spark Ads), or brand-made TikTok ads have stalled. Not for Facebook and Instagram partnership ads.
ADC.tune: posts are picked on outlier ratio and buyer fit rather than raw views; every creator has a written usage sheet with code expiry tracked; creator posts are tested against brand-made ads in equal ad groups and judged on store new customers; and disclosure and honest-use rules are hard gates, not...
ADC.title: TikTok Spark Ads with creators
ADC.outcome: a Spark Ads pack: a shortlist of creator posts with why each was picked, a signed-off usage sheet per creator (fee, code period, disclosure, link), the drafted campaign with creator and brand-made ads in two equal ad groups, and a results sheet with the winner rule, ready for the owner to approve.

ADC.when: When the owner wants ads in Hinglish, Hindi, Tamil or another Indian language, regional buyers click but do not buy, or before a festival push in one state: rewritten the way buyers speak, not translated word for word.
ADC.tune: languages are chosen from the store's orders by state and its RTO cost, not from a list of big languages; a claim lock table keeps every price, term and GST line identical; a native speaker back-translates before anything runs; and each version is paired with a page that shows what the ad promised.
ADC.title: Ad copy in Hinglish and Indian languages
ADC.outcome: for each English ad, a Hinglish version and versions in one or two chosen regional languages, field by field (primary text, headline, description, on-screen text, call to action), with a claim lock table showing every number and promise unchanged, a native speaker's back-translation sign-off, and the audience and landing page each version runs with.

ADC.when: When setting up Meta catalog (dynamic product) ads, they show broken or clumsy text, or one generic template serves every audience: text templates built from product fields. Not for building the catalog itself.
ADC.tune: every template is rendered against the feed's ten hardest rows before it ships; short custom labels replace long search-style titles in headlines; sale prices come from feed dates instead of static "Sale" text; and catalog ads are kept small and judged on new-buyer orders, not their inflated ROAS.
ADC.title: Catalog ad text
ADC.outcome: three to four text templates per product set (primary text, headline, description) using catalog fields, each tested against the 10 hardest real products in the feed, a custom label plan with the short lines to add to the feed, and a one-screen summary of which template runs for which audience.

ADC.when: When a gifting season is coming and buyers purchase the product for someone else: ad copy that answers the giver's worries (will they like it, will it arrive in time, can they exchange it).
ADC.tune: gift buyers are found in the store's own orders (different billing and shipping names, gift notes); every gift promise is written as the exact operating rule with its proof; a cutoff table by region tells each ad when to stop or switch to gift cards; and wrap cost and weaker repeat rates are...
ADC.title: Gifting ad copy
ADC.outcome: five to seven gifting copy sets (primary text, headline, description, on-screen text) written to the gift buyer, each tied to one giver worry and one recipient, a promise sheet showing every delivery, wrap, message, price-hiding and exchange line with its proof, a delivery cutoff table by region with the date each ad must stop or switch, and a one-screen summary of which set runs when.

ADC.when: When short ads get clicks but no sales, the product needs explaining or the price needs justifying: one long true-story ad (200 to 500 words) plus a short cut. Not for short copy sets to test angles.
ADC.tune: the story must be true, sourced beat by beat and consented before a word is written; the story type is chosen by what actually stops the buyer; every seam where story turns to pitch is found and rewritten; and the long ad ships with a short twin and a matched short page so the test can tell...
ADC.title: Long story ad copy
ADC.outcome: one long story ad (headline, primary text of about 200 to 500 words, description and call to action) and a short version of 40 to 80 words from the same story, each with the source of every fact, the story's consent record, a seam check and a one-screen note on who it is for and where it should send people.

ADC.when: When ads sound like the brand talking about itself, when buyers doubt the product, or when the store has reviews that say it better than any copywriter. Not for designing the review image itself: this writes the ad words.
ADC.tune: quotes are chosen to answer the store's real objections, not by star rating; every trim is recorded in a quote register that would stand up to a regulator; result claims inside reviews are held to the same proof as the brand's own; and no actor or AI voice is ever made to read a review as their own.
ADC.title: Ad copy from customer reviews
ADC.outcome: six to nine ready ad copy sets (primary text, headline, description, on-screen text), each built on one or two real review quotes and answering one buying objection, plus a quote register with the source of every quote, and the one-screen summary saying which set to test first.

ADC.when: When a sale, festival offer, anniversary, launch discount or clearance is planned and the ads need words that sell the offer without cheapening the brand.
ADC.tune: copy is only written after the discount's break-even ROAS is known; one terms box keeps every ad identical on end time, exclusions and tax wording; every "was" price is checked against the store's real price history; and a no-discount version and an end-time swap plan are part of the deliverable, not an...
ADC.title: Sale ad copy that does not cheapen the brand
ADC.outcome: three sale copy sets (each with primary text, headline, description, on-screen text and a Google headline pack) carrying the exact terms, end date and reason, one no-discount copy set built on value, a terms box to paste into every ad and page, and a dated swap plan that pauses sale ads when the sale ends.

ADC.when: When you are setting up Meta ads for your store, or you took over an account full of campaigns nobody can explain.
ADC.tune: Give it monthly spend, products with gross margin and the countries you sell to. Start from one cold campaign and add campaigns only for real business splits, grouped by concept rather than launch date (ADC-0030, ADC-0058).

ADC.when: When you are about to launch a batch of new ads and old winners keep taking all the budget.
ADC.tune: Give it your daily budget, target cost per purchase and the concepts in the batch. Put each batch of four to eight ads in its own named ad set with a small spend floor, and move unspent but worthy ads to a separate set (ADC-0016, ADC-0031).

ADC.when: When a test batch has run for a week or two and you need to know which ads to keep, leave or replace.
ADC.tune: Paste results by ad set and ad from the Meta export with spend, purchases and click rate. Judge a concept after about three times your target cost per purchase, at ad set level, and do not crown a high click-rate ad that sells nothing (ADC-0039, ADC-0059, MCR-0029).

ADC.when: When you do not know how much to spend on new ads before you judge them.
ADC.tune: Give it your target cost per purchase from your margin, the number of ads and how many days the test can run. At low daily budgets, cap impressions per ad so each one gets a fair look (ADC-0066, ADC-0004).

ADC.when: When you want to know whether your share of winning ads is normal and how many ads to make next.
ADC.tune: Paste a prospecting ad export covering at least two weeks and 20 or more ads. Count a winner only if it took a real share of spend at target cost, and expect a few ads to hold most spend under campaign budgets (ADC-0017, ADC-0014).

ADC.when: When some ads are winning and you want to spend more without losing money.
ADC.tune: Give it winning ads, product margins, cash on hand and 30 days of Shopify net sales next to Meta spend. Scale on the cost of the next customer, not the average, and judge on store cash over 30 days, not platform return (ADC-0049, ADC-0034).

ADC.when: When strong Meta returns might be coming from people who already buy from you anyway.
ADC.tune: Give it the size of your Shopify or Klaviyo customer list synced to Meta, recent CPM and current 30-day frequency on that audience. Set the spend in money from list size, CPM and a frequency cap, not as a share of budget (ADC-0021, ADC-0068).

ADC.when: When the owner wants the Facebook and Instagram (Meta) ad account audited: on taking over the account, when cost per purchase has drifted up, delivery collapsed, or before raising spend.
ADC.tune: Run it on Meta Ads Manager exports, Events Manager screenshots and your Shopify order count for the same dates. Fix data first, then structure, then creative, and be wary of advice to use flexible ads that hide which creative sold (ADC-0028, ADC-0065).
ADC.title: Meta account audit for an online store
ADC.outcome: a one-screen verdict on the Meta account, a ranked findings table with money at stake, a reconciliation table, a list of what was not checked, and audit, findings and change list files.

ADC.when: Before an ad account read, a budget change or a creative call that rests on Meta's reported sales: check which attribution setting each campaign uses and how much of the credit is view-through. Not for repairing the pixel or Conversions API.
ADC.tune: Give it the attribution setting on each campaign plus Meta's compare-attribution and incremental columns next to Shopify new-customer sales. Expect catalog and retargeting ads to shrink most on an incremental view, and expect the click-window gap to widen in November (ADC-0010, ADC-0046).
ADC.title: How much of Meta's credit is real: store attribution check
ADC.outcome: a week-by-week table of Meta against store orders, the size of the gap and its main cause, a chosen reporting basis, and store-truth factors per campaign for reading ROAS on a store basis.

ADC.when: When the owner asks which Facebook and Instagram (Meta) campaigns to scale, hold or cut, during the weekly Meta budget review, or when costs rose and spend must come down. Judged on store profit, not Meta's ROAS.
ADC.tune: Give it at least 14 days of campaign and ad set spend, results and bid settings. Its built-in rules include a 20 percent raise limit and a 70/20/10 split, so check ADC-0056 and ADC-0053 and let your own break-even numbers win.
ADC.title: Scale, hold or cut: Meta budgets from store profit
ADC.outcome: a scale, hold or cut call for every Meta campaign based on store profit, with new daily budgets, a numbered change list for approval and review dates.

ADC.when: When Meta keeps spending on people who already know you, or a new concept lost and you cannot tell why.
ADC.tune: Describe frequency, audience segment reports and what changed, with at least 7 days of data. Treat age, gender and interests as hints on broad targeting, and keep exclusions as the hard controls (ADC-0055, ADC-0029).

ADC.when: When the store needs its first or next round of Facebook and Instagram (Meta) ad ideas and copy, once the store profile is ready: concepts by product, buyer group, angle and offer, with a test plan. Not for reviewing ads already running.
ADC.tune: Give it a brand profile built from your store, the top review themes and any audit findings, and ask for primary text, headlines and calls to action per placement. Front-load the headline, since most people read nothing else, and name the buyer group in the copy (ADC-0018, ADC-0032).
ADC.title: Meta ad concepts and copy for a store
ADC.outcome: a campaign brief file with Meta ad concepts tied to profit and proof, a copy deck with character counts, visual briefs and a test plan with keep or cut rules.

ADC.when: When one ad works and you want more ads in the same voice for your best customer groups.
ADC.tune: Paste the winning ad and your top customer groups from surveys or Shopify tags. Put the target group's name in the copy instead of relying on interest targeting, and launch the variants as their own ad set (ADC-0032, ADC-0058).

ADC.when: When you are starting TikTok ads for your store and want setup, a first test and a clear read on it.
ADC.tune: Give it your pixel status, daily budget, target cost per purchase and three different styles of video. Use one broad audience rather than stacked interests, and size ad groups near twice your target cost (ADC-0035, ADC-0063).

ADC.when: When Black Friday or another big sale is coming and you need to know how many ads to have ready.
ADC.tune: Give it last year's top sale ads with their daily spend ceilings, this year's spend target and dates. Spread budget into September and October, keep evergreen campaigns running, and write scaling rules before the sale starts (ADC-0048, ADC-0050).

ADC.when: When the owner describes a Meta problem in general words ('my Facebook ads stopped working', 'ROAS is falling'), wants several Meta jobs at once, or a new store needs Meta set up: picks the right job. Not for a job that is already clear.
ADC.tune: Run the store intake once (platform, gross profit per purchase, spend, markets, stock, cash, sale calendar), then route; check tracking trust before any money or creative call.
ADC.title: Meta ads for an online store: start here
ADC.outcome: a one-screen route for the store's Meta ads work, a filled store context sheet, a money table with break-even lines, and a route plan of skills to run in order.

ADC.when: When Meta (Facebook and Instagram) sales or ROAS fell and the owner asks why, or has one hard question about the Meta account: digs down until one cause is proven. Not for a full Meta account audit.
ADC.tune: Pull the Meta export and the store order export for the same dates and attribution setting; judge every finding against gross profit per purchase.
ADC.title: Meta deep dive for an online store
ADC.outcome: a one-screen answer naming what changed and its proven cause, a bridge table, a walk-down table from campaign to ad, and a change log, saved as one dated file.

ADC.when: When starting or restarting Facebook and Instagram (Meta) ads, finding or scaling a winner, or preparing for a sale season or launch.
ADC.tune: Pick the store stage first (first 30 days, finding a winner, scaling, peak, launch); size budgets from gross profit per purchase, cash and stock, not from benchmarks.
ADC.title: Meta ads plan for an online store
ADC.outcome: a stage-based Meta ads plan: unit economics, campaigns, weekly budget, creatives and approvals, in two files.

ADC.when: When a store wants to start Snapchat ads, restart an account that spent without tracked sales, or add Snap beside Meta or TikTok for buyers under 35 in the US, UK or other markets the store sells in.
ADC.tune: the order ID is the dedup key from Snap Pixel to Conversions API, checked on one real order before spend; each ad set is funded to Snap's own learning guide inside the owner's cap; creative is full-screen 9:16 with the point in two seconds and made for sound on; verdicts read store orders, and pay-on-delivery stores count delivered orders only.
ADC.title: First Snapchat Sales campaign
ADC.outcome: a launch pack with a tracking pass on a real order, one Sales campaign built paused, the ad list to Snap's specs, and a 14-day sheet with one test and stop rule per ad set read on store orders.

ADC.when: When it is the monthly copy review, or when ads, pages, product copy and emails seem to make different promises.
