ADC.tune: It reads ad, page and email as the one path a buyer travels, quotes every promise, number and offer gap between them, scores each piece on five copy chief tests and ranks fixes by the gross profit flowing through each piece.
ADC.title: Team copy scorecard with ranked fixes
ADC.outcome: A scorecard of each live piece on awareness match, big idea, proof, objections and voice, the promise gaps between channels, ranked fixes by likely lost sales, and rewrites of the top three for the teammate who owns each channel.

GAD.when: When the owner asks for a Google Ads audit: on taking over an account, before raising spend, or when Google cost per purchase has crept up. Grades ten areas from CSV exports. Not for the weekly Google Ads check.
GAD.tune: everything from standard exports with no developer token; an overall grade that can never beat the tracking grade; fixes ranked by monthly gross profit at stake from the store's own margins; and a product profit table that shows which items lose money at current spend.
GAD.title: Google Ads account audit for a store
GAD.outcome: a Google Ads scorecard grading ten areas A to F, a ranked findings table with gross profit at stake, a product profit table, a numbered change list for approval and an audit CSV.

GAD.when: When Google Display, Demand Gen or Performance Max money may be going to junk apps, made-for-ads sites or accidental clicks: blocks bad placements with one shared exclusion list.
GAD.tune: placements are judged on store-side sessions through a free {placement} tag and on gross profit, never on clicks or view-through; one shared list plus account level protects every campaign, including new ones; and a dated log turns the clean-up into a monthly routine that compounds.
GAD.title: Display placement clean-up
GAD.outcome: a placement table sorting every Display, Demand Gen and Performance Max placement into a bucket, plus exclusion files for placements and app categories and an exclusions log, ready to upload.

GAD.when: When the owner asks which Google Search keywords make money, or an account with more than about 50 keywords needs weekly actions: sorts your own keywords into six tiers. Not for what shoppers typed or which searches to block.
GAD.tune: tiers come from profit after ads, not ROAS; a written minimum data rule protects keywords from early cuts; week-on-week moves come with a cause before any action; and every budget raise passes a marginal-cost check.
GAD.title: Keyword tiers with weekly actions
GAD.outcome: a keyword tier table placing every Search keyword in one of six tiers by profit, a tier summary with spend and profit, and a keyword actions CSV ready for Google Ads Editor.

GAD.when: When Performance Max (PMax) looks strong in Google but new customers or store profit are flat, or before scaling it: shows where its money really goes, including brand searches and returning buyers. Not for product-by-product Shopping tiers.
GAD.tune: the verdict rests on store-side new-customer orders and acquisition MER, not Performance Max's own return; a step-by-step brand-exclusion test measures real new-customer lift; asset groups get a coverage score that includes stock; and conflicting card advice on budget share is settled by the...
GAD.title: Performance Max diagnostics
GAD.outcome: a Performance Max breakdown of spend by channel and brand share, asset group scores, a settings check, the top three fixes and a dated brand-exclusion test plan with a weekly readout table.

GAD.when: When Google Search clicks cost more on keywords worth keeping, Quality Score is low, or before rewriting search ads or landing pages: finds which part is broken and routes the fix.
GAD.tune: only keywords that make money get fixed; fixes are ranked by profit at stake, not by score; every landing page fix passes a measured speed check and a written message-match check; and each fix has an owner and a recheck date matched to how slowly Google re-scores.
GAD.title: Quality Score triage for a store's Search keywords
GAD.outcome: an ad group triage table routing each low Quality Score problem to its fix with an owner and recheck date, landing page checks, and draft ads with 8 headlines and 2 descriptions per fixed group.

GAD.when: When the owner says Google wastes money on the wrong searches, new search terms pile up, or cost per purchase climbed with no clear cause: sorts search terms into negatives, hidden winners and new keywords. Not for ranking your own keywords.
GAD.tune: winners and waste are judged on gross profit after ad cost, not ROAS; every negative is tested against live keywords before it ships; failed pay-on-delivery orders are priced into the terms that bring them; and mixed-language and mixed-script queries are grouped and blocked in every spelling.
GAD.title: Search term mining for an online store
GAD.outcome: search terms sorted into six groups by gross profit, negative keyword lists checked for conflicts, new keyword and ad group ideas, and files ready to load in Google Ads Editor.

GAD.when: When Google Shopping spend grows faster than profit, before a sale or clearance, or the owner asks which products to push or cut in Shopping: tiers every product from hero to dead stock. Not for working through every Merchant Center disapproval.
GAD.tune: tiers come from gross profit per click built from Shopify costs, not platform ROAS; stock cover and lead time can override a hero call; slow stock gets a clearance tier instead of a pause; and the tiers ship as a ready supplemental feed file.
GAD.title: Shopping product tiers and feed fixes
GAD.outcome: a product tier table for Shopping and Performance Max ranked by gross profit per click, plus feed fix, bid label, pause and supplemental feed label files, ready to upload.

GAD.when: When Google spend or conversions jumped or fell suddenly, bid targets (target ROAS or CPA) look wrong, before a sale or peak season, or when deciding where extra Google money goes.
GAD.tune: every target is built from gross profit per purchase with a named rule; budgets are fitted to the client's cash ceiling at Google's monthly maximum; increases must pass a marginal-cost check; card conflicts on early targets are settled by the cash gate; and every change ships as a numbered...
GAD.title: Smart bidding diagnosis and budget shifts
GAD.outcome: a bid strategy check for every Google campaign, profit-based targets with first steps and review dates, budget moves between campaigns, and a numbered approval list the owner answers yes or no.

GAD.when: When the store spends on YouTube or Demand Gen video ads and the owner asks where viewers stop watching and whether the videos sell: a time-coded edit for each video.
GAD.tune: every video is judged on profit after ads with view-through kept out; drop-off is scored against the account's own median, not a public average; store-side signals (brand search, direct, new customers, Amazon) are read before any cut; and a regional holdout is the only proof of lift.
GAD.title: YouTube and Demand Gen video drop-off
GAD.outcome: a video scorecard placing each YouTube and Demand Gen ad in one diagnostic bucket, an opening test table, a verdict on video spend, and time-coded edit briefs for the videos worth fixing.

GAD.when: When a store has no Google Search campaign, an old one mixes brand and other searches in a tangle, or Shopping runs and the store wants Search for more sales: a ready-to-approve campaign built from scratch.
GAD.tune: max CPC and every budget are worked back from the store's gross profit per purchase, not a benchmark; the competitor campaign is capped and kept out of the trademark trap; local-language queries and pay-on-delivery wording are built in only where true; and the build ships paused with a dated...
GAD.title: Google Search campaign from scratch
GAD.outcome: one Search campaign set (brand, product and competitor campaigns) as a Google Ads Editor import sheet with every keyword, negative, ad and asset filled in, a settings sheet with bids and budgets from the store's own break-even, and a 14-day check plan, all built paused for the client's yes.

GAD.when: When Google Ads shows more or fewer sales than the store's orders, or before raising Google budget, switching to Smart Bidding or setting a target ROAS: a pass or fail check of conversion tracking.
GAD.tune: it reconciles Google with the store's own orders day by day on conversion time, with a hard rule that Google can never exceed the store; the verdict is rule-based and tells the client when not to bid; and cancelled, refunded and undelivered orders are retracted instead of counted as sales.
GAD.title: Google Ads conversion tracking check
GAD.outcome: a one-page pass or fail sheet of 10 tracking checks with the evidence for each, a 14-day reconciliation table of Google purchases against Shopify orders, a verdict (trust, trust with caution, or do not bid on this), and a numbered fix list for the client to approve.

GAD.when: When the owner wants to try Bing (Microsoft Ads) because Google Search or Shopping is profitable and the store wants more of the same buyers, often cheaper, mainly in the US and other desktop-heavy markets.
GAD.tune: only campaigns that earn gross profit on Google are copied; Microsoft's own tag and goal go live before anything spends; every imported setting gets an explicit value instead of "same as Google"; scheduled imports are set so they never overwrite Microsoft-only budgets; and the test is capped and...
GAD.title: Copy Google Ads to Microsoft Ads
GAD.outcome: an import plan naming which Google campaigns go across and why, a pre-import set-up checklist (tag, conversion goal, Merchant Center, brand split), a post-import settings sheet with the value to set for every setting, a capped six-week test budget with a stop rule, and the import schedule choice, all paused for the client's yes.

GAD.when: When products are disapproved or limited in Google Merchant Center, Shopping or Performance Max sales drop, the Diagnostics page shows red, before a sale, or after a suspension warning.
GAD.tune: every issue is ranked by the gross profit it is losing, not by the order Google lists it; product problems and account problems get different paths; no fix hides a fact or invents an identifier; and tax display and postcode price gates are checked as mismatch causes.
GAD.title: Fix Merchant Center disapprovals
GAD.outcome: a fix list for every disapproved or limited product, each row with its issue, cause, exact fix, owner and lost gross profit per week, in order of money lost, plus a separate account-level action plan if the account itself is warned or suspended.

GAD.when: When a store is starting Google Ads for the first time, restarting after a bad first try, or has a new account with no history: a 90-day plan for what to launch and spend. Not for an account with months of data.
GAD.tune: it first asks whether Google should lead at all for this product; every month's budget is worked from gross profit per purchase and checked against the client's cash; each new campaign type unlocks on a purchase count, not a calendar date; and day 30, 60 and 90 go, hold or stop rules are written...
GAD.title: Google Ads for a new store: first 90 days
GAD.outcome: a dated 90-day plan on one sheet: set-up tasks with owners, the launch campaigns, a month-by-month budget with the sum shown, the purchase counts that unlock each next campaign type, and a go, hold or stop rule at days 30, 60 and 90.

GAD.when: When a Google Ads account past its first 30 days needs its weekly check: a 30-minute routine of six checks (results, tracking, Merchant Center, wasted searches, budgets, change log). Not for a deep quarterly audit.
GAD.tune: six checks in a fixed 30-minute order, each with one allowed change, so the account is not over-managed; brand is read apart and results are judged against the store's own break-even on conversion-time columns; tracking failure freezes all bid changes for the week; and peak and festival weeks in each market and pay-on-delivery refusals are built into the reading.
GAD.title: Google Ads weekly routine
GAD.outcome: a filled one-page weekly log: six checks, each with the number found, pass or fail, and at most one proposed change, plus a short change list for the client's approval and a line on what was left alone and why. Same order every week, about 30 minutes.

GAD.when: When a rival's ads show up when people search the store's name, brand ad spend creeps up, or nobody knows whether brand ads are needed: the cheapest way to keep buyers who search the brand.
GAD.tune: it first proves who is taking brand searches and what that costs in gross profit before spending anything; it splits rivals, resellers, coupon sites and affiliates into different fixes; it uses Google's own trademark rule correctly (ad text, not keywords); and it tests whether brand ads add any...
GAD.title: Protect your brand searches
GAD.outcome: a brand protection plan for one store: an evidence table of who appears on its name, a paused brand Search and brand Shopping build with caps, the brand exclusions for every other campaign, a weekly brand watch sheet, and a trademark complaint pack if a rival uses the name in ad text.

GAD.when: When a store with steady Search and Shopping wants to reach new buyers before they search (YouTube, Discover, Gmail), or to test Google against Meta for finding new customers. Not for a pure YouTube video plan.
GAD.tune: readiness and budget come from the store's own target cost per purchase and Google's own 10 times rule, so a store that cannot fund a fair test is told before spending; prospecting excludes buyers so the test reads new customers; and Demand Gen is judged against Meta on new-customer gross profit...
GAD.title: Google Demand Gen campaign setup
GAD.outcome: a paused Demand Gen campaign build sheet (settings, ad groups, audiences, creative list with sizes and copy, product feed link), the budget worked from the store's own target cost per purchase, and a dated 6-week test plan against the store's other prospecting with the rule that decides keep, change or stop.

GAD.when: When the owner wants to start YouTube ads, has product videos sitting unused, or cannot tell if YouTube spend sells anything: campaign goal, video cuts and audience. Not for finding where viewers drop off in current videos.
GAD.tune: it picks the campaign type for the store's stage instead of defaulting to reach; it turns one master video into a cut list an editor can work from by the second; and it judges YouTube on new-customer gross profit through a region holdout with brand search, survey and Amazon side signals, never...
GAD.title: YouTube ads for a store
GAD.outcome: a one-page YouTube plan (goal, campaign type, budget, audiences), a cut list for the video editor with lengths, ratios and what each cut must show by second, a paused build sheet, and a measurement plan that says how YouTube will be judged on store sales and on what date.

GAD.when: When the Google Search ad text needs writing or refreshing, ad strength is Poor, or few people click on non-brand searches: 15 headlines and 4 descriptions per ad group. Not for Performance Max text.
GAD.tune: headlines are planned as five jobs built from the store's own search terms report rather than a template list; the load choice (15/4 or 8/2) follows the ad group's conversion volume; every offer, delivery and payment line is checked against the live page and target region; and lines are judged on...
GAD.title: Google responsive search ads
GAD.outcome: an upload sheet with, for each ad group, 15 headlines (30 characters max) and 4 descriptions (90 max), two display paths, pin settings, character counts and the landing URL, plus a one-screen summary of the angle per ad group, ready for the client to approve and paste into Google Ads or Google Ads Editor.

GAD.when: When launching Performance Max (PMax), splitting asset groups by product type, or its headlines and descriptions are generic, repeated or out of date. Not for Google Shopping feed titles.
GAD.tune: it decides text or feed-only per asset group before writing a word; every line is tested as true for every product in the listing group, not just the hero; payment, tax and delivery lines are checked by market and region; and the text is judged on store gross profit, not Google's own ROAS.
GAD.title: Performance Max asset text
GAD.outcome: one upload sheet per asset group with up to 15 headlines (30 characters, one of 15 or fewer), up to 5 long headlines (90), up to 5 descriptions (90), the business name, call to action and final URL, each with its character count and source, plus a one-screen note saying which asset groups should run with text and which feed-only.

GAD.when: When Google Shopping impressions are low, feed titles were copied from the maker or Shopify, or search terms show words the feed lacks: rewrites Merchant Center titles and descriptions. Not for titles on the store or Amazon.
GAD.tune: patterns come from the store's own converting search terms, checked against volume; changes ship as a supplemental feed so store pages stay written for people; the rollout is split in halves and judged on gross profit per product; and mixed-language and transliterated search words are kept where buyers really use them.
GAD.title: Product feed titles that match searches
GAD.outcome: a supplemental feed sheet (Item ID, new title, new description, product type) for the chosen products, one title pattern per product type with the searched words it is built from, a rules check on every row, and a two-half rollout plan with the date to read results.

GAD.when: When you are about to run Google Ads for your store for the first time.
GAD.tune: Give it your catalogue size, monthly orders, budget and whether purchase tracking already works. Start on Search and Shopping with your bestsellers, and add Performance Max only once the account has steady conversions (GAD-0033, GAD-0030).

GAD.when: When Google shows more sales than your store does, or before you raise any Google budget.
GAD.tune: Paste the conversion actions list and a screenshot of one real Shopify test order as Google recorded it. GA4 imports set as the main purchase action are a common leak, and recent days always look weak, so check GAD-0042 and GAD-0035.

GAD.when: When you took over a Google Ads account, or Google results look fine but store growth does not match.
GAD.tune: Give it campaign, search term and Shopping exports plus Shopify sales for the same dates. Look first for brand traffic hiding inside Performance Max and Shopping, which makes cold returns look better than they are (GAD-0010, GAD-0028).

GAD.when: When products show as disapproved in Merchant Center, or before you put more money into Shopping.
GAD.tune: Paste the Merchant Center diagnostics export and a few live product page prices. Price mismatches between feed and page are a top cause, and selling in several currencies needs a feed for each (GAD-0005, GAD-0049).

GAD.when: When your Shopping ads get seen but few people click or buy.
GAD.tune: Give it the Shopify product export and the search terms report filtered to converting terms. Lead titles with what people search, such as product type, material and colour, and put the brand last unless people search for it (GAD-0009, GAD-0044).

GAD.when: When you are starting Google Shopping and want spend on the few products that already sell.
GAD.tune: Give it your top 5 to 10 products by Shopify sales with cost per purchase if you have it, plus your brand terms for negatives. Concentrate cold budget on the products that convert cheapest before widening (GAD-0030, GAD-0031).

GAD.when: When Performance Max or Shopping returns look strong but new customers are not growing.
GAD.tune: Give it campaign totals, the search terms report and your brand and product names. Keep brand in its own exact-match campaigns with exclusions everywhere else, and keep brand spend a small share of the total (GAD-0003, GAD-0024).

GAD.when: When you are not sure which bid strategy to use, or spend dropped after you raised a target.
GAD.tune: Give it 30 to 60 days of campaign conversions, value and current targets, plus break-even return from your margin. Set a new target below what the campaign already achieves and raise it in small steps, because a target set too high starves the campaign (GAD-0007, GAD-0053).

GAD.when: When Search and Shopping work and you are deciding whether to add Performance Max.
GAD.tune: Give it the catalogue, daily budget, monthly conversions and break-even return. Do not launch without a clean feed and working purchase tracking, split asset groups by product type, and leave a return target off at first (GAD-0026, GAD-0016).

GAD.when: When Performance Max is spending on YouTube or Gmail and you want it pulled back to Shopping.
GAD.tune: Give it your Shopping setup, product count and placement report. Remove asset groups, turn off automatic assets and URL expansion, and check placements whenever clicks jump while return falls (GAD-0048, GAD-0055).

GAD.when: When you want a weekly routine for Standard Shopping and need to know which products to cut, fix or fund.
GAD.tune: Paste a weekly product-level Shopping export with clicks, cost, conversions and value, plus current prices. A sudden drop in click rate on one product often means a rival cut its price, so check prices before blaming bids (GAD-0034, GAD-0019).

GAD.when: When your search terms report is full of searches you never meant to pay for.
GAD.tune: Paste 30 to 90 days of search terms from Shopping, Search and Performance Max with conversions. Promote proven terms into keywords and titles, and keep brand terms as negatives in every cold campaign (GAD-0044, GAD-0028).

GAD.when: When your product solves a problem people search for in plain words and Shopping already works.
GAD.tune: Give it the problem searches buyers type, an education or advertorial page and your proof. Write the ad to the problem, not the product name, and keep most Google spend in Shopping while you test this (GAD-0025, GAD-0054).

GAD.when: When Google revenue or return fell and you want to know why before you rebuild anything.
GAD.tune: Give it 90 days of weekly results, the change history and stock-outs from Shopify. Check feed disapprovals, stock-outs and raised targets first, and make targeted fixes, since a rebuild resets learning (GAD-0037, GAD-0036).

GAD.when: When you want to raise your Google budget and are not sure the account can take it.
GAD.tune: Give it budget use, return against target and back-end store revenue by campaign. Fix an unprofitable campaign at its current budget first, and judge scaling on store revenue, not platform return (GAD-0032, GAD-0045).

ORG.when: When the owner has one clean product photo and needs more pictures plus a quick montage video this week, for posts, ads and the product page gallery. Not for ad images with text or sized for each ad placement.
ORG.tune: the real product photo is the reference for every image, so errors never compound; each image is planned for a job, including the product page gallery; the montage pace respects the flash threshold and is checked; music is cleared per platform with a sources file.
ORG.title: Photo pack and montage from one product
ORG.outcome: a pack of 10 to 15 on-brand, text-free product images, a contact sheet, and a quick-cut montage video in each size with and without music, plus a shot table and music sources.

ORG.when: When the owner says the Reels, Shorts or TikTok grid looks messy, a new video series starts, or cover titles keep getting cropped or covered. Not for the first frame of an ad.
ORG.tune: the template is built from the store's own brand tokens with only two variable slots; every title and face sits inside the crop all platforms show; product images stay real and faces carry consent; and the cover works in free tools or a simple HTML template, with no paid design tool needed.
ORG.title: Cover images for a short-video series
ORG.outcome: a locked 1080 x 1920 cover template in the store's brand, finished cover PNGs, a spec sheet, a cover log and a mock grid of the first nine covers.

ORG.when: When footage piles up unedited, the store posts little short video, or edits keep failing platform rules, and the owner wants raw clips turned into finished Reels, Shorts and TikToks with approval steps. Not for cutting one shoot into paid ads.
ORG.tune: the cut list is the approval point, so nothing renders before a yes; every file passes a per-platform check for safe zone, music licence and AI disclosure; the whole pipeline runs from one shared sheet with no chat tool; and only posts that beat the store's own baseline are passed to paid ads,...
ORG.title: Short-form video editing pipeline
ORG.outcome: finished 1080 x 1920 videos for Reels, Shorts and TikTok, each with its cut list, captions, post text and platform check table, plus a weekly work queue sheet, approved before render and before posting.

ORG.when: When the owner wants a WhatsApp group, community or channel, or a Facebook Group, for customers: to get more second and third orders, share launches, gather feedback or give best buyers a home.
ORG.tune: the community has to prove itself on reorder rate against a control group, not on member count; every perk is priced against gross profit; joining is strictly opt-in with phone-number privacy checked; and each market gets WhatsApp or Facebook formats, language groups and perks that move pay-on-delivery buyers to prepaid.
ORG.title: Customer community on WhatsApp or Facebook
ORG.outcome: a community ready to open: platform choice, purpose line, join flow, house rules, moderator rota, a 4-week post calendar, member perks with their cost, and a 90-day test sheet that shows whether members reorder more than similar non-members.

ORG.when: When comments and DMs go unanswered, team replies don't match, hate, spam or troll comments pile up, or a launch or sale is coming, and the store needs reply rules and ready answers. Not for turning 'price?' comments into sales.
ORG.tune: replies are triaged into nine types with a route that keeps order details private; honest complaints are protected while abuse and scams are removed fast; automation is held inside Meta's messaging window and hands off to a person; and each market gets language, delivery and payment-safety answers.
ORG.title: Comment and DM reply rules
ORG.outcome: a one-page rule card, a triage table for nine message types, about twenty ready answers in the brand's voice, an escalation list and a weekly check sheet, ready for whoever answers the store's comments and DMs once the client approves them.

ORG.when: When the store wants to start working with influencers or creators and has no list of who fits.
ORG.tune: every fee is capped by the store's own gross profit per order, not a rate card; the audience check uses median views and dated insight screenshots instead of follower counts; past disclosure habits are a pass or fail; and buyers are matched by language and by regions the store can deliver to...
ORG.title: Find and vet influencers
ORG.outcome: a shortlist sheet of 10 to 30 creators (name, handle, platform, tier, fit score, audience check, fake-follower flags, past brand results, disclosure check, suggested deal and maximum fee), with a one-screen summary naming the top 5 to contact first and why.

ORG.when: When Instagram followers have stalled and the owner wants reach without ad spend, through collab posts with other brands, niche creators, local businesses or community pages, or before a launch. Not for paid influencer deals or vetting creators.
ORG.tune: partners are scored on audience fit and real reach to strangers, not follower count; every collab carries its own code, UTM link and keyword so gross profit per collab can be read; gift costs come off the result; and the disclosure rules of each market (FTC in the US, ASA in the UK) are built into each brief.
ORG.title: Grow Instagram with collabs
ORG.outcome: a partner list scored for fit, a 60-day collab calendar, first message, follow-up and brief for each partner, and a tracking sheet that shows followers, store visits and gross profit per collab, ready for the client to approve and send.

ORG.when: When a creator said yes to a paid deal and the owner needs the terms written down: what they post, payment, and how long the store can use their videos in ads. Not for permission to repost customers' own photos.
ORG.tune: each usage right is bought separately with an end date, so the store pays only for what the ad plan needs; a rights register stops ads running past their licence; the disclosure clause is written for the buyer's market (such as the US or UK), not a generic hashtag; and tax steps cover VAT invoices, US W-9 and 1099 forms and any local withholding.
ORG.title: Influencer contract and usage rights
ORG.outcome: a one-page term sheet per creator deal plus a contract checklist (every point in steps 1 to 7) marked agreed, open or not needed, and a rights register showing for every creator asset where the store may use it and until when.

ORG.when: When the owner wants to start selling inside TikTok, or a TikTok Shop was opened but has no sales or creators yet. Not for fixing listings that already get views.
ORG.tune: no product is listed until its profit is worked out after TikTok's fees as read on the day, commission and spread sample cost; stock and restock time are a gate because a viral post can empty a shelf; samples go only to creators with category sales; and sellers in markets where TikTok Shop does not run are told so plainly.
ORG.title: Launch on TikTok Shop
ORG.outcome: a launch checklist with each setting written out for approval, a per-product profit sheet after TikTok's fees, the first 3 to 10 products to list, a sample budget, a target list of 20 to 50 affiliate creators, a 30-day posting and outreach calendar, and a day-30 readout template.

ORG.when: When TikTok Shop products get views but few orders, creators skip the product in the affiliate center, or before putting ad money behind a product. Not for opening a new shop.
ORG.tune: every price is checked for profit after TikTok's fees, commission and spread sample cost; listing rules are read in Seller Center on the day rather than copied from guides; one change per listing per week so results can be read; and the listing is optimised for creators in the affiliate center as...
ORG.title: TikTok Shop listing optimisation
ORG.outcome: an upload sheet with new titles, image order, video, description, variants and prices for each listing, a before and after view, a profit check per price, and a creator-appeal checklist with the changes that make affiliates choose the product.

ORG.when: When the owner asks about Pinterest: buyers plan and search there, an account was set up and ignored, or Pinterest ads are being considered and the account needs setting up first.
ORG.tune: it starts with a fit check so stores that will not earn from Pinterest stop early; the catalog reuses the store's existing feed; Pins favour products by gross profit; seasonal lead times and attribution windows are set from Pinterest's own documentation; and the 90-day verdict reads delivered...
ORG.title: Pinterest for a store
ORG.outcome: a Pinterest account ready to grow: setup checklist done, catalog connected, a board plan, 30 written Pins, a weekly posting rhythm with seasonal dates, and a 90-day results sheet, ready for the client to approve and publish.

ORG.when: When the owner asks what to post on Instagram this month, posts without a plan, has a launch or sale month coming, or reach is flat. Not for just a list of Reel ideas.
ORG.tune: hero products are chosen by gross profit and stock instead of popularity; volume is set from the team's real hours; every post carries one metric tied to a reach or selling goal; and pay-on-delivery, prepaid and language rules for each market are built into the selling posts.
ORG.title: Thirty-day Instagram calendar
ORG.outcome: one sheet with 30 days of posts, Reels and story sets, each with a dated slot, product, goal, hook, first frame, caption, call to action and judging metric, plus a one-screen summary and a mid-month review rule, ready to shoot and schedule once the client approves.

ORG.when: When the owner wants to send free product to influencers or creators before any paid deal, or past gifting brought few posts. Not for finding and vetting which creators fit.
ORG.tune: the payback rule (sales profit plus reusable content against full landed cost) is set before a single parcel ships; gifts go only to creators who asked and carry no posting obligation, which keeps reactions honest and legal; the plan assumes a realistic posting rate instead of hoping for one; and...
ORG.title: Influencer gifting campaign
ORG.outcome: a seeding plan for one round (usually 20 to 100 creators): the recipient list with units and cost, the ask and gift note, a code and link per creator, a dated dispatch and follow-up calendar, and a payback sheet with the 30-day and 60-day verdict rule.

ORG.when: When the owner has run out of Reel ideas, has a shoot day coming, or product videos get views from followers only. Not for a dated month of posts.
ORG.tune: every idea starts from a sourced product seed (reviews, questions, specs) instead of a trend list; ideas are scored on gross profit, ease and proof before anyone shoots; audio rights and claims are checked before the shoot; and winning Reels have a clear path into ads.
ORG.title: Reel ideas from your products
ORG.outcome: a sheet of twenty Reel ideas, scored and ranked, each tied to one product with its hook, first frame, shot list, audio, caption opener and proof source, ready for a phone shoot and for the content calendar.

ORG.when: When customers tag the store in photos or videos and the owner wants to reshare them on social, the website, emails or ads, with a recorded yes. Not for paid creator contracts.
ORG.tune: nothing is used without a register row holding the exact ask, the exact yes and a screenshot; paid-ad rights are always a separate ask with an expiry; incentives trigger the right label for each market; and past reshares are cleaned up rather than ignored.
ORG.title: Repost customer content with permission
ORG.outcome: a rights register sheet, ready permission messages for four scopes, a weekly find-ask-record routine, and a use checklist that blocks any customer photo or video without a recorded yes, ready for the social and ad teams once the client approves the wording.

ORG.when: When the ad folder is full but the social feed is empty, ads and posts are made by different people, or a winning ad has an idea followers have never seen. Not for making new ads from old winners.
ORG.tune: winners are picked by profit against gross profit per order, not ROAS; organic rights are checked asset by asset before anything is reposted; each winner becomes three native formats with different goals; and the routine runs both ways, sending organic winners back to ads.
ORG.title: Repurpose ads into organic posts
ORG.outcome: a one-hour weekly routine with a winners sheet, a rights check, and three ready organic posts per winning ad (Reel recut, carousel, story set) with captions, plus a return list of organic winners for the ad team, ready for the client to approve and post.

ORG.when: When posts get comments like 'price?' or 'link?' that never become sales, or before turning on Instagram comment-to-DM automation. Not for WhatsApp sales chats or general comment reply rules.
ORG.tune: the single private reply is written to sell on its own because the platform allows no second message until the buyer answers; prices are public, not hidden behind DMs; each keyword is unique so every post's sales and gross profit can be counted; and automation is labelled, with a person behind it.
ORG.title: Sell in Instagram DMs
ORG.outcome: a DM sales kit: a keyword plan for the next 8 posts, a first-DM template per post type, reply flows for price, size, delivery and story replies, a hand-off card, tracked links, and a weekly sheet reading orders and gross profit per post.

ORG.when: When the owner wants to start an affiliate program, asks what commission to offer, or the current program pays for sales the store would have got anyway. Not for TikTok Shop affiliate creators.
ORG.tune: the commission is a ceiling worked back from each product group's own gross profit, not an industry rate; commission is held past the return window and paid on pay-on-delivery orders only after delivery; brand bidding and coupon-site leaks are banned in the terms from day one; and a free manual route works...
ORG.title: Affiliate program setup
ORG.outcome: a program spec (commission, cookie window, holding period, approval and removal rules, banned sources, payout and tax steps), a settings list ready for the client to approve, a terms page draft, and a creative pack of 10 to 15 approved assets with captions and disclosure lines.

ORG.when: When the owner wants to sell live on TikTok (or Instagram or YouTube live) and needs a first show, or a weekly series, that does not flop.
ORG.tune: every live offer is checked for profit at the live price before the show; anchors and giveaways come with their break-even and crowd-size conditions; disclosure lines are written into the script at start, end and every recap; and stores where TikTok Shop is not open get the same plan on Instagram Live and YouTube with...
ORG.title: TikTok LIVE selling plan
ORG.outcome: a show plan for one live (or a 4-week series): the product and offer table, a minute-by-minute run of show, the full host script, a promotion schedule, a staffing sheet with roles, a tech and stock checklist, and a post-show readout template.

ORG.when: When a TikTok Shop is live but few creators promote it, free samples go out and few videos come back, or commission rates were set without checking profit. Not for an affiliate program on the store's own site.
ORG.tune: every commission rate is capped by the product's own profit after TikTok costs; free samples go only to creators with fit and category sales, with a monthly cap tied to last month's profit; collaboration rules are read in Seller Center on the day instead of copied from guides; and creators are...
ORG.title: TikTok Shop affiliate creators
ORG.outcome: a rate card (open and targeted commission per product), a sample policy, a target list of 30 to 100 creators in priority order, a one-page creator brief, invite and follow-up messages, and a weekly scorecard template.

ORG.when: When the owner wants to run ads for TikTok Shop products, GMV Max spends but profit is unclear, or a Shop sale day is coming. Not for boosting creators' videos with Spark Ads.
ORG.tune: each product's break-even ROI is built from Seller Center settlements including affiliate and ads commissions; the ROI target can never go below that line, whatever TikTok suggests; promotion-day boosts need their own approved cap; and the weekly read is contribution after ads on settlements...
ORG.title: TikTok Shop GMV Max ads
ORG.outcome: a GMV Max plan: a product profit table with break-even ROI per product, the product list for the campaign, ROI target and daily budget, creative and affiliate rules, the drafted campaign settings, and a weekly profit read sheet, ready for the owner's yes.

ORG.when: When the owner asks which influencers actually bring sales, creator spend is growing, before rebooking anyone, or the profit team needs creator costs in the P&L.
ORG.tune: every creator is judged on gross profit against full cost, including product, shipping and commission fees; pay-on-delivery orders count only when delivered; codes, links and survey answers are merged without double counting, with survey-only sales kept apart; and the rebook call has written rules that also...
ORG.title: Track creator sales
ORG.outcome: a code and link naming rule, a filled creator results sheet (one row per creator per month), a one-screen summary of who to rebook, renegotiate or drop, and a 30-minute monthly routine to keep it current.

ORG.when: When a vetted shortlist exists and nobody has written to the creators yet, and the store needs the first DM or email and the follow-ups.
ORG.tune: every offer carries a number capped by the store's own profit per order; the deal type changes by tier instead of one rate card; gift messages say posting is optional and ask for a label, which keeps the store inside US, UK and EU rules; and creators get messages in their own posting...
ORG.title: Influencer outreach messages
ORG.outcome: a message pack for each creator on the shortlist: one personal first message, follow-up 1 and follow-up 2, the offer terms for their tier, and four reply templates, ready for the client to approve and send.

ORG.when: When the owner wants to start on YouTube Shorts, already makes Reels or TikToks and wants a second short-video channel, or wants buyers who search on YouTube.
ORG.tune: the route to the store is built on YouTube's real link rules (related video to a long video with the clickable link) instead of a dead URL in the caption; products are chosen by gross profit; audio and AI disclosure are checked before upload; and results are read as store sessions and orders, not...
ORG.title: YouTube Shorts plan
ORG.outcome: a 60-day Shorts plan with channel setup done, three formats, a dated list of the first 24 Shorts with hooks and related video links, two to four long product videos that carry the store link, and a results sheet that tracks store visits and orders, ready for the client to approve and publish.

ORG.when: When you have posted for a few weeks and cannot tell which kind of post works.
ORG.tune: Give it at least 20 posts with views, shares, saves, comments and the share of views from non-followers. Judge by your goal, shares for growth and comments for buyers, and turn a format that wins again and again into a named series (ORG-0019, ORG-0011).

ORG.when: When your product videos get few views and you think the first three seconds are the problem.
ORG.tune: Give it the product, the post idea and the buyer it is for. Keep on-screen hook text short and simple, and make sure the first frame shows the product being used (ORG-0016, ORG-0017).

ORG.when: When you have a product and a phone and want a plan for what videos to film this week.
ORG.tune: Tell it who can go on camera, what the product does on screen and who buys it. Pick two or three expert formats or a numbered series that shows the product every time, and post many videos on one topic for one buyer (ORG-0015, ORG-0018, ORG-0023).

ORG.when: When your store's social posts get few views and you want to rule out setup problems first.
ORG.tune: List each account, its country settings and its last 20 posts with views. Creator-style accounts set up in the target country usually reach further than brand accounts, and one hero platform plus email beats spreading thin (ORG-0013, ORG-0022).

ORG.when: When one of your posts got far more views than usual and you want to run it as an ad.
ORG.tune: Give it 30 or more recent posts with views so it can find real outliers against your normal. Run a post that beat your usual views by a wide margin as-is first, and ignore high-view rival videos with low engagement, since those are often paid (ORG-0035, ORG-0010).

ORG.when: When your videos get views but few people reach your store or email list.
ORG.tune: Give it a free guide, size chart or quiz worth a comment, your DM tool and your Klaviyo list setup. Swap link-in-bio for a comment keyword, but keep calls to action off posts until they reach steady views (ORG-0021, ORG-0014).

ORG.when: When you want a steady supply of creator videos for ads without paying a studio.
ORG.tune: Give it product cost, shipping cost, margin and how many videos you need a month. Tier creators by job, a few for authority and many smaller ones for volume, and keep partner-ad terms in writing (ORG-0004, ORG-0009).

ORG.when: When a creator sends you a price and you cannot tell if it is fair.
ORG.tune: Give it your recent Meta CPM, the creator's last 10 video views and your product and postage cost. Price the post off your own paid reach, and offer a floor or a commission for shop sellers rather than a share of ad spend (ORG-0041, ORG-0036).

ORG.when: When you want to find creators yourself instead of paying an agency.
ORG.tune: Describe your buyer from reviews and order data, the platforms they use and the hours your team has. Scouts should match creators to the buyer, not to follower counts (ORG-0040, ORG-0004).

ORG.when: When you have long videos or lots of footage that could be cut into many short clips by other people.
ORG.tune: Give it your footage, a capped budget, a do-not-say list and who approves clips. Pay only for approved clips, re-post stories that already won in new formats, and get claims checked first (ORG-0037, ORG-0026).

ORG.when: When the founder wants to post regular videos and keeps running out of ideas.
ORG.tune: Feed it real buyer questions from support tickets, reviews and DMs. Keep most videos tightly on the exact buyer, give help without asking for the sale, and stick to one topic long enough for the platform to learn who to show it to (ORG-0001, ORG-0003, ORG-0023).

ORG.when: When you want to sell through live auctions or live shows and need a run order and a profit check.
ORG.tune: Give it your stock list with costs, show length and current follower count. Start with many short shows if you have no audience, promote big shows three times, and check giveaways and low opening bids against margin (ORG-0005, ORG-0006, ORG-0007, ORG-0008).

ORG.when: When a creator or athlete already uses your product daily and you are thinking about a long deal.
ORG.tune: Describe the person, how long they have used the product and your company's stage. Sign only people who already use it, think in multi-year terms, and take the outline to a lawyer and accountant (ORG-0039, ORG-0034).

ORG.when: When you want buyers or a launch waitlist to bring in new customers.
ORG.tune: Give it product margin, repeat rate and what you can give as a reward. For a launch, product rewards that grow with each referral can beat cash, so read ORG-0030 before choosing rewards.

ORG.when: When you want to rethink where your buyers really pay attention and what free help would earn it.
ORG.tune: Bring your last month of posts, the platforms your buyers use and what you sell. Use the lens to plan useful posts with no ask, and let paid ads carry the selling (ORG-0003, ORG-0022).

ORG.when: After a vetted shortlist and message pack exist, when outreach is spread across team inboxes and nobody knows who replied, or when creator posts went live without clear labels.
ORG.tune: every send is a batch the owner approved, from the owner's own accounts, with one store contact per creator; follow-ups stop at two; terms are written once in a deal summary before anything ships; every post is checked against the label rules of the creator's market (FTC in the US, ASA in the UK), with label times by video length, before further fees are paid.
ORG.title: Influencer outreach pipeline
ORG.outcome: a pipeline sheet with one row and a dated stage per creator from draft to label check, a batch send plan, a deal summary for every yes, and a weekly one-screen status.

EML.when: When emails land in spam or promotions, opens, clicks or email revenue have fallen for weeks, or on taking over an email and SMS account.
EML.tune: every gap is sized in gross profit with the store's own best period as the target and labelled as attributed, not proven; deliverability is fixed before anything else; and the API path is read-only through a connector or a key the owner keeps, never pasted into chat.
EML.title: Email account health audit
EML.outcome: a checklist table of email and SMS setup checks with pass or fail and money at stake, a flow table, a numbered change list for approval and an audit CSV file.

EML.when: When the owner wants one campaign or flow email written from what worked in the store's own past emails, and there are at least three months of send history. Not for a full welcome, cart or sale series.
EML.tune: the patterns come from the store's own clicks and revenue per recipient, not opens or a formula list; any discount must pass a gross profit check before it goes in; and every price, deadline, stock count and product claim is traced to a source or cut.
EML.title: Email copy from the store's own history
EML.outcome: one finished email (eight subject lines, preview text, opener, body and call to action) built from patterns in the store's own send history, with a claims check table and a test plan.

EML.when: When the owner asks which automated emails, texts or WhatsApp messages the store should have, needs flows planned from scratch, or wants existing flows sorted by value. Not for writing the messages: this plans the flows.
EML.tune: flows are ranked by the gross profit gap from the store's own numbers, not a standard list; timing comes from the store's real days between orders and usage cycles; every SMS and WhatsApp step must pay for itself; and stores that offer pay on delivery get order confirmation and prepaid nudges tied to failed-delivery losses.
EML.title: Email, SMS and WhatsApp flow plan
EML.outcome: a ranked flow build plan for email, SMS and WhatsApp, with every message's trigger, delay, purpose, exit rule and target metric, ready for a builder to set up in Klaviyo or a similar tool.

EML.when: When every email goes to the whole list, the account has dozens of unused segments, or the owner asks who each campaign should go to and which groups to exclude (segments in Klaviyo or a similar tool).
EML.tune: buyer windows come from the store's own reorder gap; engagement ignores Apple privacy opens; active subscribers, open complaints and buyers who keep refusing delivery are excluded from every campaign by default; and each segment carries a size check so tiny segments never feed a split test.
EML.title: Email segments that matter
EML.outcome: a segment sheet of fourteen segments, each with its purpose, the Klaviyo definition written line by line, a size check against the list, where it is used, and a naming convention, plus a cleanup list of old segments to retire.

EML.when: When the owner tests email subject lines every week but revenue never moves, or asks what to A/B test in emails and texts and whether the list is big enough to tell.
EML.tune: every test is sized with the sum shown before it runs, so small lists stop chasing order effects they cannot see; flow timing and offers are tested before subject lines; results are read in gross profit per recipient after message costs; and a separate holdout answers whether a flow adds sales at...
EML.title: Email A/B test plan
EML.outcome: a ranked test list for the next quarter, each test with its hypothesis, the metric that decides it, the sample needed per variant against what the list can supply, how long it runs, and the reading rule, plus a results log that records gross profit per recipient, not just opens.

EML.when: When few visitors sign up, the popup covers the page as soon as it loads, or the owner wants a better sign-up offer to grow the email, SMS or WhatsApp list.
EML.tune: the offer is chosen by gross profit per subscriber rather than sign-up rate; mobile triggers protect both the product view and search ranking; speed is measured before and after with old popup code removed; and chat-first markets get a phone-first form with a WhatsApp opt-in and a sender registration check.
EML.title: Grow the email and SMS list with popups
EML.outcome: a ready-to-build popup spec (offer, triggers, page rules, both form steps with every line of copy and consent text, success screen), the offer cost per subscriber in gross profit, a before-and-after speed check, and a test plan sized to the store's traffic.

EML.when: When the owner asks what emails and texts to send this month, or campaigns are decided on the morning they go out. Not for automated flows.
EML.tune: every send is checked against stock cover before it is planned; offer sends come only from the profit plan's allowed depths; each send carries an attributed gross profit goal that adds up to the month's target; and each market's moving holiday and festival dates and courier cutoffs are planned from the current year's calendar.
EML.title: Monthly email and SMS calendar
EML.outcome: a calendar sheet for one month with every campaign send (date, day, time, channel, segment, theme, products, offer, gross profit goal, writer, approval status), a one-screen summary, and the stock and profit checks that each send passed.

EML.when: When customers run out and forget to reorder, the owner wants 'time to restock' reminders for used-up products, or one fixed 30-day reminder goes out for every product. Not for the full sequence after a first order.
EML.tune: each reminder day comes from cleaned reorder gaps counted from delivery and checked against the label's usage cycle; days scale with the quantity bought; stock-outs pause the branch before the flow sells what the store cannot ship; and success is a reorder lift over a holdout, not attributed...
EML.title: Replenishment reminder timing
EML.outcome: a table of reminder days for every used-up product (first and second reminder, scaled by quantity, with the evidence behind each day) and a flow build spec a builder can set up as written, with a 10% holdout to prove the reminders add reorders.

EML.when: When every customer gets the same campaigns, one-time buyers from two years ago and regulars alike, and the owner wants buyers grouped by how recently, how often and how much they buy (RFM).
EML.tune: recency cutoffs come from the store's own reorder gap instead of fixed defaults; spend is scored on gross profit so heavy returners never pass as top customers; frequency uses order counts so one-order-heavy lists still split; and phone-only buyers, pay-on-delivery buyers and failed deliveries are handled before anyone is scored.
EML.title: Customer segments by recency, frequency and spend
EML.outcome: one sheet with every customer scored 1 to 3 on recency, frequency and gross profit, grouped into seven named segments, plus a one-page plan per group (goal, message type, channel, offer rule, frequency cap, exit) and the matching segment definitions for the email tool.

EML.when: When the owner wants to send WhatsApp offers and broadcasts, move from the WhatsApp Business app to the API, or a number was restricted. Not for answering buyers' chats one to one.
EML.tune: journeys go live before any broadcast; every template is sorted so no offer hides in a utility message; each journey and broadcast is costed at the current per-message rate against gross profit; pay-on-delivery confirmation and a prepaid nudge are tied to the store's real failed-delivery cost; and India's COD and RTO specifics go to Ishita (ishita-india-commerce).
EML.title: WhatsApp marketing setup
EML.outcome: a setup checklist for the account and number, the opt-in wording for each capture point, a starter template set (category, purpose, variables, button) ready to submit, the catalog link steps, a journey list, written broadcast rules with a size and cost sheet, and a weekly quality check.

EML.when: When the store is about to send its first marketing SMS or WhatsApp and the owner asks what consent, sender registration (DLT in India, 10DLC in the US), quiet hours and opt-out rules apply. Not for setting up the WhatsApp account and templates.
EML.tune: one register covers each country's SMS sender registration (such as US 10DLC) and WhatsApp opt-in side by side; every subscriber without a consent record is suppressed rather than guessed; a monthly STOP test proves opt-outs reach every tool; the skill names what a lawyer must confirm instead of giving rulings; and India's DLT registration goes to Ishita (ishita-india-commerce).
EML.title: SMS and WhatsApp compliance
EML.outcome: a compliance register per market and channel (consent wording, what is recorded, sender registration status, template status, quiet hours, opt-out handling, frequency disclosure), a setup checklist with owners and dates, and a monthly audit sheet, plus a short "confirm with a lawyer" list.

EML.when: When repeat orders slip, many past buyers have gone quiet, or the owner is about to send a 'we miss you' discount to everyone. Not for writing the win-back emails: this decides who gets which offer.
EML.tune: the lapse line comes from the store's own reorder gap; every offer is capped so the returning order still earns gross profit; complainers, returners and repeat parcel refusers are fixed or excluded instead of discounted; and success is read from a holdout, not attributed revenue.
EML.title: Win back lapsed customers
EML.outcome: a lapsed-customer sheet split into five groups, an offer ladder per group with the maximum discount each can carry and still earn gross profit, the contact sequence and channel per group, the sunset cutoff, and a holdout design to measure what came back.

EML.when: When people add to cart or start checkout but leave, and the store's recovery emails are missing, run on one trigger, or open with a discount by default. Not for shoppers who only viewed a product.
EML.tune: a written discount rule tied to gross profit, new versus returning buyer and a real enforced expiry, decided before any copy; each email answers a ranked reason from the store's own checkout data; pay-on-delivery and prepaid shoppers get different messages; and the text follows each market's exact consent rules.
EML.title: Abandoned cart and checkout emails
EML.outcome: seven recovery emails and one text written in full (three for added to cart, four for started checkout, one text alongside checkout email 1), a timing and exit sheet, and a one-page discount rule with its gross profit check, ready to load as drafts for the client to approve.

EML.when: When known shoppers look at products but leave without adding to cart, and the store has no browse email or one generic one for everyone. Not for people who left items in the cart.
EML.tune: the emails split by the question each product type raises rather than one generic reminder; codes are kept out except the shopper's own unused welcome offer; every fit, result or delivery line is traced to the store's guides, claims list or exact reviews; and identity-matched visitors without...
EML.title: Browse abandonment emails
EML.outcome: two or three browse emails written in full for each of the store's product types (up to four types), with subject lines, preview, body, a dynamic product block spec, timing, entry filters and exit rules, ready to load as drafts for the client to approve.

EML.when: When the owner wants a personal plain-text note from the founder: designed emails feel like ads, a launch or comeback is coming, or a welcome, cart or sale sequence needs a closing email.
EML.tune: the email comes from a short founder interview and their own writing, and only goes out after the founder approves every line; every fact is on a checked fact sheet; replies have an owner and a written plan; and the win-back version separates unhappy buyers so they get a fix, not a sales pitch.
EML.title: Founder plain-text email
EML.outcome: one plain-text founder email written in full (two subject lines, preview, body of about 120 to 250 words, one text link, P.S.) in a launch version or a win-back version, plus the interview notes it came from, a fact sheet, and a reply plan with the three likely replies and answers, ready for the founder to read, edit and approve.

EML.when: When the store sends only order confirmations, or asks for a review before the parcel arrives, and needs the first 30 days of emails after an order written in full. Not for timing reorders to win a second order.
EML.tune: timing comes from the store's delivery data and each product's time to a felt result; selling pauses whenever there is an open problem; the review ask follows Google and FTC rules, the same ask to every buyer; and order messages stay free of offers so they remain transactional in the US and...
EML.title: Post-purchase emails, first 30 days
EML.outcome: five post-purchase emails written in full (thank-you, reassurance, how-to, check-in, review request) with two subject lines, preview, body, button and timing each, first-buyer and repeat-buyer branches, and the exit and pause rules, ready to load as drafts for the client to approve.

EML.when: When a new product, flavour, colour or collection goes live in two to four weeks and the owner needs teaser, early-access, launch and last-call emails. Not for a sale on existing products.
EML.tune: waitlist and VIP customers get time, not deeper discounts; last-call emails exist only when something truly ends and nothing is quietly extended; stock counts, ship dates and tester quotes are checked on the day; and resends go to engaged non-clickers rather than unreliable non-openers.
EML.title: Product launch email sequence
EML.outcome: a launch sequence of seven to nine emails written in full (teasers, waitlist and VIP early access, launch, proof, questions, last call), each with two subject lines, preview, body, button, send date and time and target segment, plus a segment map and a stock and claims sheet, ready to load as drafts for the client to approve.

EML.when: When the owner needs one email, plus a matching SMS or WhatsApp text, for a one-day offer, a weekend sale, a bundle or a free-gift deal. Not for a multi-day sale series like Black Friday.
EML.tune: nothing is written until the offer clears gross profit, stock and price history; one offer sentence locks every number across email, terms and text; the email replaces a weaker send instead of piling on; and the text version follows the real US, UK and EU sending rules.
EML.title: Promotional campaign email
EML.outcome: one campaign email written in full (three subject lines, preview, headline, body, button, offer terms block) and one text version (SMS under 160 characters, or a WhatsApp marketing template), with the segment, send time and a check table, ready to load as a draft for the client to approve.

EML.when: When a multi-day sale is set (Black Friday and Cyber Monday, Diwali or another festival or holiday sale, an end-of-season sale or the brand's own sale days) and each day needs its email. Not for a single one-day offer email.
EML.tune: urgency is real by rule (one written end, timers that never reset, no extension of a final sale); one terms block locks every number; every send has a daily stop check on spam, unsubscribes, stock and terms; and the sale is held to break-even at each discount depth while subscribers and VIPs are...
EML.title: Sale countdown emails
EML.outcome: seven to nine sale emails written in full (announcement, early access, open, best sellers, what is left, final day, final hours), each with two subject lines, preview, body, an identical offer terms block, send time and segment, plus a daily stop-and-check sheet, ready to load as drafts for the client to approve.

EML.when: When the owner wants texts or WhatsApp messages added to existing flows or campaigns: welcome, cart recovery, delivery updates, COD (cash on delivery) confirmation, review asks or sales. Not for live sales chats or the full COD confirmation routine.
EML.tune: every message is written to the channel's hard limits and checked for its true category before submission; each campaign text must pay for itself against gross profit; WhatsApp-first markets get journeys with order confirmation, and SMS meets each country's registration rules; and messages that invite replies come with a written...
EML.title: SMS and WhatsApp messages
EML.outcome: a message set for the store's flows and campaigns (up to 12 messages), each as exact SMS text or a WhatsApp template with category, header, body, footer, buttons, variables and sample values, character counts, send timing and a cost per send, ready to submit for template approval or load as drafts once the client says yes.

EML.when: When an email is written and the owner wants subject lines and preview text that earn clicks and orders, not just opens. Not for writing the email body.
EML.tune: every subject must be paid off by a named line in the email; angles are spread so the test teaches the store something; Gmail's and US law's honesty rules are checked pair by pair, not just a spam word list; and results are judged on clicks and revenue, never inflated opens.
EML.title: Subject lines and preview text
EML.outcome: ten subject line and preview text pairs for one send, grouped into five angles with two pairs each, every pair with its character counts, the email line that pays it off, a pass on the spam and honesty check, and a recommended pair plus a test pair, ready to paste into the email platform.

EML.when: When every email is a discount, the list is tired, or the owner wants a regular newsletter people open by habit, one that teaches or entertains and still sells.
EML.tune: every topic comes from the store's own tickets, reviews or product facts; each issue gives the reader something to use today before it sells; claims come only from the approved list kept in one shared file; and the series is sized to what the team can keep up and judged on clicks and revenue per...
EML.title: Value newsletter email
EML.outcome: one newsletter issue written in full (two subject lines, preview, body of about 200 to 350 words, one product tie-in, P.S.), the repeatable format sheet for the series, and a bank of the next eight issue topics with their source and product link, ready to load as a draft for the client to approve.

EML.when: When new subscribers get no welcome emails or a generic set copied from a template, or the owner asks whether to give a sign-up discount and how big.
EML.tune: the offer is costed against gross profit per order and checked against repeat behaviour by discount code before any copy is written; every deadline must be enforced by the platform; each email answers a doubt taken from the store's own reviews and tickets; and there is always a no-discount...
EML.title: Welcome email series
EML.outcome: four to six welcome emails written in full (two subject lines, preview text, body, button and P.S. each), a timing and exit sheet, and a one-page offer decision with its gross profit check, ready to load as drafts in the email platform for the client to approve.

EML.when: When first-time buyers rarely come back, the win-back email is one generic coupon, or the list is about to be cleaned, and the emails need writing in full. Not for deciding which lapsed groups to target.
EML.tune: unhappy buyers are pulled out and sent a fix, not a coupon; the start date comes from the store's own reorder gap per product; offers escalate only to the smallest rung that keeps gross profit above zero; and the series ends in an honest keep-me choice and a sunset rule based on clicks and site...
EML.title: Win-back email series
EML.outcome: a win-back series of three to four emails written in full (two subject lines, preview, body, button each), a fix-first note for unhappy buyers, the offer ladder with its gross profit check, timing from the store's own reorder gap, and the sunset step with its suppression rule, ready to load as drafts for the client to approve.

EML.when: When your email flows were set up a while ago and nobody has checked which ones are missing or firing on the wrong trigger.
EML.tune: Feed it a Klaviyo flow export (trigger, filters, delays, message count) plus last 90 days of flow revenue per recipient. The usual store trap is an 'abandoned cart' flow that really fires on Checkout Started, so check EML-0018 and EML-0019 first and compare delays to EML-0064.

EML.when: When people join your list through a pop-up but the welcome flow is still the default or earns little.
EML.tune: Give it the sign-up offer, top five sellers from a Shopify sales-by-product report, founder story and three real reviews. Read EML-0047 and EML-0058 before picking the offer size, and keep the first 72 hours dense as in EML-0060.

EML.when: When your cart emails give away a code in the first message or only start once checkout begins.
EML.tune: Bring gross margin per order, shipping and returns terms and current flow timing from Klaviyo. Build a separate Added to Cart flow (EML-0018), hold any discount until late in the flow (EML-0044), and if you also text, send email and SMS together as in EML-0012.

EML.when: When past buyers have gone quiet and your win-back still fires at the tool's default 90 days.
EML.tune: Pull days between first and second order from a Shopify order export so the trigger matches your real reorder gap, not a template. Screen out buyers with a return or complaint first (EML-0050), and for subscriptions time the offer as in EML-0006.

EML.when: When your product gets used up and most buyers still order only once.
EML.tune: Give it how many days one unit lasts per product and real delivery times, then time reminders near 75 percent of use (EML-0049). Most second orders land inside 30 days (EML-0062), so check the stage split in EML-0053 before adding offers.

EML.when: When first-time and repeat buyers get the same flow emails and the same discounts.
EML.tune: Give it your flow list and how you define new, returning and loyal from Shopify order counts. Split at the top of each flow (EML-0053) and keep active subscribers out of sale sends (EML-0001).

EML.when: When your pop-up signs up only a small share of visitors and you do not know what to change first.
EML.tune: Give it current pop-up sign-up rate, average order value and margin. Ask for the phone on step two with the same offer (EML-0038), and check the offer against your subscription offer so the pop-up does not undercut it (OFF-0037).

EML.when: When you send every campaign to your whole list and your open rate keeps sliding.
EML.tune: Give it list size, send pace and the Klaviyo fields you have for opens, clicks, site visits and orders. Define engaged without Apple privacy opens (EML-0011) and set a clear unengaged rule (EML-0042) before any suppression.

EML.when: When you have just set up or switched your email tool, or email revenue looks too good to be true.
EML.tune: Paste SPF, DKIM and DMARC records plus Klaviyo smart sending and attribution settings. Check the attribution window against EML-0013 and EML-0056 before trusting any flow revenue number.

EML.when: When opens have dropped for weeks and your emails seem to be landing in spam or promotions.
EML.tune: Bring 60 days of campaign results by segment and spam complaint counts from Klaviyo. Follow the narrow-then-widen pacing in EML-0021, judge recovery against EML-0059, and clean out only after the consent check.

EML.when: When you only email around sales and want a steady plan for the month.
EML.tune: Give it monthly revenue, list size, launch and restock dates and who writes each send. Set the pace from EML-0041 and the content mix from EML-0016, and plan one owned moment per quarter (EML-0055).

EML.when: When you need to decide which launches and sales deserve a text this month and how often to send.
EML.tune: Give it SMS list size, cost per text and last month's SMS click and unsubscribe rates. Start from about one campaign a week (EML-0025, EML-0039) and let a holdout settle frequency as in EML-0036.

EML.when: When a text is written and you want its cost and rule problems checked before it goes to the whole list.
EML.tune: Paste the exact text, list size and send time. Watch for one extra character or an emoji doubling the billed parts (EML-0024), and use images only where EML-0028 says they pay.

EML.when: When the month ends and you want to know what your email and texts really earned and what broke.
EML.tune: Feed Klaviyo campaign and flow exports, Shopify orders for the same dates and list growth. Read revenue per recipient by cohort (EML-0057) rather than attributed share, which EML-0056 warns mostly measures opens.

EML.when: When your buyers already chat on WhatsApp, as many do in Brazil, Mexico and much of Europe, and you want to sell and answer questions there.
EML.tune: Give it opt-in counts, order volume and your top support questions. Lean on automated journeys over broadcasts (EML-0048), and only message people who opted in, since the number can be banned.

SEO.when: When Google shows the store's products without price or star ratings, after installing a review app, or when Search Console reports structured data (product schema) errors.
SEO.tune: it audits and removes the theme and app blocks that clash before adding anything; ratings are marked up only from verified reviews shown on the page; variant, sale and out-of-stock pages are tested, not just one product; and it tells the client plainly what rich results Google no longer shows.
SEO.title: Product schema and rich results
SEO.outcome: a schema audit of each page template (what exists, what is broken, what is duplicated), a JSON-LD spec per template mapped to Shopify fields, the theme changes on a duplicate theme, and a test log showing each template passing the Rich Results Test, ready for the client to publish.

SEO.when: When Google Search Console shows many 'Duplicate without user-selected canonical' or 'Crawled, currently not indexed' pages, or the store has near-empty or copied product and collection pages. Not for a full technical SEO check.
SEO.tune: no page with clicks, links or sales is removed without a redirect; each decision uses the store's own 12-month data and gross profit; Shopify's three hiding methods are chosen by what else they switch off, including AI channel listing; and rewrites are batched and human-reviewed instead of...
SEO.title: Fix duplicate and thin pages
SEO.outcome: a page decision sheet (URL, type, clicks, links, orders, decision, target, how to apply), a redirect CSV for Shopify's bulk import, a rewrite list for the pages worth saving, and a one-screen summary, ready for the client to approve.

SEO.when: When key collection or product pages sit on Google's first or second page (positions 4 to 20) and need a push from links on the store's own pages.
SEO.tune: link targets are chosen by gross profit and near-win position, not by gut; strength is traced from pages with real outside links using free Search Console data; template blocks fix every page at once before manual links; and stock decides whether a product or its collection gets the link.
SEO.title: Internal linking plan
SEO.outcome: a link sheet listing every link to add or change (from page, to page, anchor text, placement, reason), link block rules for each page template, an orphan and dead-end fix list, and a one-screen summary, ready for the client to approve.

SEO.when: When opening a second country, Google shows the wrong country's pages, hreflang errors appear, or before translating the store. Not for opening a country in Shopify with its prices and currency.
SEO.tune: no market gets SEO work until its landed gross profit is positive; a language is published only when its main content is truly translated and reviewed; same-language markets with different prices still get their own tags; and the test log proves reciprocity and Google's chosen canonical for each...
SEO.title: SEO for selling in more than one country
SEO.outcome: a market structure decision (subfolders, domains or separate store) with the runner-up, an hreflang map for every market version, a translation and localisation list by page, a test log showing tags are reciprocal and valid, and a one-screen summary, ready for the client to approve.

SEO.when: When the owner asks what buyers search for on Google, or collection and product pages are about to be written or rewritten and need target keywords. Not for picking blog post topics.
SEO.tune: pages are ranked by gross profit per order and stock, not search volume; intent is read from the live results page in each selling country; clashes come from the store's own Search Console data; and mixed-language and pay-on-delivery buyer terms are part of the seed list.
SEO.title: Keyword research for collections and products
SEO.outcome: a keyword map sheet with one row per collection and product URL (primary keyword, variants, monthly searches, intent, difficulty, CPC, gross profit per order, priority), a list of page clashes to fix, up to 10 new collection ideas, and a one-screen 90-day focus plan.

SEO.when: When collection pages do not show up on Google or sit below the top results, after keyword research, or when new collections are added.
SEO.tune: collections are worked in order of gross profit and near-win position; filters become indexable collections only when search, stock and margin all agree; copy is checked to be in the page HTML for AI crawlers; and handle changes always carry a redirect and a client yes.
SEO.title: Collection pages that rank
SEO.outcome: a collection SEO sheet for the top 5 to 15 collections (title tag, meta description, H1, handle, intro copy, below-grid guide, sub-collection links, filter decisions), a redirect list for any changed handle, and a theme fix list, ready for the client to approve and publish.

SEO.when: When traffic from Google drops, after a site move or theme change, before an SEO push, or when pages will not show up in Google. Not for writing page titles and copy.
SEO.tune: each Search Console reason is translated into its usual Shopify cause; issues are ranked by the gross profit of the pages they hide; AI crawlers and CDN bot settings are part of the audit; and risky edits like robots.txt.liquid need their own client yes.
SEO.title: Technical SEO audit for Shopify
SEO.outcome: a ranked issue list (issue, URLs affected, gross profit at stake, fix, owner, how to verify), a redirect sheet ready to import, a theme fix list for a duplicate theme, and a one-screen summary of what to fix this week.

SEO.when: When product images have empty or file-name alt text, after a big catalogue upload, before a translated market launches, or when an accessibility check fails.
SEO.tune: each image is drafted from what it actually shows, sorted by type, with variant colours tied to the store's own option names; a measured review sample with a stop rule catches errors before import; and image problems that block Shopping or slow pages are flagged on the same pass.
SEO.title: Image alt text for the whole catalog
SEO.outcome: an import-ready Shopify product CSV with alt text for every product image, a pattern sheet per image type, a review log with error rate and fixes, and a one-screen summary, ready for the client to approve and import.

SEO.when: When the owner wants blog posts that bring buyers from Google, such as comparisons, 'best X for' posts and buying guides, once collection and product pages for that topic exist. Not for short answer pages to specific buyer questions.
SEO.tune: topics are ranked by the gross profit of the products they link to; blogs wait until the money pages are ready; every comparison is fair, dated and checked against US, UK and EU rules; and AI drafting is capped and always edited by a named person.
SEO.title: SEO blog posts that sell
SEO.outcome: a 90-day post list (up to 10 topics ranked by profit), plus 3 to 5 posts written in full for this batch, each with a one-page brief and outline, title tag, meta description, product links and a claims file, ready for the client to approve and publish.

SEO.when: When you are deciding whether search is worth your time or an agency's fee for your store.
