SEO.tune: Give it margin per order, order value, monthly hours and cash, and a few target terms with search volume. Search takes months, so if you need sales this quarter expect a not-now answer. Read SEO-0008 and SEO-0013.

SEO.when: When you have a few hours a month for search and want one routine you can repeat.
SEO.tune: Give it your platform, catalogue size and Search Console access. Put collection pages before blog posts, since they carry most organic revenue on stores with many products. Read SEO-0001 and SEO-0003.

SEO.when: When you have a pile of keyword ideas and need to know which ones deserve a page.
SEO.tune: Paste keyword exports from Google Keyword Planner, Ahrefs or Semrush with volume and difficulty, plus your product list. Keep terms with buying intent and difficulty a small store can win, and drop terms for things you do not sell. Read SEO-0008.

SEO.when: When you need each page to target its own search term so your pages stop competing.
SEO.tune: Give it your catalogue, current page addresses and the checked keyword list. Map one topic to one page and mark each as a collection, product or blog page. Read SEO-0012, SEO-0003 and SEO-0011.

SEO.when: When you sell a range but have only a few broad collections and want more ways to be found.
SEO.tune: Give it your product export with tags and attributes plus keyword data. Build a sub-collection for each searched variant, such as a style or a price band, each aimed at one search. Read SEO-0012, SEO-0001 and SEO-0003.

SEO.when: When you are launching a collection, or one ranks poorly with only a name and a product grid.
SEO.tune: Give it the collection, its target keyword and the pages that rank for it now. Put the keyword first in the title and alone in the H1, and show 36 to 48 products per page. Read SEO-0005.

SEO.when: When you are writing or fixing a product page for a product people search for by name.
SEO.tune: Give it supplier specs, your own product facts, reviews and the target term. Put specifications in a table and keep the page live with a back-in-stock note when it sells out. Read SEO-0007 and AEO-0031.

SEO.when: When Search Console shows many duplicate or crawled but not indexed pages on your Shopify store.
SEO.tune: Give it a duplicate of your theme and a crawl or Search Console page indexing export. Make product grid links point to plain product addresses, then rebuild breadcrumbs so they do not depend on the old path. Read SEO-0004.

SEO.when: When a site audit gives you hundreds of warnings and you need the few that matter for sales.
SEO.tune: Paste a crawler export and Search Console page indexing data. Rank fixes on the collection and product pages that earn money first, and ignore warnings on pages nobody visits. Read SEO-0003 and SEO-0013.

SEO.when: When you want a 90-day search plan for one product category instead of spreading effort thin.
SEO.tune: Pick your best-margin category and give it the main rivals and the questions buyers ask. Start with the most-aware searches, such as one brand versus another and alternatives, and cover Google and AI answers together. Read SEO-0009, SEO-0010 and AEO-0024.

SEO.when: When shoppers search for your rivals by name and you want comparison pages built in the right order.
SEO.tune: Give it your top rivals, Search Console queries that name them and honest product facts. Stick to the formats that tend to pay: you versus a rival, alternatives, best for a use, and buying guides. Read SEO-0011 and AEO-0006.

SEO.when: When your collections sit just off page one and rivals have many more sites linking to them.
SEO.tune: Give it your linking domains and those of three rivals from Ahrefs or Semrush. Size the gap against the rival average, point early links at the home page and top collections, and avoid paid links. Read SEO-0006 and SEO-0002.

SEO.when: When you have a few months of Search Console data and want to know what to work on this month.
SEO.tune: Export queries and pages for the last three months. Push pages that rank just off page one with many views, and turn real queries into FAQ answers. Read SEO-0013 and AEO-0005.

SEO.when: When organic clicks fell and you need to know which pages lost them and why.
SEO.tune: Export Search Console by page and query for the drop period and the period before. If the position held but clicks fell, look for an AI answer above you before you change the page. Read AEO-0005 and AEO-0019.

SEO.when: When an SEO or AI search agency sends you a proposal and you are about to sign.
SEO.tune: Paste the proposal, sample reports and any promises about links or page counts. Flag paid link schemes and plans to publish hundreds of AI-written pages, which often rise and then crash. Read SEO-0002, AEO-0018 and AEO-0033.

AEO.when: When buyers keep asking the same detailed questions (sizing, fit, compatibility, care, delivery), or ChatGPT and other AI assistants answer them with rivals' pages. Not for long buying-guide blog posts.
AEO.tune: questions come only from counted buyer sources and logged assistant sub-searches; pages are ranked by the profit of the products they lead to; every section is written to stand alone when quoted, with sourced numbers and honest "no" answers; and delivery, payment and tax questions are answered for each market.
AEO.title: Answer pages for buyer questions
AEO.outcome: a question bank grouped into page topics and ranked by profit, plus 5 to 10 answer pages written in full (title, direct answer, facts table, sections, sources, product links, refresh date), with a claims file, ready for the client to approve and publish.

AEO.when: When buyers say they asked ChatGPT or another AI assistant, rivals get named and the store does not, or assistants describe the store wrongly. Not for the monthly check once fixes are live.
AEO.tune: every change is tied to products with real gross profit and stock; third-party work comes only from sources the assistants actually cited for the store's questions; tactics that fake people, hide paid mentions or plant hidden AI instructions are ruled out; and results are judged against an...
AEO.title: Get recommended by AI assistants
AEO.outcome: a baseline table of 20 to 40 buying questions across assistants (named or not, cited sources), a ranked change list in three layers (found, matched, chosen) with owner and effort, a third-party source work queue, a brand facts page draft, and a one-screen summary, ready for the client to approve.

AEO.when: When products do not show up in ChatGPT, Google or other AI shopping results, before turning on agent checkout, or after a catalogue import with gaps.
AEO.tune: every SKU gets a pass or fail per field agents read, ranked by the gross profit of what fails; policies and price sync are treated as gates that block whole channels; stale app metafields are cleaned because the catalog reads the admin, not the theme; and pay-on-delivery buyers are planned for when an AI channel only takes prepaid.
AEO.title: Product data for AI shopping agents
AEO.outcome: a per-SKU completeness sheet with pass or fail on every field AI shopping channels read, a policy checklist, a channel status table, a ranked fix list with the Shopify field or feed rule for each fix, and a one-screen summary, ready for the client to approve.

AEO.when: When the owner wants a monthly check of whether ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Google's AI answers name the store, once AI visibility fixes have started going live. Not for the first baseline and fix list.
AEO.tune: the panel is weighted to the store's highest-profit products and kept fixed so trends mean something; no-search answers are discounted; mention share is joined to purchases, gross profit and survey answers, not clicks alone; and every finding leaves the report as a fix handed to a named skill.
AEO.title: Track AI answer visibility
AEO.outcome: a monthly report (one screen: mention share by assistant, change since last month, wrong facts, top cited sources, fixes), the filled panel sheet, an AI traffic and survey table, and a fix list handed to the right skills.

AEO.when: When you want one run from shopper questions to a list of who AI names today and the page fixes that close the gap.
AEO.tune: Give it your products, rivals and real customer questions from email, chat and reviews. Save the first run as a baseline so you can rerun the same questions later. Read AEO-0001, AEO-0012 and AEO-0035.

AEO.when: When you want to know if AI search bots can reach and read your product pages before any other AI work.
AEO.tune: Give it your robots.txt, your CDN bot settings and a few product page links. Reload key pages with JavaScript turned off to check that reviews and FAQs still show. Read AEO-0028, AEO-0002 and AEO-0008.

AEO.when: When you need a robots.txt for AI bots and an llms.txt file written for your store.
AEO.tune: Paste your current robots.txt and sitemap address. Allow the AI search crawlers you want, keep cart and account pages blocked, and have a developer apply the files. Read AEO-0028 and AEO-0008.

AEO.when: When you run a Shopify store and want your catalogue data ready for AI shopping tools.
AEO.tune: Give it read access to the Shopify admin so it can check product data, categories and descriptions. AI shopping tools read the back-end catalogue, so fill product category, specs and variants in the admin, not only on the page. Read AEO-0003.

AEO.when: When you need the long, specific questions shoppers ask AI about products like yours.
AEO.tune: Feed it support emails, chat logs, review questions and return reasons. Use the follow-up search wording in page titles, H1s and first sentences, and answer fit and compatibility questions in full. Read AEO-0016 and AEO-0031.

AEO.when: When you want to see which stores AI assistants name for your shopper questions and which sources they cite.
AEO.tune: Run about five core questions in ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini and Google's AI answers, both signed in and signed out. Free ChatGPT may answer without searching, so note whether citations appeared. Read AEO-0001, AEO-0015 and AEO-0012.

AEO.when: When your AI panel shows rivals named and you missing, and you need to know what to fix first.
AEO.tune: Give it the panel results and the rival pages that were cited. Work each engine on its own terms, since Reddit, Google rankings and outside lists each move different engines. Read AEO-0024, AEO-0034 and AEO-0032.

AEO.when: When you want to know which outside sites AI keeps citing so you can get your store onto them.
AEO.tune: Give it five buyer questions and any budget you have for placements or free product. Go after the best-of lists and review sites already cited, and fix wrong facts there first. Read AEO-0029, AEO-0014 and AEO-0001.

AEO.when: When AI tools state a wrong price, size or delivery time for your product, or never quote your page.
AEO.tune: Give it the product page, real specs, shipping and returns rules, and review data. Put facts and a spec table in plain page text that loads without JavaScript. Read AEO-0006, AEO-0002 and AEO-0030.

AEO.when: When a guide, blog post or FAQ ranks in Google but never gets named in AI answers.
AEO.tune: Give it the page plus any original data, tests or customer results you can add. Open with a short direct answer, use question headings with answers that stand alone, and refresh the page often. Read AEO-0023, AEO-0021 and AEO-0009.

AEO.when: When AI and Google show best-of lists for your buyers' question and your store is not on them.
AEO.tune: Give it the buyer question, rival products with real specs and your honest pros and cons. Keep the list fair and place your product only where it truly fits, or readers and AI will discount it. Read AEO-0006, SEO-0011 and AEO-0021.

AEO.when: When an AI assistant tells shoppers the wrong price, returns rule or product detail about your store.
AEO.tune: Paste the AI answers word for word with the date and the tool used. Publish one official facts page and repeat the corrected fact on your site, your social posts and the outside pages AI cites. Read AEO-0011, AEO-0017 and AEO-0014.

AEO.when: When AI answers in your category cite Reddit threads and you want an honest plan to take part.
AEO.tune: Give it the threads AI cites and the team member who will reply under their own name. Answer comparison questions that name rivals in buyer subreddits, and never use hidden brand accounts. Read AEO-0027 and AEO-0024.

AEO.when: When you think AI assistants send you buyers but you cannot see them in your reports.
AEO.tune: Give it your GA4 channel groups, your checkout survey tool and your 404 report. Add an AI channel, add AI assistants to the how-did-you-hear question and redirect the broken links AI sends people to. Read AEO-0020, AEO-0010 and AEO-0008.

AEO.when: When your shipping, returns or privacy pages are thin, buried or hard for AI tools to quote.
AEO.tune: Give it Shopify admin access and policy wording you have already approved. It loads clean text versions, so keep legal review as a separate step. Read AEO-0011 and AEO-0002.

CXP.when: When most customers buy once and never come back, and the owner wants emails and texts timed to each product's real reorder gap to win a second order. Not for writing the first 30 days of emails in full.
CXP.tune: every timing is measured from the store's own reorder percentiles, usage cycles and delivery times; incentives pass a gross profit check and only reach buyers past the median; and buyers with an open return or ticket are taken out of the selling messages until the problem is solved.
CXP.title: Post-purchase repeat-buyer sequence
CXP.outcome: a reorder table per product and a timed email and SMS sequence with subject, preview, body outline and exit rule for every message, plus build notes and a sequence file, ready to set up.

CXP.when: When the owner wants more reviews: a product has few, the review rate is low, reviews say little, or the store wants photo and video reviews. Not for replying to bad reviews.
CXP.tune: asks are timed to when each product has done its job, not a fixed day; prompts make reviews answer real buyer doubts; incentive rules differ by destination under Google and FTC rules; and moderation is equal for good and bad reviews, with WhatsApp and local-language asks where buyers use them.
CXP.title: Review collection system
CXP.outcome: a review request plan per product (timing, channel, question prompts, photo and video ask, incentive rule), the moderation policy, the display plan for product pages, and a monthly tracker, ready to set up in the review app or by hand.

CXP.when: When the support team types the same answers every day, replies differ from agent to agent, or a new support hire needs ready replies in week one. Not for a chatbot's answers.
CXP.tune: macros are ranked by the store's own ticket count times handling time; every reply opens with the facts to check before promising; offer caps come from gross profit per order; and pay-on-delivery refunds, language and tax invoice cases are built in.
CXP.title: Support replies for top tickets
CXP.outcome: twenty saved replies for the twenty most common ticket reasons, each with a trigger tag, the checks to run first, the fill-in fields, a short and a long version, the agent's no-approval offer and the bend-the-rule line, ready to paste into the helpdesk as macros.

CXP.when: When 'where is my order?' is the top support question, contacts per order are rising, or the store is changing courier or 3PL. Not for messages about one delay or stockout.
CXP.tune: tickets are bucketed by the last tracking scan to find the exact anxious moment; the shipped message waits for the first real scan; fulfilment problems are fixed before messages hide them; failed deliveries, pay on delivery and postcode-level delays get their own handling; and India's NDR handling goes to Ishita (ishita-india-commerce).
CXP.title: Cut where-is-my-order tickets
CXP.outcome: a one-page diagnosis of the store's order-status tickets, a tracking page spec, four proactive messages written in full per channel, an order-status FAQ block, and a before and after measure, ready to build at draft level.

CXP.when: When the owner wants a points or rewards program and needs to know if it will pay. Not for a refer-a-friend program or a VIP club for top buyers.
CXP.tune: the program must earn back its cost in extra returning orders, computed from the store's own gross profit; a random holdout, not member spend, decides if it stays; points are never earned on refunded or undelivered orders; and expiry follows the store's real repeat cycle.
CXP.title: Loyalty program design
CXP.outcome: a one-page program design (earn rules, burn rules, expiry, tiers if any), a cost model sheet showing reward cost per order and the break-even lift in repeat gross profit, a holdout test plan, and the launch message set outline, ready for the client to approve and set up.

CXP.when: When the owner wants a refer-a-friend program, or the current one costs more per new buyer than paid ads. Not for points or rewards on repeat orders.
CXP.tune: the reward is capped by the store's own allowed cost per new customer; referrers are paid only after delivery, payment and the return window, so pay-on-delivery orders and refunds cannot be gamed; asks fire at real high points; and the program is kept only if referred buyers beat paid ones on 90-day gross profit.
CXP.title: Referral program design
CXP.outcome: a one-page referral design (reward for both sides, payout timing, rules), a fraud checklist, an ask calendar with the trigger for each ask, five message outlines with exact wording, the terms text, and a tracker that compares referred buyers with paid ones.

CXP.when: When a customer is angry, threatens a bad review or chargeback, or agents either refund too much or argue back. Not for public replies to reviews already posted.
CXP.tune: offer caps by role come from the store's gross profit per order; safety, legal and review-pressure cases are taken out of agents' hands; the playbook aims for one complete reply rather than a delighted recovery; and failed-delivery, language and consumer-helpline cases are built in for each market.
CXP.title: Handle angry customers
CXP.outcome: an escalation playbook the team can use today: a case triage card, the five-move reply with wording per channel, a role-by-role offer ladder with caps, the escalation triggers and owners, and a case log layout.

CXP.when: When one to three star reviews sit unanswered, replies sound defensive, or a run of complaints follows a bad batch or courier problem. Not for an angry customer still in a live chat or email.
CXP.tune: replies are written for the next buyer and sorted by review type; the problem is fixed privately before any public word; nothing is ever traded for a changed review, under Google and FTC rules; and clusters become a product or shipping fix rather than more apologies.
CXP.title: Reply to negative reviews
CXP.outcome: a reply sheet with a public reply (under 80 words) and a private follow-up for every unanswered one to three star review, a report list for reviews that break platform rules, and a cause log, ready for the client to approve and post.

CXP.when: When the owner has no measure of how happy buyers are, scores exist but nobody acts on them, or before building loyalty or referral programs (NPS and satisfaction surveys).
CXP.tune: surveys are timed to when each product has done its job; no survey is sent without a named person to call back unhappy buyers; NPS never gates reviews; and scores are read against the store's own past with response counts shown, with WhatsApp surveys and undelivered orders left out where buyers pay on delivery.
CXP.title: NPS and satisfaction surveys
CXP.outcome: two ready surveys (post-delivery recommend survey and post-ticket satisfaction question) with exact wording and timing, the scoring and reading rules, a close-the-loop routine with reply templates for unhappy buyers, and a monthly score sheet.

CXP.when: When customer messages are scattered across email, WhatsApp, Instagram and site chat, replies get missed, or the store is about to hire or outsource support.
CXP.tune: targets are sized from the store's own workload and hours, not copied from benchmarks; order status volume is sent to a shipping fix before anyone is hired; a free path runs on Gmail and the WhatsApp Business app; and chat-first markets get a WhatsApp-first queue, language queues and call logging for pay-on-delivery checks.
CXP.title: Helpdesk and response time setup
CXP.outcome: a one-page desk design (channels connected, tag list, queues and owners, routing rules, hours and response targets) plus a setup checklist the agent or owner can follow in the chosen tool, and a weekly scorecard layout.

CXP.when: When the store adds a chatbot or AI assistant to site chat or WhatsApp, or the current bot gives wrong or risky answers. Not for sales scripts that people use in chat.
CXP.tune: the bot answers only from approved, sourced text and never invents policy; the handoff rule carries the context so buyers never repeat themselves; launch waits for a 50-chat test with zero invented facts; and WhatsApp escalation, language and payment question rules are built in.
CXP.title: Train a support chatbot
CXP.outcome: a bot knowledge pack (approved question and answer set, order-lookup rules, a never-do list and the handoff rule with its message), a 50-conversation test sheet with pass or fail per answer, and a weekly review sheet, ready to load into any chatbot tool.

CXP.when: When the owner asks what customers complain about most and what it costs: every month, after a launch or bad batch, or when teams blame each other. Not for writing ready replies to tickets.
CXP.tune: themes are ranked by cost per 100 orders, not raw counts; service failures, pre-sale doubts and expectation gaps go to different owners; every fix is measured the next month; and tickets in every buyer language are read in the original.
CXP.title: Turn support tickets into insights
CXP.outcome: a monthly report with the top ten ticket themes ranked by cost, each with counts per 100 orders, two to three verbatim quotes, an owner and a dated fix, a pre-sale doubts list for ads and pages, and a fix tracker that shows whether last month's changes cut tickets.

CXP.when: When a small group of customers brings in much of the profit and the owner wants to reward best customers without discounting, or after customer segments are built. Not for points for every customer.
CXP.tune: VIPs are chosen on 12-month gross profit with heavy returners and parcel refusers removed; every perk is priced per member per year against a written cap; service effort is fixed before any delight is added; and an at-risk alert on each VIP's own buying gap catches slippage before win-back is needed.
CXP.title: VIP customer program
CXP.outcome: a VIP list with the qualifying rule, a perk menu priced per VIP per year and capped against their gross profit, a welcome and keep-buying plan with messages per step, an at-risk alert rule, and a results sheet with a holdout.

CXP.when: When too few buyers come back for a second order and you do not know whether to fix the product, offer, flows or who you acquire.
CXP.tune: Feed it a full Shopify order export with discount codes and first-order source. Split cohorts by discount and ad angle (CXP-0016), and do not read Shopify's returning customer rate as a repeat rate (MEA-0021).

CXP.when: When your inbox fills with 'where is my order' messages and buyers only get the carrier's link.
CXP.tune: Give it monthly orders, WISMO ticket counts from your help desk and real delivery days by region. Rate your WISMO share against CXP-0012, show a padded delivery date (CXP-0010), and send the proactive updates in CXP-0014.

CXP.when: When the only message after an order is the store's plain confirmation and you want more second orders.
CXP.tune: Give it each product's pairings, how-to steps and delivery time. Send the thank-you and cross-sell soon after the order (EML-0062) and mirror the reassurance then how-to order in EML-0051.

CXP.when: When refunds take days, returns cost more than some items are worth, or support needs approval for every fix.
CXP.tune: Bring return rate by product, cost to process one return and refund timing from Shopify. Set keep-it rules for low-value items (CXP-0018) and fast refunds or exchange first (CXP-0007, CXP-0015).

CXP.when: When refunds are a real cost each month and you cannot tell which products or listings cause them.
CXP.tune: Run it monthly on Shopify refunds and return reasons with product, order date and refund date. Remember Shopify books returns on the refund date (MEA-0011), so match each return to its order month before comparing.

CXP.when: When reviews say 'never used' or 'how do I' tickets and returns keep rising.
CXP.tune: Paste return reasons, 2 and 3 star reviews and how-to tickets. Fix effort before adding delight (CXP-0009), and for slow-acting products frame a trial at onboarding (CXP-0003).

CXP.when: When cancels or returns pile up in the first two weeks after a first order.
CXP.tune: Give it time to results, delivery wait and the routine customers use. Front-load messages before delivery and stay quiet in the high-cancel window (EML-0004), and survey for the habit that keeps people (EML-0005).

CXP.when: When subscription churn is high and you do not know which day or message makes people cancel.
CXP.tune: Feed cancels with dates and order numbers from Recharge or Skio, plus the emails subscribers received. Look for the spikes in CXP-0021 and EML-0002, and compute churn the way MEA-0027 does.

CXP.when: When your subscription save rate is low or you only offer a discount to people who cancel.
CXP.tune: Give it cancel reasons with counts and what your portal can show. Benchmark the save rate (CXP-0001), offer skip or delay rather than open pause (CXP-0005), and fix cadence first when 'too much product' leads (OFF-0040).

CXP.when: When your rebill reminder and order receipt are still the plain app default and cancels spike at the first rebill.
CXP.tune: Give it subscription products, rebill schedule and any gift plan. Rebuild the reminder benefits first with the delay button high (EML-0003), and announce gifts ahead rather than surprising (CXP-0006).

CXP.when: When you want something in the box that brings buyers back but need to know if it pays.
CXP.tune: Give it average order value, margin, packaging cost and orders a month. Cost each tier against CXP-0008 and work out the repeat lift needed to break even (CXP-0013) before ordering inserts.

CXP.when: When support must ask before sending a fix or a small gift, or you want to surprise top buyers.
CXP.tune: Give it weekly support cases by type and who can approve spend. Keep delight away from service failures (CXP-0017), set a fixed weekly budget (CXP-0022), and give reps a small no-approval limit (OPS-0009).

CXP.when: When your best buyers get the same treatment as one-time buyers and you want perks that are not discounts.
CXP.tune: Give it customer spend tiers from Shopify and margins. Check first that second orders are healthy, and where buyers respond to points, test expiring coins with reminders (CXP-0019).

CXP.when: When reviews pile up unanswered or you worry a reply to an angry buyer will make things worse.
CXP.tune: Feed it recent reviews from your review app and Google with star, date and product. Reply to fix the problem, not to win praise, since recovery rarely beats no problem at all (CXP-0011).

CXP.when: When you need to decide whether to spend on delight or on making service easier.
CXP.tune: Bring your top ticket reasons and how many steps each takes a customer to solve. Ask it to rank moments by customer effort, using CXP-0009 and CXP-0017 as the bar.

CXP.when: When returns or bad reviews rise for a product, after a new batch or supplier, or once a month for your top sellers.
CXP.tune: Every return is sorted into maker, transit, listing promise or buyer fit before the factory is blamed, defects are costed with the full cost of a return, and the fixed lot is tracked on its own for 90 days.
CXP.title: Link factory defects to your returns
CXP.outcome: A table matching return reasons and review complaints per SKU to factory defects, the cost of each in refunds and lost reviews, and the new checks to add to the defect list and inspections, with a 90-day check on the next lot.

CXP.when: When monthly subscription churn is high, the cancel flow saves under about 15%, cancels jump after a campaign or billing email, or failed payments end subscriptions.
CXP.tune: Cancels are read by day since the first order so each spike gets its own cause and fix, saves and gifts are priced against gross profit, failed payments are recovered by decline type, and cancel stays as easy as sign-up.
CXP.title: Cut subscription churn
CXP.outcome: A churn map by day since the first order, rebuilt billing reminder and confirmation, a cancel flow with one save per reason, failed payment recovery, a subscriber-only calendar and a tracker in cancels per 100 subscribers and gross profit.

COG.when: When the owner asks what a product really costs once it reaches the warehouse (factory price, freight, duty, customs), before a first order, to know if it can make money at the planned price.
COG.tune: freight is split by what set its price; import VAT is kept in its own column because it is cash, not cost, for a registered store; US duty uses the transaction value base; cost is divided by sellable units after defects; and the same sheet runs backwards from the selling price so every quote...
COG.title: Landed cost per unit
COG.outcome: a landed cost sheet (one row per SKU per shipment) with the cost of each unit delivered to the warehouse, the target ceiling worked back from the selling price, and a one-screen note on what moved the number.

COG.when: When products are not selling and cash is tied up in stock, storage fees are rising, a season or expiry date is close, or the warehouse needs room for new stock.
COG.tune: the floor price treats purchase cost as sunk and comes from the cost to sell one more unit by route; the cause check stops discounting products that were only hidden; routes run in a ladder from brand-safe to liquidation with cash counted at 30, 60 and 90 days; and pay-on-delivery, sales tax and "was" price rules for each market are built in.
COG.title: Clear slow-moving stock
COG.outcome: a clearance sheet with a row per slow product (stock, days of cover, floor price, chosen route, markdown steps with dates, expected units and cash back), a one-screen summary of the cash this plan frees in 30, 60 and 90 days, and the draft set-up list for the client to approve.

COG.when: When the owner needs a manufacturer or supplier for a product (Alibaba, IndiaMART, trade fairs or local), a backup to a single supplier, or a cheaper place to make it. Not for comparing price quotes.
COG.tune: the shortlist starts from a target landed cost and signed deal-breakers rather than search results; local checks (tax number match, the safety marks your market needs, how advances are paid) sit beside the global ones; starred red flags cut a supplier outright; and the backup supplier is planned from the first day instead of after...
COG.title: Find and vet suppliers
COG.outcome: a supplier shortlist sheet with 3 to 5 vetted suppliers (and every rejected one with its reason), a red-flag check for each, and the list of who receives the request for quote next.

COG.when: When the owner asks how many units of each product to plan for, a buying cycle is due, or purchase orders need unit numbers per product for the next 13 weeks. Not for when to reorder each product.
COG.tune: weekly series cleaned of stockout and one-off weeks; moving holidays shifted to this year's dates in every market; promotion lift paired with its pull-forward dip; returning-buyer demand built from cohorts; and a weekly bias tracker that fixes the method, not just the number.
COG.title: Demand forecast per product
COG.outcome: a 13-week unit forecast per product or variant (low, base and high) in one sheet, with the seasonal index, promotion lift and launch assumptions written beside each line, a one-screen summary of the top movers and risks, and a weekly accuracy tracker.

COG.when: When a preferred supplier's minimum order (MOQ) is more than the store can sell or pay for, or the owner wants a lower unit price or better payment terms.
COG.tune: walk-away points come from gross profit per order and the cash forecast, not from the other quote; the minimum order is capped by sell-through days; payment terms are bargained as money; and every price win is protected by a spec lock, inspection and a 90-day return watch on the first cheaper lot.
COG.title: Negotiate minimum order and price
COG.outcome: a one-page negotiation plan (target, fallback and walk-away for minimum order, price and payment terms), the trades the store can offer, and 5 ready messages in order, each approved by the client before it is sent.

COG.when: When the owner must choose a supplier on real samples, not photos, or wants a quality checklist and inspection before paying the factory's balance.
COG.tune: the checklist is written before samples arrive and sorted by what a buyer would return; every sample faces the same reference; the inspection limits are agreed before production and tied to the balance payment; and new stock gets a 90-day return watch so a quality slip shows up before the next...
COG.title: Samples and quality check
COG.outcome: a sample order plan (which suppliers, which stages, cost and dates), a filled quality checklist for this product with pass or fail rules, a sample decision sheet, and a pre-shipment inspection brief that must pass before the balance is paid.

COG.when: When the store keeps selling out or sits on too much stock, the owner asks when to reorder and how much, or a supplier, lead time or sales speed changes. Not for Amazon FBA shipments.
COG.tune: speed is measured only on days the product could sell; the buffer follows a gross-profit grade instead of one flat number; the last safe order date turns the sheet into a red list the media buyer acts on; and orders are cut to the cash the store really has, C products first.
COG.title: Reorder points and safety stock
COG.outcome: one reorder sheet (Google Sheet or CSV) with a row per product or variant showing daily sales speed, full lead time, safety stock, reorder point, order quantity, the last safe order date and a red, amber or green status, plus a one-screen summary of the purchase orders to place this month and the cash they need.

COG.when: When the owner wants to know which suppliers are reliable, as a review at the end of each quarter, rating quality, on-time delivery, cost and response with the profit each one's misses cost.
COG.tune: supplier misses are priced in gross profit lost, not just scored; quality is measured on product-fault returns tied back to the lot; missing tax paperwork counts as a cost when it blocks a VAT reclaim; and a red supplier is never dropped before a backup passes a real batch.
COG.title: Supplier scorecard
COG.outcome: a quarterly scorecard sheet with one row per supplier (scores, band and the gross profit their misses cost), a one-screen summary, and an action list with owners and dates for every amber or red supplier, plus a short note to send each supplier.

COG.when: When the owner wants a custom, private-label or modified product made and needs exact specs (materials, sizes, labels, packaging) before asking factories for quotes.
COG.tune: buyer complaints become spec lines; the label section carries each market's labelling rules (US textile rules, UK and EU marking and pack quantity wording) side by side; retail and shipping packaging are specified apart because they land in different cost lines and feed Shopify's shipping set-up; and the sheet is tested on a...
COG.title: Product spec sheet for a factory
COG.outcome: a versioned spec sheet (one document plus a measurement table and label and packaging artwork list) that any factory can quote and produce from, and that the store owns and can take to another factory.

COG.when: When a supplier shortlist exists and the owner needs real prices: one quote request to send and a side-by-side comparison of the answers. Not for finding suppliers.
COG.tune: quotes are forced into one format before they arrive; every quote is compared as landed cost at the quantity the store will really buy; deposits become days of cash; and duty and VAT or sales tax are treated by the rules of the destination country rather than one generic percentage.
COG.title: Request for quote and quote comparison
COG.outcome: one request for quote (RFQ) document and message to send to 3 to 5 suppliers, and a comparison sheet that ranks their answers on landed cost per unit at the planned order size, terms and risk, with one recommendation.

COG.when: When you want factories to quote on your own version of a product and need a clear first message.
COG.tune: Give it the product, the top buyer complaint from rival reviews and your target order size. Write sizes in exact numbers, never words like centred. Read COG-0005 and COG-0011 first.

COG.when: When you are about to ask factories for quotes and have only photos and a description.
COG.tune: Add drawings, fabric weight and treatments, measurements, graphics, hardware and labels. Never send a factory a product without a tech pack, and plan three sample stages. Read COG-0007, COG-0011 and COG-0005 first.

COG.when: When you need a first factory or a backup and have a list of listings to sort.
COG.tune: Use each factory's answers on capacity, certificates and the brands it already makes for, from Alibaba, IndiaMART or trade fairs. Line up a backup so you are never tied to one source. Read COG-0012, COG-0013 and COG-0003 first.

COG.when: When you have quotes from two or three factories and must pick one before you send a deposit.
COG.tune: Paste each quote with unit price by volume, minimum order, lead time, sample cost and deposit terms. Let factories know you hold other quotes, and weigh a lower minimum against the cash it frees. Read COG-0003, COG-0004 and FIN-0005 first.

COG.when: When you have a factory quote and want the cost per sellable unit before you place an order.
COG.tune: Add freight by air and by sea, duty for your import country, inbound fees and an allowance for defects. Compare a small and a bulk order, since unit cost falls fast with volume. Read COG-0010, COG-0009 and FIN-0007 first.

COG.when: When a factory quotes one price per unit and you want to know what is inside it.
COG.tune: Ask each factory to split every SKU into parts, sub-suppliers, labour, overhead and margin, in the same layout. This pays most once your yearly product spend is large, so read COG-0001 first, then COG-0002.

COG.when: When your volume is growing and you want lower unit costs at your next order.
COG.tune: Bring the bill of materials and a 12-month volume plan from your sales forecast. Ask for breaks line by line, tied to how fully your order keeps the factory's workers busy, and hold a real backup quote. Read COG-0002, COG-0003 and COG-0001 first.

COG.when: When a factory sent a sample and you need to decide if it can move to the next stage.
COG.tune: Check the sample line by line against the tech pack and keep the approved one as the gold standard. Test any cheaper new supplier on samples before you trust it with bulk. Read COG-0007 and COG-0009 first.

COG.when: When your order is nearly finished and you are about to pay the balance.
COG.tune: Give it the order, the tech pack and the approved sample, and set the pass rule before the inspector visits. Pay the balance only after the inspection passes, and order extra units if you skip it. Read COG-0006 and COG-0009 first.

COG.when: When you are launching a product on a fixed date, such as before a holiday peak.
COG.tune: List each step from sample to warehouse with real lead times for production and for sea or air freight. Launch with a small air batch and restock by sea. Read COG-0008 and COG-0007 first.

COG.when: When you have overseas orders in transit and the team keeps asking where they are.
COG.tune: Feed it purchase orders, forwarder details and expected arrival dates, and send the warehouse a notice before each one lands. Count units on receipt so short shipments are caught the same week. Read COG-0008 and COG-0009 first.

COG.when: When you depend on one or two suppliers and want terms that protect you as you both grow.
COG.tune: Bring your buying volume, growth plan and current terms. Ask a sole supplier for continued supply if it changes hands and for best-price terms, and have a lawyer draft the contract. Read COG-0013 and FIN-0023 first.

COG.when: When one supplier would hurt you badly if it stopped and you want a backup plan.
COG.tune: Give it your supplier list, spend, defect rates and lead times. Treat moving production out of China as a trade between lead time and cost, not price alone. Read COG-0004, COG-0013 and COG-0003 first.

COG.when: When you are preparing a hard price or terms talk with a factory and do not want to split the difference.
COG.tune: Bring the bill of materials, your backup quotes and what the factory needs from you, such as steady volume. Pair it with COG-0003 on keeping alternatives visible and FIN-0004 on offering to share the cost of longer terms.

COG.when: When the product is chosen and suppliers must quote on the same terms, when the owner wants to use Accio but does not know what to type, or when marketplace replies are too many and too vague to compare.
COG.tune: one brief block feeds Accio, Alibaba.com, 1688, Global Sources, Made-in-China, IndiaMART and TradeIndia so answers compare; Accio is told not to contact anyone until the owner picks names and says yes; badges are judged by the dated audit report; Trade Assurance and IndiaMART payment cover are checked for what they really protect; Indian quotes are read ex-GST with the GSTIN checked.
COG.title: Accio and Alibaba sourcing prompts
COG.outcome: a prompt pack (Accio find, verify and send messages, an Alibaba.com RFQ, a 1688 note and an IndiaMART or TradeIndia enquiry) filled from one spec, and a reply check sheet marking each supplier keep, ask or cut with the reason.

COG.when: When you have a BOM or supplier quotes and want to know what each part should cost before the next order or negotiation.
COG.tune: lines are ranked before they are priced, every material price names the market the factory really buys in with a date, scrap compounds by BOM level, conversion is built from press time or sewing minutes, and a quote below should-cost is read as a quality risk.
COG.title: Should-cost for every part of your product
COG.outcome: A sheet with one row per BOM line: material quantity with scrap, the market price with its named source and date, conversion, overhead and fair margin, the should-cost, the quoted price, the gap, and a target price with a walk-away range.

COG.when: When a product's cost is too high for its margin and you need ways to cut it without more returns or bad reviews.
COG.tune: each lever carries the store's own return reasons as evidence, risky savings are halved or zeroed until a test proves them, carton fit and price tiers are priced in money, and a material change always brings its claim change.
COG.title: Cost-down options rated for return risk
COG.outcome: A ranked list of 5 to 12 levers, each with the saving per unit and per year, the return and review risk with the evidence, the test to run first and who signs off.

COG.when: When your margin depends on commodity prices, container freight or exchange rates and you want a scheduled check instead of surprises.
COG.tune: each BOM line is tied to the market its factory buys in, moves become cents per unit through the driven share and the lag instead of passing through whole, the dollar is watched beside the supplier's currency, and one fixed two-minute report lands on schedule.
COG.title: Weekly materials, freight and currency watch
COG.outcome: A level 1 routine that maps each BOM line to a public series, runs on your schedule, and reports what moved, cents per unit per SKU, anything past a trigger line and a 3, 6 and 12 month COGS range.

COG.when: When cost moves keep catching the team out and nobody agrees when to act.
COG.tune: action lines are worked back from the store's margin floor and watch lines from each series' own noise, every line already names the move, the teammate and the cash check, and index clauses move both ways on the driven share only.
COG.title: Cost trigger rules: buy ahead, reprice, renegotiate or re-source
COG.outcome: A one-page rule table: each driver, its watch line and action line, the move it starts, the teammate who owns it and the cash check, plus index-linked price wording, ready to run with the weekly watch.

COG.when: When you write to factories on Alibaba.com, Accio, 1688 through an agent, WeChat or email and need the message to land in Chinese.
COG.tune: every message carries one ask with numbers that survive translation, a separate back-translation catches drift before sending, a reply guide says what common factory phrases really commit to, and agreed terms are confirmed by email and logged with the owner's yes.
COG.title: Supplier messages in English and Simplified Chinese
COG.outcome: Each message in English and Simplified Chinese with an English back-translation, a note on tone and what a likely reply means, and a log of every message sent with your yes.

COG.when: When you are about to place a first order, or a repeat order where terms have drifted.
COG.tune: the balance follows a passed inspection rather than a ship date, the Incoterm is chosen for container goods with a named place, remedies carry fixed figures, moulds are owned on paper with IDs and a release date, and the Chinese copy is back-translated because it is the one that counts.
COG.title: Purchase order and supply terms
COG.outcome: A PO and supply terms with price, MOQ, payment split or Trade Assurance, Incoterm, quality standard and AQL, ship date, late and defect remedies and tooling ownership, in English and Chinese, flagged for a lawyer to check before you sign.

COG.when: When you are about to send your own design, mould or tech pack to a factory in China.
COG.tune: it guards against what Chinese factories really do (use your design and go round you), binds the entity that makes the goods in its own language and courts, and shares the design in stages so the most valuable files go out last.
COG.title: NNN agreement to protect your design
COG.outcome: A plain-words brief and draft NNN (non-use, non-disclosure, non-circumvention) in Chinese and English, with the right parties, products and remedies, a share and hold-back list, and a checklist for a China-qualified lawyer.

COG.when: When a sample is approved and before production starts, so the factory and the inspector check against the same standard.
COG.tune: the defect list starts from the store's own return reasons and reviews, every line has a number and a yearly cost, and the inspector's sealed golden sample is sent by the store so nobody can swap the standard.
COG.title: Golden sample and defect list
COG.outcome: A golden sample record with photos and measurements, and a defect list split into critical, major and minor, each with how to check it, its tolerance and the return reason it prevents.

COG.when: When any production order is placed, from the first booking to the inspector's report.
COG.tune: limits are agreed before production and tied to the balance, inspections follow the real production clock, each report call is written against the accept and reject numbers with the cost of shipping defects shown, and the level tightens or relaxes on the supplier's record.
COG.title: AQL inspection plan and pass, rework or reject calls
COG.outcome: An AQL plan in the ISO 2859-1 style (general inspection level II, limits per defect class, on-site tests), an inspection schedule for each stage, booking requests for your yes, and a pass, rework or reject call on each report before you pay the balance.

COG.when: When a new product is about to be sampled, so the factory and lab know what it must pass.
COG.tune: the plan is built before the first sample so the factory makes and the lab tests the same thing, every rule is marked confirmed or to confirm for the compliance lead, no lab cost or date is guessed, and label lines reach the spec and artwork before anything is printed.
COG.title: Test and certificate plan before sampling
COG.outcome: A plan per market listing the tests and certificates the product needs (for example CPSIA and a children's product certificate in the US, CE or UKCA and REACH in Europe and the UK), the lab, the sample count, the cost and timing, set with meenakshi-compliance.

COG.when: When colour matters to the brand and samples keep coming back the wrong shade.
COG.tune: each material gets its own approval against one physical standard the store holds, dips are judged under two named lights so colour does not shift at home, rejections come with a direction a dye house can act on, and the approved colour is carried through to the product page.
COG.title: Colour standard and lab dip approval
COG.outcome: A colour spec per material with the Pantone reference and a physical standard, the light source to judge under, a lab dip request for the factory, and an approval log with photos taken under the same light.

WLD.when: When the owner wants a joint product or drop with another brand to reach a new audience without buying it all through ads, or a partner brand has pitched an idea.
WLD.tune: partners are scored on a shared buyer with evidence from the store's own surveys and reviews; the cheapest format comes first so a minimum order never sinks the idea; the money is checked for both brands before the pitch; and new customers from the partner are counted with codes and the survey,...
WLD.title: Collab drop with another brand
WLD.outcome: a partner shortlist with scores and evidence, a pitch message and one-page proposal for the top three, a term sheet checklist, a unit economics table for both brands, and a dated drop plan (stock, page, ads, emails, measurement). Nothing is sent, signed or ordered without the client's yes.

WLD.when: When the owner wants the store in press, magazines or gift guides, usually 6 to 20 weeks before a gifting season (Mother's Day, Father's Day, Black Friday, the holidays, Diwali or another local festival).
WLD.tune: every target is a named writer with a dated piece in the store's price band, and every row carries a pitch-by date worked back from lead time; claims are checked against a proof sheet before any pitch; paid placements are logged and judged as ads; and coverage is tied to orders through UTM links...
WLD.title: Pitch the store to press and gift guides
WLD.outcome: a press tracker with 20 to 40 named targets (outlet, writer, recent relevant piece and date, price band, lead time, contact source, status), three ready-to-fill pitch emails, a one-page media kit, and a coverage log that links each mention to sessions and orders. Nothing is sent without the client's yes.

WLD.when: When the store is offered a stall, booth or pop-up space, or the owner wants to try selling in person at a market or trade show and needs a go or no-go.
WLD.tune: the decision uses the low end of a footfall model, not the organiser's best case; the online halo is measured against a city without the event and kept out of break-even; event stock can never starve the website; and tax registration for selling in another state is flagged before booking.
WLD.title: Pop-up shop or trade show plan
WLD.outcome: a one-page go or no-go for one event with costs, the break-even line and the realistic sales range side by side, plus a stock list, staff rota, payment and lead capture set-up and a post-event scorecard, ready for the client to approve before any booking fee is paid.

WLD.when: When the owner wants to 'try Pinterest', Snapchat, YouTube or Reddit ads, or the main ad channel has stalled and a second one is being considered.
WLD.tune: a wild bet only runs once the base channel is healthy; the new channel's attribution window is matched before launch so 28 and 30-day defaults cannot flatter it; the maximum loss is agreed in money before budget is sized; and the pass line is read on store new customers with an eye on halo in...
WLD.title: Test a new ad channel
WLD.outcome: a one-page test plan for one channel (why this one, maximum loss, budget per day, length, creative set, tracking checklist, and the pass, extend or fail line), plus a results sheet filled at the end with the decision, ready for the owner to approve before any spend.

WLD.when: When you are excited about a bold store idea and want the worst case written down before you commit.
WLD.tune: Give it the bet, the cash and stock it ties up, and your monthly contribution margin from Shopify. Wild bets never replace your proven channels, so cap the loss first and check the fails-when line of the matching card.

WLD.when: When you want a stunt that gets press and talk for your store without a big ad budget.
WLD.tune: Give it your product benefit, your brand tone and the big rival you stand against. The stunt must act out the product's benefit, and mocking stunts fail for brands built on trust or care (WLD-0005, WLD-0001).

WLD.when: When you are launching a product or brand with a small ad budget and want attention before you pay for ads.
WLD.tune: Give it the product, your rivals and any partner brands you could launch with. Treat collabs and stunts as awareness, not profit, and check minimum order sizes before planning a one-off variant (WLD-0011, WLD-0005).

WLD.when: When you want to try a personal note or gift for your best customers and see if it brings them back.
WLD.tune: Give it a Shopify customer export ranked by spend and orders. Start with the top 10 to 50 against a control group, send real notes rather than printed fakes, and expand only if reorders beat control (WLD-0007, WLD-0010).

WLD.when: When you want to sell a product in limited drops that truly sell out.
WLD.tune: Give it real stock counts, drop dates and email and SMS list sizes from Klaviyo. Drops only work for products people do not need on demand and after the brand already has fans, and an unsold drop hurts (WLD-0009).

WLD.when: When a product sold out or is coming back and you want to use that as proof in ads, emails and the product page.
WLD.tune: Give it dated order reports, the sold-out window and the restock date. Use only true, dated facts and push the restock across email, SMS and social on the same day (WLD-0012).

WLD.when: When you want the first box to feel special or to prove your quality in a way customers can test.
WLD.tune: Describe the product, pack and what rivals cut corners on. Put a quality test in the box only if your product truly wins it, and keep any surprise gift for top buyers free of discount codes (WLD-0006, WLD-0003).

WLD.when: When a long-time subscriber cancels suddenly and you want to answer with care, not just a discount.
WLD.tune: Give it cancel reasons from Recharge or Skio and what your portal can branch on. Add a gentle branch for a death or life change with a no-return refund and a note, and watch the cost if such cancels are common (WLD-0002).

WLD.when: When you have an unproven, exciting idea such as a new sales channel and do not know how much to put in.
WLD.tune: Describe the idea, its best case and the cash and hours you can lose without harm. Set a loss cap and a stop date, and check local rules first for anything that looks like a bet or a lottery (WLD-0008, WLD-0004).

WLD.when: When your wild idea sounds bold but you cannot say why it would work for your store.
WLD.tune: Paste the idea and what most stores in your niche do instead. Use it to find the true but unpopular belief behind the bet, then pick the matching wild card and test it small.

WLD.when: When you want cheap, odd ideas that change how customers feel about your store, not just what it costs.
WLD.tune: Bring a customer problem, such as cancels, slow repeat orders or a dull box, and ask for low-cost ideas that change how it feels. Test every idea against a control group before you roll it out (WLD-0007, WLD-0003).

WLD.when: When you want people to talk about a stunt, drop or restock and share it with friends.
WLD.tune: Bring the stunt or drop idea and the buyer it is for. Use the lens to find what makes it worth retelling, and drop ideas whose hook has nothing to do with the product (WLD-0005, WLD-0012).

FIN.when: When cash feels tight, profit looks good but the bank balance does not, or before a big stock order, a sale, a hire or a financing offer. Not for a sales forecast or monthly P&L.
FIN.tune: every receipt is timed by the store's measured payout and pay-on-delivery remittance lag, not by order date; reserved money and labels on the card are handled the way Shopify actually runs them; the lowest week, not the ending balance, drives the actions; and slow stock is treated as cash to release before...
FIN.title: Thirteen-week cash forecast
FIN.outcome: a 13-column cash sheet (receipts, payments, closing cash per week) with the lowest week and every week under the buffer flagged, a downside case, and a short action list for each short week, ready to update every Monday.

FIN.when: When bulk, corporate or wholesale enquiries arrive and quotes, proforma invoices and tax invoices are handled by email and guesswork. Not for setting the wholesale price list.
FIN.tune: one numbered document chain from quote to credit note that matches the VAT or tax invoice rules field by field; e-invoice steps where the country requires them; a bank-change fraud warning on every payment document; bulk orders kept in the store's own stock records so the website never oversells; and India's GST invoice and e-way bill steps go to Ishita (ishita-india-commerce).
FIN.title: Bulk order quote and invoice
FIN.outcome: three ready templates (quote, proforma, tax invoice) with the store's details filled, a document numbering rule, a one-page process from enquiry to cash received with owners and timings, and a collections schedule, all approved by the client and the store's accountant before first use.

FIN.when: When a lender, platform or payment provider offers a loan or cash advance repaid from sales, before a big stock buy or peak season, or when the owner is thinking of borrowing to grow.
FIN.tune: the cost is an annual rate computed at the store's own sales forecast, so fast repayment is shown as expensive; repayments are dropped into the weekly cash forecast to find the lowest week; the money is approved only for uses with measured payback; and supplier terms and slow stock are costed as...
FIN.title: Should you take revenue-based financing?
FIN.outcome: a one-page verdict (take it, take it with changes, or decline) with the effective annual cost, the repayment schedule by month in base and downside, the lowest cash point, the alternatives compared, and a list of contract terms to accept, negotiate or refuse.

FIN.when: When the owner asks what sales to expect next month, at month end, or wants the gap to a sales target and what would close it. Not for cash in the bank week by week.
FIN.tune: new and returning revenue are forecast from different drivers; cost per new customer rises with planned spend and is floored by cost per click; pay-on-delivery revenue is counted only if delivered; and every forecast comes with a range and a stock cap, not one hopeful number.
FIN.title: Next month's revenue forecast
FIN.outcome: a one-page forecast of next month's orders and net revenue by week, with a low, base and high range, the input table behind it, and the gap to the owner's target with what would close it.

FIN.when: When the owner asks whether the store really made money last month, in the first week after each month ends, with a profit and loss (P&L) laid out for an online store.
FIN.tune: returns are accrued to the month that caused them instead of the month Shopify books them; the P&L stops at two contribution lines before fixed costs so spend decisions are not distorted; first-order and returning profit are split; and the month ends with three actions ranked by money, not a list...
FIN.title: Monthly store profit and loss
FIN.outcome: a one-page monthly P&L for the store (this month, last month, same month last year, and each line as a share of net revenue), a first-order versus returning split, and the three things to act on with their money at stake.

FIN.when: When payouts, COD remittances or marketplace settlements don't match orders, payment fees look higher than agreed, or every month before closing the books or building the P&L.
FIN.tune: it reconciles at four levels (order, payment, payout, bank) instead of comparing two totals; every delivered pay-on-delivery order is traced to its remittance; fee rates are checked by payment method against the contract; and each gap is typed so timing differences are not chased as losses while real money...
FIN.title: Reconcile payouts and payment fees
FIN.outcome: a gap register listing every unmatched or short amount by type, with order, payout and bank references, the total money at stake, the effective fee rate per gateway against the agreed rate, and draft claims ready for the client to approve.

FIN.when: When you want one monthly P&L in the same layout every month to see where the money goes.
FIN.tune: Feed it Shopify sales shown gross to net (refunds, discounts, shipping collected), plus cost of goods, shipping, ad spend and fixed costs. Read it in four buckets against targets for your kind of product. Read FIN-0016 and FIN-0010 first.

FIN.when: When your gross margin looks too good or too bad and you suspect costs are in the wrong place.
FIN.tune: Paste cost lines from your Xero, QuickBooks or Tally export. Inbound freight, duty and the branded box go in cost of goods, while the plain shipping carton and return postage do not. Read FIN-0007, FIN-0008, FIN-0009 and FIN-0017 first.

FIN.when: When a mixed shipment has arrived and you need the true cost per unit for each product.
FIN.tune: Paste the supplier invoice, freight bill, duty and exchange rate, then update cost per item in Shopify. Spread freight by weight or volume, not by unit count alone. Read FIN-0007 and FIN-0017 first.

FIN.when: When your P&L is positive but cash feels tight and you suspect new customers cost more than they bring.
FIN.tune: Tag Shopify orders as first or repeat and assign ad spend to new customers. Treat discounts and ad spend as one pool spent to win a buyer. Read FIN-0015 and FIN-0029 first.

FIN.when: When your payback estimate looks short but the bank balance says otherwise.
FIN.tune: Feed it first orders grouped by month from Shopify, with later orders and gross margin. Use cohorts with real churn, not one average customer. Read FIN-0014 and FIN-0029 first.

FIN.when: When sales are up but the bank balance is low and you do not know where to look first.
FIN.tune: Give it the P&L, stock by SKU with sell-through and your supplier terms. Cutting ad spend while stock piles up can deepen the drop, and faster sell-through often frees the most cash. Read FIN-0027, FIN-0028 and FIN-0026 first.

FIN.when: When you plan to grow fast and want to know whether cash or ads will hold you back first.
FIN.tune: Feed it stock levels, supplier terms, lead times and the growth plan. Growth funded by stock hits the cash cycle wall, so read FIN-0011 first and FIN-0013 for slow stock.

FIN.when: When you are about to place a large stock order and want to know if you can pay for it.
FIN.tune: Use your sales forecast, lead time, landed unit cost and cash on hand, and model a slow-sales case. Compare supplier terms, a credit line and purchase-order finance before you raise equity. Read FIN-0020, FIN-0011 and FIN-0022 first.

FIN.when: When you pay deposits and balances up front and want more cash room from your factory.
FIN.tune: Give it your order cycle, lead time and payment history with the supplier. Float is payment terms minus factory-to-warehouse time, so ask for longer terms in steps and offer to share the cost of funding them. Read FIN-0005, FIN-0004 and FIN-0023 first.

FIN.when: When a lender, partner or buyer wants a forecast, or you want to know how much cash the store needs before it pays for itself.
FIN.tune: Feed it ad budget, cost to win a customer, prices, cost of goods and repeat rates from your own cohorts. Judge any change on 60- to 180-day cash, not 30 days. Read FIN-0029 and FIN-0016 first.

FIN.when: When you are pricing a new product and want the lowest price that still hits your profit target.
FIN.tune: Work down from your profit target and overheads, then add the expected cost to win a buyer, returns, shipping and landed cost. If the price lands above what buyers will pay, drop the product rather than trim the target. Read FIN-0012 and PRD-0006 first.

FIN.when: When a retailer or distributor asks for your wholesale price and you want to know what you would keep.
FIN.tune: Give it shelf price, landed cost, the retailer and distributor cuts, trade spend and freight. Retail chains take a large share, so the product needs a high gross margin to survive there. Read FIN-0002, PRD-0010 and FIN-0024 first.

FIN.when: When you want your real profit each month and to know which cost line moved.
FIN.tune: Each month give it Shopify sales and refunds, cost of goods, Meta and Google ad spend and fixed costs. Report gross to net every month so your accountant sees refunds and discounts, not only net sales. Read FIN-0010 and FIN-0016 first.

FIN.when: When you are about to change your company setup, start selling in new states or countries, or sell the business and need the right tax questions.
FIN.tune: State your jurisdiction first, such as UK VAT, EU VAT or US state sales tax, and bring entity type, sales by region and the decision. It prepares questions for your accountant and files nothing. Read FIN-0017 so your cost-of-goods treatment matches your filings.

FIN.when: When you are thinking about selling your store and want to get ready for buyers.
FIN.tune: Gather three years of P&L, audited accounts if you have them, customer cohorts and supplier terms. Show that the brand runs without the founder, and expect buyers to price on profit and growth. Read FIN-0001, FIN-0021, FIN-0018 and FIN-0025 first.

FIN.when: When setting prices, a budget or a big buy, and you need to know where product costs are heading.
FIN.tune: each BOM line is tied to a named public price series with its measured lag and pass-through, high and low cases come from each series' own volatility, duty changes are listed by market with a legal source and date, and the last forecast is graded against invoices.
FIN.title: COGS forecast with base, high and low cases
FIN.outcome: A COGS per SKU forecast at 3, 6 and 12 months with base, high and low cases, the driver and lag behind each, the gross margin each leaves, and a log scoring the last forecast against real invoices.

OPS.when: When nobody checks the ad accounts every day, problems are found days late, and the owner wants checks and short reports to run on a schedule without building a server. Not for doing one daily review now.
OPS.tune: it runs on schedulers the store already has, with platform rules locked to notify only; performance alerts switch on only when gross profit per purchase exists; alert rules suppress known false alarms such as low-spend daily ROAS and Google's late-filling days; and a shadow week tunes the...
OPS.title: Scheduled ad-operations assistant
OPS.outcome: a schedule of ad checks (breakage monitor, daily review, weekly and monthly jobs) on free schedulers in notify-only mode, with role briefs, alert rules, a work queue and a shadow-week report, ready to switch on.

OPS.when: When packing eats the founder's day, orders grow fast, peak season is coming, deliveries are slow or wrong, or a 3PL (outside warehouse) quote needs checking.
OPS.tune: both options are costed per order at today's volume, double and peak with the owner's time priced; a 3PL is scored on accuracy, peak record and exit terms before price; US sales tax and UK or EU VAT effects of stock location are raised before a multi-site choice; and the move is timed away from peak...
OPS.title: Choose a 3PL or fulfil in-house
OPS.outcome: a one-page decision (stay, hire, outsource or split) with cost per order for each option at three volumes, a scored comparison of up to three 3PL quotes, a ready-to-send request-for-pricing pack, a question list for 3PL calls, and the service terms to put in the contract.

OPS.when: When shipping costs feel high, parcels are slow or lost, pay-on-delivery cash arrives late, a new region opens, or a courier or aggregator pitches new rates.
OPS.tune: every option is priced on the store's own three-month parcel mix with billable weight and pay-on-delivery share; coverage is weighted by real orders, including pay on delivery and reverse pickup; each carrier's own failed-delivery rate and remittance days go into cost and cash; and the switch runs as a pilot with pass...
OPS.title: Compare shipping carriers
OPS.outcome: a comparison sheet that prices each carrier or aggregator on the store's real shipment mix, a scorecard on speed, coverage, pay on delivery, returns and claims, a one-screen recommendation (main carrier, backup and routing rules), and a 2 to 4 week pilot plan with pass or fail lines.

OPS.when: When COD (cash on delivery) parcels come back undelivered, fake or doubtful orders get shipped, or the team confirms orders by hand with no script or timing. Not for deciding which orders get COD at all.
OPS.tune: the prepaid offer rides in the free 24-hour window opened by the buyer's own confirmation instead of spoiling the utility template; every order ends in one outcome tag; the routine must show RTO saved above its own cost; and a small holdout tells the store whether confirmation is really what cut...
OPS.title: Confirm COD orders by chat or call
OPS.outcome: a written COD confirmation routine for the team: a queue rule, a timing card, a confirmation message, a reminder, a call script with 6 branches, a post-confirmation prepaid message, 7 outcome tags, a cost check and a weekly tracker that shows parcels saved and orders lost.

OPS.when: When COD orders keep coming back undelivered (return to origin, RTO) and eat margin, COD share is high, a new region or product opens to COD, or ads bring orders that never get delivered. Not for the confirmation call and message scripts.
OPS.tune: the break-even return-to-origin rate is computed per product, so one pincode can be allowed for a high-margin item and prepaid-only for a thin one; thin pincodes roll up instead of being blocked on a handful of orders; the tracker counts orders lost as well as parcels saved; and the confirmation...
OPS.title: Cut return-to-origin on COD orders
OPS.outcome: a rule table (segment, evidence, action, owner, timing) that sorts each new COD order into allow, confirm, nudge to prepaid or prepaid only; a pincode and pattern risk sheet built from the store's own orders; the break-even return-to-origin rate per product; and a weekly tracker that shows parcels saved against orders lost.

OPS.when: When orders run late, an item sells out after purchase, a courier problem hits, or peak season is near, and buyers need clear updates. Not for routine 'where is my order' tracking messages.
OPS.tune: every late-order message carries a real wait-or-cancel choice timed to US notice rules; offers stay out of WhatsApp order updates so they remain utility messages; make-goods are capped and each frequent trigger is sent back to the process that caused it; and pay-on-delivery, SMS registration and language notes are built in.
OPS.title: Delay and stockout messages
OPS.outcome: a trigger table (event, rule, channel, send time, owner) and a filled message set of 10 messages in email, SMS and WhatsApp versions, each with a wait-or-cancel choice where needed, plus a make-good rule card for support and a one-screen summary for the client to approve.

OPS.when: When wrong items, missing items or damage show up in complaints, a new packer joins, peak season is coming, or packing must move out of the founder's hands.
OPS.tune: release times are worked back from the courier pickup and the promise shown on site; a weight check and packed-order photo catch errors and settle delivery and courier disputes; every release is reconciled before the team leaves; and tax invoice, pay-on-delivery and customs paperwork checks sit next to each market's restricted goods rules.
OPS.title: Pick, pack and ship routine
OPS.outcome: a one-page daily routine with times and owners, a step card for each station (pick, pack, label, hand over), a box and protection guide per product, the exception rules, an error and damage log with weekly targets, and a one-screen summary for the owner.

OPS.when: When the owner wants to take orders before stock arrives: stock is on the way, a launch is weeks off, a best seller is about to sell out, or past pre-orders caused angry buyers and refunds.
OPS.tune: pre-orders open only on a confirmed purchase order; the cap is net of defects and units held for in-stock buyers; payment method follows the date gap and keeps pay on delivery off; and one promised date runs through page, cart, confirmation and updates, with US, UK and EU delay rules built in.
OPS.title: Pre-orders and backorders
OPS.outcome: a set-up sheet per product (mode, cap, promised date, payment method, settings), the buyer-facing wording for the product page, cart, checkout note, confirmation and three update messages, a delay and refund rule card, and a one-screen summary of what goes live once the client approves.

OPS.when: When returns are handled in email chaos, refunds are slow, return costs are rising, or the store is writing its first returns and exchanges policy.
OPS.tune: each outcome is costed per return before the policy is set; exchange and credit are offered first but the refund is never hidden; pay-on-delivery buyers get a safe refund path; and every reason code is wired to the person who fixes it, so returns drop instead of just being processed.
OPS.title: Returns and exchanges process
OPS.outcome: the policy terms in a table, the portal flow screen by screen with its wording, the warehouse inspection and restock checklist, a reason-code list, the Shopify or app settings to apply, the cost per return for refund, exchange and store credit, and a one-screen summary for the owner to approve.

OPS.when: When several agents or people work on the store and the owner cannot see what each is doing, or approvals and blockers sit for days; run before the weekly meeting. Not for the weekly sales and growth numbers pack.
OPS.tune: it runs on one fixed status note from every agent, so the owner sees work, blockers and approvals in one place; only numbers outside their normal range are discussed; it checks clashes between agents before they reach buyers; and priorities are capped and tied to the quarter's plan, with new...
OPS.title: Weekly store operating review
OPS.outcome: a one-page review ready the day before the meeting (numbers page, exceptions, blockers, approvals queue, clashes, decisions to make, next week's priorities), a filled status note from each agent, an updated decision log, and a 45-minute agenda.

OPS.when: When most of your yearly profit lands in a few peak weeks and you cannot afford late shipping or a stockout.
OPS.tune: Give it last year's daily Shopify sales, ticket counts and current 3PL terms. Check customs papers and backup plans (OPS-0001), and plan whether to hide stock rather than sell out (OPS-0019).

OPS.when: When you are moving to your first warehouse partner or replacing one that ships late or loses stock.
OPS.tune: Give it a 12-month order forecast, product sizes and weights and ship-to countries. Vet bids on error rate and past Q4 surges (OPS-0008), and write a pick-on-time promise with penalties (OPS-0015).

OPS.when: When your warehouse or courier bill arrives each month and you pay it without checking.
OPS.tune: Paste the invoice, the rate card and the Shopify orders export for the same month. OPS-0012 suggests overcharges are common, so run it monthly, not only after peak.

OPS.when: When you are about to make a first or second hire, or nobody clearly owns refunds, reorders or ad budget.
OPS.tune: Give it revenue, lowest-month revenue and who does what today. Size core payroll to the slow month (OPS-0010), match generalists or specialists to your stage (OPS-0003), and push specialist roles offshore where OPS-0007 fits.

OPS.when: When growth has stalled and you think one hire, like a media buyer, will fix it.
OPS.tune: Give it revenue, net margin, ad spend and honest skill ratings for the founders. Check OPS-0020 and OPS-0016 before hiring a buyer, and OPS-0004 before agreeing a pay plan tied to spend.

OPS.when: When support fell behind at your last sales peak and you do not know what each ticket costs.
OPS.tune: Feed 12 months of tickets by type from your help desk, support costs and a sales forecast. Expect more contacts as order value rises (OPS-0006) and blend offshore and local agents by ticket type (OPS-0013).

OPS.when: When your support inbox has piled up and the same questions keep coming back.
OPS.tune: Export open tickets with tags from Gorgias or your help desk. Treat 'where is my order' as a shipping fix, not a reply to write faster (CXP-0012), and keep replies low effort for the customer (CXP-0009).

OPS.when: When late or stuck parcels reach you as angry tickets before you spot them yourself.
OPS.tune: Run it each morning on open Shopify orders with fulfilment and tracking status. Use it to hold your 3PL to its pick-time promise (OPS-0015) and catch delays before they turn into WISMO (CXP-0012).

OPS.when: When you use more than one carrier and suspect one is slower or costlier than it should be.
OPS.tune: Run it on Shopify shipments with tracking for at least a few hundred orders. It uses what customers paid for shipping, so check real cost against carrier invoices (OPS-0012) and promised dates (CXP-0010).

OPS.when: When you keep running out of best sellers while slow lines pile up in the warehouse.
OPS.tune: Give it weekly sales by SKU from Shopify, supplier lead times and stockout days. Forecast only from in-stock days (OPS-0014) and use total door-to-door lead time (COG-0008).

OPS.when: When ads and posts take weeks to approve and your team keeps missing trends.
OPS.tune: Describe who makes and who approves creative today. Pre-approve a trend budget and a fast turnaround (OPS-0018), and decide when to move a channel from agency to in-house (OPS-0002).

OPS.when: When your team repeats the same order, stock or reporting chores every week and one person holds the know-how.
OPS.tune: List weekly chores with owner and time spent, such as order tagging, restock emails and report pulls. Collect requests and review them on a set rhythm as in OPS-0021, and run the tool beside the manual way until they match.

OPS.when: When your product sells well online and a big retailer is interested or on your list.
OPS.tune: Give it online sales proof, unit cost and how much stock cash you can tie up. Plan stock so you never miss a purchase order (OPS-0022), and check landed cost before agreeing terms (FIN-0007).
