OPS.when: When you want to keep the team lean, hire for attitude and stay ready for a bad year.
OPS.tune: Bring payroll as a share of revenue and your slowest month. Test your plan against OPS-0010 and OPS-0017 and ask what the store must keep doing to stay low cost.

OPS.when: When a product is about to be imported into a market for the first time, or after a duty bill that did not match the plan.
OPS.tune: each product is described the way customs reads it, the code is worked through the classification rules in order and checked in each market's own tariff, added duties and the value basis follow that market's law, and unclear codes get a ruling plan before the goods ship.
OPS.title: HS code and duty research per product
OPS.outcome: A sheet with the likely HS code per product and market, the tariff line, duty rate, any added duties, the official source and date, and a flag for broker review or a binding ruling where the code is unclear.

OPS.when: When stock is about to land in a new market such as the US, UK, EU, Canada or Australia.
OPS.tune: the importer of record is settled first, each market's list covers customs, tax and product safety duties together, and every item has a filer, a lead time and a start date counted back from the first arrival.
OPS.title: Import setup checklist by market
OPS.outcome: A checklist per market (for example US importer number, ISF and customs bond; UK and EU EORI and import VAT), with who files each item, the lead time, and the documents your broker will ask for.

OPS.when: When stock is moving from booking to warehouse receipt, for every inbound shipment.
OPS.tune: every shipment is tied to the stock-out dates of the SKUs it carries, buffers come from measured schedule reliability, alerts fire on filings and free time as well as dates, and every slip comes with priced options against sales protected.
OPS.title: Inbound shipment tracker with delay alerts
OPS.outcome: A tracker sheet with booking, vessel or flight, departure and arrival dates, customs status and free-time end per shipment, alert rules for slips, and quoted against real cost and days logged after each arrival.

AMZ.when: When Amazon sends a warning or IP complaint, listings or the account are deactivated, a health metric crosses Amazon's line, or as a monthly health check.
AMZ.tune: every metric is traced to the actual orders behind it before any words are written; the plan of action reports changes already made, with dates and numbers; documents must be real and only those that prove a line go in; and nothing reaches Amazon or a rights owner without the client's fresh yes.
AMZ.title: Fix Amazon account health
AMZ.outcome: a repair file with one row per account health issue (metric or policy, cause, fix, owner, date, documents), plus a ready-to-submit plan of action for each issue that needs one, written as root cause, actions taken and prevention, with an evidence list, for the client to approve before anything is sent to Amazon.

AMZ.when: When the owner is asked 'why are you not on Amazon?', site growth has slowed, or before signing up to any marketplace (Amazon, Flipkart, Etsy, Walmart and others). Not for listing products once an Indian marketplace is chosen.
AMZ.tune: every marketplace is ranked on gross profit per order after ads, returns and fees pulled on the day, not on traffic or commission alone; a channel that forces the price below the site fails outright; failed-delivery and return losses and payout lags are in the maths; and the choice ends in a 60-day...
AMZ.title: Choose the next marketplace
AMZ.outcome: a one-page ranking of 3 to 6 marketplaces for this store, each with gross profit per order after all fees and ads on its top SKUs, a risk and cash score, one recommendation and a runner-up, and a 60-day test plan with a pass or fail line, for the client to approve before any account is opened.

AMZ.when: When a product is about to launch on Amazon with no reviews and the owner wants the first reviews within Amazon's rules (Vine, Request a Review).
AMZ.tune: the client signs a written do-not-do list before launch; reviews are tracked per 100 delivered orders from the product's own baseline, not a borrowed benchmark; every early complaint is routed to a product, listing or packaging fix with an owner; and Vine is costed as a launch expense at landed...
AMZ.title: Early Amazon reviews within the rules
AMZ.outcome: a dated plan for the first 60 days of reviews on one product: Vine enrolment details and cost, a Request a Review routine for every eligible order, a compliant package insert text, a do-not-do list the client signs, and a weekly tracker of reviews per 100 orders with the product and listing fixes the first reviews point to.

AMZ.when: When Amazon ads have run past their first 14 days and the owner wants the weekly clean-up: which shopper search terms to add as keywords and which to block. Not for building the first campaigns.
AMZ.tune: verdicts use break-even ACOS from gross profit, not a flat ACOS goal; a term is judged only after a click count set by its own conversion rate; every negative is checked against live keywords and the brand; and winning terms flow back into the listing, not only into ads.
AMZ.title: Amazon search term harvesting
AMZ.outcome: a weekly harvest sheet: every search term with its verdict and reason, a bulk upload file with new exact keywords, product targets and negatives, a change log, and a short list of buyer words to add to the listing, ready for the client to approve in 30 to 45 minutes.

AMZ.when: When a product is newly listed and ready for Amazon ads (Sponsored Products), a first PPC try burned money with no structure, or after a listing rebuild. Not for the weekly search term clean-up.
AMZ.tune: bids are worked back from gross profit after Amazon's fees, not from suggested bids; the launch loss is a capped sum the client signs; keyword verdicts wait for a click count set by conversion rate; and refused or undelivered orders cut the affordable bid.
AMZ.title: Amazon PPC launch
AMZ.outcome: a build sheet for 4 Sponsored Products campaigns ready to create paused in the Amazon Ads console, with every keyword, negative, bid and budget written down, a launch spend cap for the client to approve, and a 14-day check list with the action rule for each day.

AMZ.when: When an Indian store wants to sell on Flipkart, Myntra, Nykaa or Meesho, beyond its own site and Amazon, and asks which products to list and at what price. Not for choosing which marketplace to open first.
AMZ.tune: each channel is judged on profit per order after returns and cash-on-delivery refusals, not on commission; prices stay in line with the brand's own site and under MRP; sale event discounts are modelled before opting in; and pack declarations and BIS marks are checked before any listing goes up.
AMZ.title: List on Flipkart, Myntra, Nykaa and Meesho
AMZ.outcome: a channel decision sheet showing, for every product, the gross profit per order on each marketplace after every fee, return and RTO cost, with a list, price or skip verdict; a price sheet that keeps MRP and the brand's own site in line; and a listing sheet per marketplace with every required field filled, ready for the client to upload.

AMZ.when: When the owner asks how much stock to send to Amazon FBA and when, before each reorder or FBA shipment, or products keep running out or getting storage surcharges. Not for stock in the store's own warehouse.
AMZ.tune: every fee is read from Amazon on the day because the 2026 fee changes make course figures wrong; cover has both a floor and a ceiling set by fees, not one flat number; it prices a split between FBA and cheaper storage; and it writes the stock-to-ads rule into the ad skills.
AMZ.title: FBA inventory plan
AMZ.outcome: a 90-day FBA plan sheet: for each product, sales per day, weeks of cover now, the date the next shipment must leave, units and boxes per shipment, the fee cost of holding more or less, and the flag list of products about to run out or age into surcharges, ready for the client and supplier to act on.

AMZ.when: When a brand starts selling on Amazon, a reseller or copycat edits its listings, or A+, Vine and Sponsored Brands are locked because the brand is not registered. Not for losing sales to another seller's offer.
AMZ.tune: it protects who owns the mark before anything is filed; it files the word mark that Brand Registry accepts and enrols on the pending number instead of waiting; store pages are built from the brand's own search data; and protection runs on test buys so genuine resellers are never reported as fakes.
AMZ.title: Amazon Brand Registry and brand store
AMZ.outcome: a set-up file in four parts: the trademark filing plan with the exact mark, classes and owner; the Brand Registry application checklist with every field filled; a Brand Store page plan (pages, tiles, copy, links) ready to build; and a weekly brand protection routine with a log, all for the client to approve and submit.

AMZ.when: When the Buy Box (Featured Offer) share drops, ads stop serving, another seller appears on the listing, or the price shows only under 'See all buying options'.
AMZ.tune: it uses Amazon's own factor list, which says reviews and Prime do not count, instead of the common "lowest price wins" belief; every price move sits above a profit floor; it checks the brand's own prices elsewhere as a cause; and it treats genuine resellers as a supply-chain leak, not an IP case.
AMZ.title: Win and keep the Buy Box
AMZ.outcome: a one-page diagnosis per affected ASIN naming what is losing the Featured Offer, the fix for each cause with its owner and date, a price floor and repricing rule the client can set in Seller Central, and a weekly watch list so the problem is caught in days, not weeks.

AMZ.when: When listing a new product on Amazon, the listing was copied from the supplier or store page, Amazon rewrites or suppresses the title, or before running ads to a listing that does not sell. Not for titles across several marketplaces.
AMZ.tune: bullets are built from rival 1 to 3 star reviews, not a feature list; search terms are counted in bytes, which matters for accented and non-Latin words; every claim needs a document or is cut; and the listing is only written once the product makes money after Amazon's fees.
AMZ.title: Amazon listing
AMZ.outcome: one listing file for one product, ready to paste into Seller Central or a flat file: a title with its character count, five bullets, a description, a search terms line under 249 bytes, an A+ plan of 5 modules (7 if Premium), a keyword map showing where each buyer word lives, and a claims sheet with the proof for every claim.

AMZ.when: When you want to sell on Amazon but only have an interest or a category, not a product.
AMZ.tune: Feed it a keyword tool export for your seed phrases and screenshots or notes on page one. Favour products described in many ways (AMZ-0003) and read the page-one price spread first (AMZ-0001).

AMZ.when: When you have one or more Amazon product ideas and are about to ask a factory for quotes.
AMZ.tune: Give it planned price, landed cost, page-one results and cash on hand. Screen out low-priced products (AMZ-0004) and products whose sellers earn far more than you can stock for (AMZ-0005).

AMZ.when: When you want to build a better version of a rival's Amazon product from what its buyers complain about.
AMZ.tune: Paste rival reviews grouped by star, ideally from listings rated in the low 4s that still sell well (AMZ-0002). Turn 1-star themes into your product spec, not just ad lines.

AMZ.when: When you have a price and a factory quote and want the real profit per unit after every Amazon fee.
AMZ.tune: Give it price, landed cost, measured size and weight, return rate and ad spend per sale. Count the delivered cost with marketplace fees (MEA-0037) and test whether click costs erase the margin (AMZ-0004).

AMZ.when: When you have a brand name and are about to order stock for Amazon.
AMZ.tune: Give it the brand name, logo, selling country and category. Start the trademark early, because many protection and content tools open only after registry.

AMZ.when: When you have chosen a product and need the search phrases for its title, bullets and backend.
AMZ.tune: Feed keyword exports for your seed phrases and two or three rival ASINs. A new brand should win long-tail phrases first (AMZ-0003), so keep the filters tight.

AMZ.when: When you have product facts and a keyword list and need the Amazon title, bullets and backend terms written.
AMZ.tune: Give it the keyword tiers, verified product facts and rival titles. Use the complaint themes from your review mining (AMZ-0002) in the bullets, and make no claim you cannot prove.

AMZ.when: When you are about to launch an Amazon product and need a first ad plan with safe limits.
AMZ.tune: Give it unit profit after fees, keyword tiers, rival ASINs and a daily budget you can lose. Set bids from break-even ad cost (AMZ-0004), and count Meta ad value that lands on Amazon (MEA-0029).

AMZ.when: When your Amazon launch is weeks away and you have an email list or audience to bring.
AMZ.tune: Give it launch date, price, list size and the discount cash you can spend. Off-Amazon demand can rank you before ads do (AMZ-0007), so send your own audience in, and never plan paid or swapped reviews.

AMZ.when: When you are sending your first shipment to Amazon or need a date to restock.
AMZ.tune: Give it weekly sales, factory and freight lead times and case sizes. Plan on total lead time (COG-0008) and the stock a seller of your size needs (AMZ-0005).

AMZ.when: When you have closed Amazon shipments and want to find money Amazon owes you for lost units or wrong fees.
AMZ.tune: Feed 90 days of shipment, receipt, fee and returns reports from Seller Central plus measured product sizes. Run it monthly so claims are filed inside the window.

AMZ.when: When another seller jumps onto your listing, buyers report fakes, or a reseller undercuts your price.
AMZ.tune: Give it your ASINs, brand registry status and the hijack or fake reports you have. Use the complaint drafts as a starting point and check them before sending.

AMZ.when: When you sell on Amazon and want the same margin, stock and refund checks done every month.
AMZ.tune: Give it the month's Seller Central fee, inventory, returns and business reports. Read margin on delivered cost (MEA-0037) and size restocks on in-stock days only (OPS-0014).

AMZ.when: When you want to sell on Amazon in another country and need to pick which marketplace to open first.
AMZ.tune: Give it products, landed cost and the countries you are weighing, such as Amazon.com and Amazon.co.uk. Confirm tax and customs points with an adviser, and see how small a share Amazon can be for a strong direct brand (PRD-0017).

SEC.when: When the store is new and access is being handed out, a staff member or agency leaves, there was a suspicious login, or nobody knows who has admin rights.
SEC.tune: every tool the store depends on sits in one map, not just Shopify; access is set by job, with two owners and two-step login on every critical tool; the offboarding checklist runs across all tools in one sitting; and the agent never touches a password, code or key.
SEC.title: Lock down staff and app access
SEC.outcome: an access map (one row per person or app per tool) with current and target access, a change list to approve, a two-step login and recovery record, an offboarding checklist covering every tool, and a monthly review sheet.

SEC.when: When visits jump with no sales, conversion rate falls for no clear reason, an ad source sends clicks that never engage, or before ranking channels by profit.
SEC.tune: the check starts from the store's own normal gap between Shopify and GA4 instead of treating any gap as an attack; each source needs three signs and a count before it is called a bot; key numbers are shown raw and cleaned so profit rankings can be trusted; and wanted AI and search crawlers are...
SEC.title: Spot bot traffic in analytics
SEC.outcome: a bot traffic report (sources scored real, doubtful or bot, with the sessions and share each makes up), a before-and-after table of key numbers (sessions, conversion rate, cost per sale, revenue per session) with bots removed, and a filter list for GA4, Shopify reports and each ad platform, ready to apply after the client's yes.

SEC.when: When small or odd orders spike, failed payments flood in, chargebacks rise, or pay-on-delivery orders arrive with fake names and numbers. Not for answering a chargeback already filed.
SEC.tune: rules come only after the store's own pattern is counted; every rule has an owner, a time limit and a tag the weekly check counts; the incident routine runs on a cancel pattern the client signed in advance; and pay-on-delivery fraud gets its own hold-and-confirm path instead of a blanket ban.
SEC.title: Stop fake orders and card testing
SEC.outcome: a pattern report from the store's own data, a settings list to turn on, an order rules table (hold, review, cancel) with owners and time limits, a one-page incident routine for an attack in progress, and a weekly check sheet with alert lines, ready for the client's approval.

SEC.when: When a chargeback or bank dispute arrives, the dispute rate climbs toward the payment provider's warning line, or several disputes were lost in a row.
SEC.tune: each dispute starts with a fight-or-accept call on expected recovery; evidence is matched to the reason code from the platform's own list; nothing is submitted without the client's fresh yes or edited from the original record; and every lost or fought dispute feeds a counted prevention list.
SEC.title: Win chargeback disputes
SEC.outcome: one dispute pack per open chargeback (reason, deadline, fight or accept call, evidence checklist with files named, a response letter under 300 words), a dispute log with deadlines, and a prevention list of the 3 to 5 store changes that would have stopped most of the last 6 months of disputes.

SEC.when: When you see failed logins, bursts of odd orders or tiny test charges, or you want AI shopping agents in but abusers out.
SEC.tune: Describe traffic, login, sign-up, reset, gift card and checkout flows and what bot protection you run. Gate by action, not identity (SEC-0007), and set login limits per user and per IP (SEC-0011).

SEC.when: When chargebacks are creeping up or real buyers complain their cards are declined.
SEC.tune: Give it monthly orders, average order value, chargeback count and Shopify Payments settings. Leave AVS off unless risk reviews say otherwise (SEC-0003) and keep the chargeback rate well below the 0.9 percent line (SEC-0004).

SEC.when: When a dispute has just landed on Shopify Payments and you need to know what proof to send before the deadline.
SEC.tune: Give it the dispute reason code, order number and amount. Check whether 3D Secure already shifted liability (SEC-0005), and weigh the fee against the order value before fighting (SEC-0004).

SEC.when: When you are setting up payments or think your checkout settings are losing buyers or adding risk.
SEC.tune: Share platform, plan, country and current payment and checkout settings. Check fraud and 3D Secure choices against SEC-0003 and SEC-0005, and confirm card data never touches your own systems (SEC-0006).

SEC.when: When your bank or payment provider asks which PCI form you fill in or for proof you comply.
SEC.tune: Describe every way you take cards, including phone orders and any app that sees card numbers. Most small Shopify stores sit at Level 4 (SEC-0006), so the main job is keeping card data out of your hands.

SEC.when: When someone has left the team or an agency finished a project and you are not sure who still has admin access.
SEC.tune: List staff and collaborator accounts with permissions, installed apps and backups. Rerun each quarter and after every staff change, and confirm no app or person stores card data (SEC-0006).

SEC.when: When you are adding staff and want to know if store and customer sign-ins are safe enough.
SEC.tune: Describe staff and customer login, password reset and second-step setup. Set rate limits per username and per IP (SEC-0011), and do not lean on a CAPTCHA alone (SEC-0010).

SEC.when: When new staff, contractors or an agency will touch your store or ad accounts, or someone nearly fell for a fake login.
SEC.tune: List the accounts that matter most, such as Shopify, Meta Business, Google Ads, Klaviyo and the domain registrar. Fix shared logins first, then run the drill with the whole team.

SEC.when: When years of apps, pixels and scripts have piled up and you cannot say what each one can see.
SEC.tune: List every app, pixel and theme script with who owns it, from the Shopify apps page and theme code. Remove what nobody owns and revoke the keys, since unused apps are open doors.

SEC.when: When you have old subdomains from past campaigns or test stores and do not know who can log in to your registrar.
SEC.tune: List domains, subdomains, where each points and who has registrar and DNS logins. Clean up records left from old landing pages first.

SEC.when: When you are not sure whether your robots.txt or CDN settings block the AI crawlers you want.
SEC.tune: Give it your store URL, robots.txt and a product page. Check that CCBot and GPTBot are not blocked by accident (SEC-0001, SEC-0002), then publish the reviewed file yourself.

SEC.when: When your own AI shopping or support assistant can change orders, refunds or prices and you must decide what needs a person.
SEC.tune: List every action the assistant can take, from answering to refunding. Give it no power over prices or policies (SEC-0008), and verify only at high-risk actions like checkout and gift cards (SEC-0007).

SEC.when: When your store's AI assistant reads product reviews, emails or web pages and can use tools.
SEC.tune: Describe what text the assistant reads and which tools it can call. Add rate limits and alerts for bots that ride on your assistant for free (SEC-0008).

SEC.when: When a vendor sells you a bot shield or agent-ID badge and you need to judge what it really stops.
SEC.tune: Bring the vendor's claim and the abuse you actually see in orders and logins. Weigh it against SEC-0009 and SEC-0010, and ask what each control costs real shoppers.
